Hampshire Instruments Awarded Third DoD Contract for X-Ray Semiconductor Technology 

By Chris Hayden 
570 words 
14 October 1988
Business Wire 
Pg. 1 
English
Copyright Business Wire 1988 

Marlborough, MA, US -- 

Hampshire Instruments Inc., a manufacturer of X-ray production equipment for the semiconductor industry, Friday announced that it has received a $1.5 million contract from the Department of Defense, under the Very High Speed Integrated Circuits (VHSIC) and Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit (MMIC) programs. 

This award represents the third phase of contracts awarded to Hampshire to supply X-ray lithography equipment and technology for the next generation of advanced military microelectronics. 

This contract, together with previous awards, total $3.3 million for this program in the past 12 months. Offices of the Naval Research Laboratories and the VHSIC program will manage the 13-month contract. 

Hampshire will provide X-ray reticle technology to the VHSIC/MMIC project. Reticles, containing original microcircuit patterns, have long been a stumbling block in the development of X- ray semiconductor production equipment. Hampshire is developing an advanced reticle technology, geared to its laser-based Series 5000 X-ray wafer stepper, but equally applicable to synchrotron based X- ray sources. 

A consortium of MMIC device manufacturers will use Hampshire's Series 5000 to develop ultra-dense military chips. Now getting under way, the MMIC effort calls for integrated circuits with features ranging from one-half to one-quarter micron. As prime contractor, Hampshire will subcontract some development work to Sanders Associates, a wholly owned subsidiary of Lockheed Corp. 

Subcontracts are to be awarded to Stanford University, Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Nanostructures Inc. to aid in reticle development. 

"This effort is vital to the future of the U.S. semiconductor industry," said Moshe J. Lubin, Hampshire's president and chief executive officer. "Our work will transfer quickly to the private sector. It means that U.S. companies will be competitive in the worldwide race to produce equipment required for the super-dense chips of the 1990's." 

X-ray lithography provides the advantages of short wavelength and fine resolution, plus an almost unlimited depth of field. The latter greatly diminishes the problems associated with compensating for irregularities in wafer topography and the substrate surface. This allows the Series 5000 to work equally well on both gallium arsenide and silicon wafers. A further advantage of X-ray systems is that they are relatively immune to organic particle contaminates. 

Using an extremely bright pulsed industrial laser, the Hampshire Series 5000 generates "soft" X-rays in the range of 0.8 to 2.2 nanometers. Soft X-rays provide the short wavelengths required for ultra-high density chip fabrication, while using conventional chemical processes (single layer novolak resists). The Series 5000 achieves a resolution limit of 0.3 micron and a depth of field that exceeds 30 microns. 

In the Hampshire system, a focused laser radiation on a metallic target induces a plasma that generates intense soft X-rays. The brighter intensity of the Hampshire X-ray source translates into faster exposure and higher throughput. The high intensity source is coupled with an interferometrically controlled water stage and a dark field site-by-site alignment system. 

Moshe J. Lubin and James M. Forsyth, formerly of the Laboratory for Laser Energetics at the University of Rochester, N.Y., founded Hampshire in Rochester, N.Y., in 1984. In 1987, the company opened a Customer Support Center in Marlborough. Hampshire has scheduled commercial shipments of its Series 5000 X-ray stepper for next year.

Novell names Jim Tolonen as chief financial officer; Eliason named senior vice president and treasurer

(Copyright (c) 1989, Business Wire) 

PROVO, Utah--(BW)-Novell Wednesday named Jim Tolonen as chief financial officer. 

Tolonon was most recenty chief financial officer for Excelan Inc., now a wholly owned subsidiary of Novell. Ron Eliason, former Novell chief financial officer, was named senior vice president and treasurer. 

In his new position, Tolonen is responsible for multiple operations functions including accounting, budgeting, MIS and financial reporting. Eliason is responsible for Novell's asset management functions including treasury, taxes, fixed asset management, auditing, transporation and travel, and facilities management. 

Both are jointly responsible for contributing to efforts in investor relations and credit management. 

We welcome the addition of Jim Tolonen to our executive ranks,'' said Raymond Noorda, Novell president and chief executive fficer. We're confident his lengthy experience in computer industry finance will contribute substantially to the company's efforts to grow in profitability.'' 

Tolonen joined Excelan as chief financial officer in 1983. Prior positions include management of the financial department for Boschert Inc., a Sunnyvale, Calif-based electronics firm (1979-83); head of the financial department for Dynapol, a molecular engineering company (1975-79); and certified public accountant for Arthur Anderson Co, (1972-75). 

He earned a bachelor of science degbree in mechanical engineering and a master of business administration degree from the University of Michigan. 

Eliason joined Novell in 1985 as chief financial officer and treasurer. Previously, he was vice president of the commercial banking division of First Security Bank of Salt Lake City. Before that he served in various capacities, including visiting professor of finance at Brigham Young University, president of Western Home Bank and president of Ramada Mortgage and Realty. 

He holds a master of business administration degree from Stanford University and a bachelor of science degree in physics from the University of Utah. 

Novell is the leading independent provider of open, high-performance networking connectivity products. The company's NetWare operating system has become a standard for personal-computer-based local area networks, with more than 400,000 operating systems installed worldwide. 

Novell common stock is traded on the NASDAQ National Market System under the symbol NOVL.

Genex and Catalytica announce feasibility study for potential venture

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Genex Corp. (NASDAQ:GNEX) and Catalytica Inc. announced Wednesday that they have entered into an agreement with three venture capital firms to conduct a short-term feasibility study to identify new products or processes that advantageously combine their technologies. 

If the feasibility study, which is scheduled to be completed by the end of the year, is successful, the parties contemplate additional investment to fund product development. The venture capital firms providing the feasibility study and development funding are the Mayfield Fund, Primus Capital and New Enterprise Associates. 

The joint venture is designed to leverage the strengths of Genex and Catalytica in the development of novel processes to make pharmaceutical, specialty and other fine chemicals. A combination of biological and chemical techniques will be used to make products at lower cost or with fewer adverse environmental effects than is possible with traditional chemical techniques alone. 

Commenting on the new program, Gary Frashier, president and chief executive officer of Genex, said: ``While we won't know for certain until the feasibility study is completed, I am optimistic about our ability to create some innovative and potentially advantageous approaches to specialty and fine chemical production. 

``The two companies have first class, synergistic skills. Catalytica is a leader in molecular engineering of catalysts and in chemical catalysis; Genex in protein engineering and biocatalysis. And the participation of our venture partners assures a strong business urgency and focus for the joint effort.'' 

Dr. James Cusumano, chairman and chief technical officer of Catalytica and the leader of the joint effort, said: ``This feasibility study can lead to an exciting new venture if our concepts bear up under the close scrutiny we will now give them. This stage is always the toughest on new ideas, but early and frequent assessment of a developing technology is crucial to guiding it to commercial success.'' 

Genex Corp. is an applied biotechnology company that uses proprietary protein engineering expertise to design, manufacture and market specialized proteins and affinity protein products for the research, diagnostic and commercial bioseparation marketplace. 

Catalytica designs, develops and commercializes proprietary catalysts and process technologies based on advanced molecular design that are economically and environmentally advantageous. Product areas include commodity and specialty chemicals and energy-related products.

IBM scientists position individual atoms -- first to build structures one atom at a time 

1,185 words 
4 April 1990
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1990, Business Wire) 

SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Scientists at IBM's Almaden Research Center here have demonstrated the ability to position individual atoms on a surface and have used this technique to build structures one atom at a time. 

This achievement creates the potential for a wealth of future applications. Among the possibilities are: building custom-made molecules atom-by-atom, altering individual molecules, making ultra-small electrical circuits far smaller than is possible today, storing data on an atomic scale at densities more than a million times greater than is now possible and perhaps even duplicating structures atom-for-atom. 

More immediately, the new technique will assist scientists in studying the fundamental behavior of atoms on surfaces. This knowledge is crucial to everyday industrial processes, such as catalyzing chemical reactions and manufacturing semiconductors. 

Writing in an article in the April 5 issue of Nature, a British science journal, physicists Donald M. Eigler and Erhard K. Schweizer described how to move individual atoms across the surface of a metal crystal. 

Eigler is a research staff member at Almaden; Schweizer was a visiting scientist at Almaden on leave from the Fritz-Haber-Institut in Berlin when this work was done in November 1989. 

To demonstrate their new technique, the scientists first moved atoms of the element xenon into a pattern forming the letters ``IBM.'' Later, they created the first-ever atomic cluster built one atom at a time -- a chain of seven xenon atoms bound together. 

These demonstrations required the atoms to be cooled to minus 269 degrees Celsius (minus 453 degrees Fahrenheit), which is only slightly warmer than the absolute zero of temperature. 

In the ``IBM'' written with xenon atoms, each letter is about 500,000 times smaller than those on this page. The atoms are separated by only about 50 billionths of an inch, or 13 Angstroms. (The Angstrom is a unit of distance commonly used by scientists because the diameter of most atoms is 1-4 Angstroms. One Angstrom is equal to 100 trillonths of a meter, 4 billionths of an inch, or about a millionth the diameter of a human hair). 

The atoms in the chain are much closer -- within 20 billionths of an inch, or 5 Angstroms. Eigler said he realized the xenon atoms in the seven-atom chain were bonded together because he could relocate up to three of them at a time by moving an end atom. 

The ability to position individual atoms has the potential to advance fabrication techniques to a scale of less than a billionth of a meter, more than 500 times smaller than that currently used in semiconductor chip manufacturing. 

``For decades, the electronics industry has been facing the challenge of how to build smaller and smaller structures,'' Eigler said. ``For those of us who will now be using individual atoms as building blocks, the challenge will be how to build up structures atom by atom.'' 

The scientists used a scanning tunneling microscope (STM) both to move the atoms into place and to view their progress. The STM, invented in the early 1980s by Nobel Prize-winning scientists at IBM's Zurich Research Laboratory, can image individual atoms on a metal or semiconductor surface by scanning the tip of a needle over the surface at a height of only a few atomic diameters. By plotting the path of the STM tip, the scientist can make an atomic resolution image of the surface. 

Eigler and Schweizer discovered that by bringing the STM tip slightly closer to a xenon atom on the surface, they can drag the atom across the surface when they move the STM tip parallel to the surface. At the desired position, the scientists raise the STM tip, leaving the atom fixed in its new location. The process is like moving a magnet by the motion of another magnet nearby, but not touching. 

The shape of the surface is important. To another atom, even an atomically smooth surface would look like the bumpy, waffled surface of a large egg carton. To move over the surface, the atom must traverse its depressions and crests. 

Eigler and Schweizer's method requires that the STM operator maintain a delicate balance of several attractive forces between the atoms. For example, the atom's attraction to the tip must exceed the lateral force that prevents an atom from riding over a crest into the next depression. But to keep an atom from flying off the surface, the force that binds it to the surface must be stronger than the atom's attraction to the STM tip. 

``The beauty of this technique is that we can tune the attractive forces by controlling the height of the STM tip above an atom,'' Eigler said. ``Despite our ability to tune these forces, however, I expect this process will only work with particular combinations of atoms and surfaces.'' 

In creating these structures, the scientists also had to plot their course across the surface carefully so the atom being moved would not collide with, or get close enough to be attracted to, any other xenon atoms along the way. 

The achievement grew out of Eigler's desire to understand how atoms and molecules interact with surfaces. To do this, Eigler built an STM that could operate with extraordinary sensitivity and precision. He reduced contamination and unwanted atomic motion by placing the STM in a high vacuum and cooling it with liquid helium to minus 269 degrees Celsius. 

He also carefully isolated the STM from vibrations as faint as those from the sound of a person's voice and heat sources as weak as a nearby human body. As a result, Eigler's STM can resolve vertical changes in an atom's apparent shape as small as 8 trillionths of an inch (0.002 Angstrom) -- far smaller than any single atom. 

Xenon is a heavy, unreactive gas at room temperature and is found naturally in air in very low concentrations (1 part in 10 million). Commercially, the gas is used to fill electronic flash tubes for photography and lasers.

Plastic recycling research and development firm formed to provide solutions to post-consumer waste problems 

394 words 
23 May 1990
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1990, Business Wire) 

ANAHEIM, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--A new research and development firm, Replatec Co., in Anaheim, has entered the plastic recycling field to provide engineering and technical consulting services...it was announced jointly Wednesday by co-founders, molecular engineer William Baskind, president, and G.P. ``Skip'' Humphrey Jr., vice president, marketing. 

Baskind said: ``The plastic recycling problem is expanding more rapidly than available technology. It will be our objective to provide laboratory and consulting services not only to test materials for physical characteristics but also to provide economic studies to recommend optimization of post-consumer wastes.'' 

Typical products made from commingled post-consumer waste find application in agriculture, marine and civil engineering, garden and horticulture, recreational and industrials. 

Converting the entire commingled post-consumer plastic waste stream has immediate economic value as a reconstituted plastic material. Given new life, it can be used by injection molders or extruders to manufacture a variety of products. 

Replatec will provide scientific laboratory services in conjunction with Polymer Testing Laboratories in Orange County. Clients will be able to obtain analysis of their products by differential scanning colorimity, infrared, ultra violet and visual spectro photometry, physical mechanical, optical, thermal and flammability ratings. 

At this stage of recycling, it appears that municipalities, states and private organizations will need the expertise of dedicated technical and engineering development firms for post-consumer waste problem solving. 

One ``quick fix'' employed to the disadvantage of clean air people is to incinerate wastes into a fine ash from garbage and plastic materials, reprocessing the material for landfill and other use. This is undesirable because of potential economic loss of the salvageable plastic as well as health hazards caused by the high content of lead and other heavy metals. 

The initial business development plan for Replatec will start with client-customers in the Southern California area with whom they are now in preliminary discussion. The first assignment may be in conjunction with a plastic recycling firm engaged in production of playground equipmnet for parks and recreation. 

For further information contact: William Baskind, president, Replatec Co., 132 N. Wade Circle, Anaheim, Calif. 92807; 714/974-5072 (phone) or 714/282-7133 (fax).

Two IBM achievements named ``Best of What's New'' 

515 words 
13 November 1990
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1990, Business Wire) 

SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Two scientific accomplishments by researchers at IBM's Almaden Research Center here were named Tuesday as among the year's most outstanding achievements by the editors of Popular Science magazine. 

The manipulation of individual atoms by Drs. Donald Eigler and Erhard Schweizer was cited as the Grand Award winner in the ``Science and Technology'' category. 

The compact blue-laser device developed by Drs. William Kozlovsky and Wilfried Lenth was honored as being among the top 10 developments in the ``Computers & Electronics'' category. 

These selections are part of the magazine's 3rd Annual ``Best of What's New'' feature in its December issue. The 32-page section, unveiled today in New York City, highlights the editors' choices for the 10 most innovative achievements or products introduced in 1990 in each of 10 categories (a) that the magazine regularly features during the year. A Grand Award was given in each category to the most significant development during the year in that field. 

Eigler and Schweizer's work was the world's first demonstration of the ability to position individual atoms at will. Eigler developed the method that employs a scanning tunneling microscope cooled to nearly absolute zero both to move the atoms and make images to record the results. 

Eigler first positioned 35 xenon atoms to spell ``I-B-M'' in block letters. Later, Schweizer, a visiting scientist, used the same technique to move seven xenon atoms next to each other into a straight row, thus forming the first atomic cluster ever made one atom at a time. 

The achievement creates the possibility that some day custom molecules and structures with desirable properties could be built atom-by-atom. This research was first reported in the April 5 issue of Nature, the British science journal. 

No one has found a way to make a compact and efficient blue laser based on semiconductor technology alone, so Kozlovsky and Lenth used a technique called ``frequency doubling'' to convert infrared light from a semiconductor diode laser into blue. They used a new electrical feedback system that controls the frequency of the diode's output precisely, which is essential for stable and efficient operation of their blue source. 

The system's overall efficiency for converting electrical input power to blue light is about 10 percent -- very high for any laser system, but especially notable for one emitting a blue beam. 

Such a light source could lead to optical data storage devices operating at about four times present storage densities or play an integral part in other applications, such as in biomedical diagnostics and color displays. This research was disclosed at several scientific conferences during 1990, including the Conference on Lasers and Electro-Optics held in May in Anaheim, Calif. 

(a) The categories are: Audio & Video; Auto Technology; Aviation & Space; Cars; Computers & Electronics; Environmental Technology; Home Technology; Photography; Recreation; and Science & Technology.

Himont's commitment to research and technology is apparent: 20% of the company's employees work in research or technically related functions, a figure well above the industry average for materials producers. Our capability in molecular engineering to meed defined targets and our drive to realize commercial success in the shortest time possible will have a positive impact in the development of the next generation of high performance fibers,'' said John Haylock, director of worldwide product development, Technology, HIMONT Inc. 

Allied-Signal comprises more than 40 businesses, which serve some of the world's most demanding industrial customers with innovative products, systems and services that respond to their needs for ever higher quality and performance standards. The company has 500 manufacturing plants, technical centers, and sales offices and other facilities in 46 countries plus the United States, and a total worldwide workforce of 107,000. 

Himont, headquartered in Wilmington, is the world's leading producer and marketer of polypropylene resins and a major producer of a broad range of specialty composites, alloys and advanced materials. Himont is the leading lincensor of technology related to the production of polypropylene and also develops and markets catalysts used in its manufacture. 

The Ferruzzi Group is a leading international industrial system, which operates through Montedison in the chemical, pharmaceutical and energy sectors, as well as in the agro-industrial sector, with an aggregate turnover of approximately $30 billion.

Los Alamos researchers identify structure of superconductor grains deposited as thin films 

968 words 
27 March 1991
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1991, Business Wire) 

LOS ALAMOS, N.M.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Researchers at Los Alamos National Laboratory have for the first time imaged and identified the structure of individual grains of high-temperature superconducting material deposited as a thin film. 

The images show that as atoms of the high-temperature superconducting material are deposited on a surface, they form individual grains that build upward as spiraling terraces. As the grains grow taller, their bases spread outward until individual grains touch one another, creating a continuous, microscopically thin film. 

The Los Alamos researchers are exploring the contribution of the spiral structure and the boundaries where grains touch for giving the thin films their capacity to carry a higher electrical current than a wire or bulk ceramic object made from the same material. 

By studying thin films grown through sputtering, a process in which particles are emitted onto a surface, the new visual details should lead to improvements in using this process to produce superconducting films. In combination with other measurements, the pictures of microscopic structure could enabel researchers to understand better how thin films behave and thereby improve their superconducting properties. 

The research appears in the March 29 issue of Science magazine. The authors are Marilyn Hawley, postdoctoral fellow with the Materials Technology Group; Ian Raistrick, deputy group leader for Electronics Research; Jerome Beery, a former contract employee with Los Alamos; and Robert Houlton, technician in Electronics Research. 

The study was submitted to Science magazine last December. Raistrick also presented the results at the American Physical Society meeting in Cincinnati on March 18. 

``We've shown that these films are not composed of a single crystal but instead consist of many individual grains,'' Raistrick said. ``Each grain grows by adding material to the edge of a spirally rising step. The steps grow outward as the structures grow up. This is by far the most graphic description yet of the real microstructure of the films.'' 

Completely independent work with essentially the same results was submitted in February and published in the March 28 issue of Nature magazine. The work was done at IBM's Zurich Research Laboratory by Christoph Gerber, Dario Anselmetti, J. Georg Bednorz, Jochen Mannhart and Darrell Schlom. 

The new superconducting materials, which offer virtually no resistance to the flow of electricity and operate at much higher temperatures than previous such materials, were discovered some five years ago. Since then, researchers have done extensive theoretical and experimental analyses of the new materials to understand their behavior in the hopes of developing them into usable products. The new materials have potential application in energy transmission, magnetic field detectors, high-strength magnets used in medical imaging and various electronic uses. 

One such application involves using the superconducting material in the form of a thin film deposited on an underlying substance, or substrate. Previous attempts to image the structural features of thin films using scanning tunneling microscopy were stymied because of degradation of the surfaces of the films that caused poor surface conductivity. 

Scanning tunneling microscopy measures the electronic state at a material's surface and uses this information to provide a three- dimensional view of surface structures. 

As researchers have improved their techniques for producing a microscopically thin layer of material, the surface condition of the films has improved so researchers can now use scanning tunneling microscopy to provide high-resolution images of the films at the scale of an atom, about one angstrom. The steps of the spiraling terraces of the grains are measured to be about 12 angstoms high or smaller, roughly 50 billionths of an inch. 

Atomic force microscopy produces lower resolution images, but serves to verify that the features seen with the tunneling technique relate to topological structures, not just electronic features, in the material. 

``Scanning tunneling microscopy is a tool that gives us additional information for improving our basic understanding of how the thin films grow, what their structure is and what the role of the structure is in determining the material's properties,'' said Hawley. 

``We're still at the infant stage in using this technique to study the growth mechanism, but when the film conditions are good, scanning tunneling microscopy quickly provides high-resolution images that let us measure the sizes, distribution and orientations of the grains.'' 

``Scanning tunneling microscopy looks at a scale intermediate between the atomic level and the average, bulk structure,'' said Raistrick. ``This intermediate scale is hard to look at but it happens to be the right scale for studying the relationship between grain structure and the properties of high-temperature superconducting materials.'' 

Raistrick notes that two structural anomalies result from the spiral growth pattern. As a grain grows, the atomic planes of the material form a spiral ramp winding around the center line of the grain; this feature extends from the top of the grain to its interface with the substrate. The second anomaly is the large number of grain boundaries formed when neighboring ``island'' grains impinge on one another. 

``These two structural features are strong candidates for creating the magnetic-flux pinning in thin films that leads to their high current-carrying capacity,'' Raistrick said. 

The researchers also are exploring the role of the microstructure in determining the surface resistance at high frequencies of the material. This has importance for the use of thin film superconductors in microwave communications systems. 

Los Alamos National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary research organization that applies science and technology to problems of national security ranging from defense to energy research. It is operated by the University of California for the Department of Energy. 

NOTE TO EDITORS: Photographs of the microscopic superconducting grains are available by calling 505/665-7777. 

CONTACT: Los Alamos National Laboratory, Los Alamos John R. Gustafson, 505/665-7777 17:33 ET

Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1991, Business Wire) 

LOS ALAMOS, N.M.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Researchers at Los Alamos National Laboratory have for the first time imaged and identified the structure of individual grains of high-temperature superconducting material deposited as a thin film. 

The images show that as atoms of the high-temperature superconducting material are deposited on a surface, they form individual grains that build upward as spiraling terraces. As the grains grow taller, their bases spread outward until individual grains touch one another, creating a continuous, microscopically thin film. 

The Los Alamos researchers are exploring the contribution of the spiral structure and the boundaries where grains touch for giving the thin films their capacity to carry a higher electrical current than a wire or bulk ceramic object made from the same material. 

By studying thin films grown through sputtering, a process in which particles are emitted onto a surface, the new visual details should lead to improvements in using this process to produce superconducting films. In combination with other measurements, the pictures of microscopic structure could enabel researchers to understand better how thin films behave and thereby improve their superconducting properties. 

The research appears in the March 29 issue of Science magazine. The authors are Marilyn Hawley, postdoctoral fellow with the Materials Technology Group; Ian Raistrick, deputy group leader for Electronics Research; Jerome Beery, a former contract employee with Los Alamos; and Robert Houlton, technician in Electronics Research. 

The study was submitted to Science magazine last December. Raistrick also presented the results at the American Physical Society meeting in Cincinnati on March 18. 

``We've shown that these films are not composed of a single crystal but instead consist of many individual grains,'' Raistrick said. ``Each grain grows by adding material to the edge of a spirally rising step. The steps grow outward as the structures grow up. This is by far the most graphic description yet of the real microstructure of the films.'' 

Completely independent work with essentially the same results was submitted in February and published in the March 28 issue of Nature magazine. The work was done at IBM's Zurich Research Laboratory by Christoph Gerber, Dario Anselmetti, J. Georg Bednorz, Jochen Mannhart and Darrell Schlom. 

The new superconducting materials, which offer virtually no resistance to the flow of electricity and operate at much higher temperatures than previous such materials, were discovered some five years ago. Since then, researchers have done extensive theoretical and experimental analyses of the new materials to understand their behavior in the hopes of developing them into usable products. The new materials have potential application in energy transmission, magnetic field detectors, high-strength magnets used in medical imaging and various electronic uses. 

One such application involves using the superconducting material in the form of a thin film deposited on an underlying substance, or substrate. Previous attempts to image the structural features of thin films using scanning tunneling microscopy were stymied because of degradation of the surfaces of the films that caused poor surface conductivity. 

Scanning tunneling microscopy measures the electronic state at a material's surface and uses this information to provide a three- dimensional view of surface structures. 

As researchers have improved their techniques for producing a microscopically thin layer of material, the surface condition of the films has improved so researchers can now use scanning tunneling microscopy to provide high-resolution images of the films at the scale of an atom, about one angstrom. The steps of the spiraling terraces of the grains are measured to be about 12 angstoms high or smaller, roughly 50 billionths of an inch. 

Atomic force microscopy produces lower resolution images, but serves to verify that the features seen with the tunneling technique relate to topological structures, not just electronic features, in the material. 

``Scanning tunneling microscopy is a tool that gives us additional information for improving our basic understanding of how the thin films grow, what their structure is and what the role of the structure is in determining the material's properties,'' said Hawley. 

``We're still at the infant stage in using this technique to study the growth mechanism, but when the film conditions are good, scanning tunneling microscopy quickly provides high-resolution images that let us measure the sizes, distribution and orientations of the grains.'' 

``Scanning tunneling microscopy looks at a scale intermediate between the atomic level and the average, bulk structure,'' said Raistrick. ``This intermediate scale is hard to look at but it happens to be the right scale for studying the relationship between grain structure and the properties of high-temperature superconducting materials.'' 

Raistrick notes that two structural anomalies result from the spiral growth pattern. As a grain grows, the atomic planes of the material form a spiral ramp winding around the center line of the grain; this feature extends from the top of the grain to its interface with the substrate. The second anomaly is the large number of grain boundaries formed when neighboring ``island'' grains impinge on one another. 

``These two structural features are strong candidates for creating the magnetic-flux pinning in thin films that leads to their high current-carrying capacity,'' Raistrick said. 

The researchers also are exploring the role of the microstructure in determining the surface resistance at high frequencies of the material. This has importance for the use of thin film superconductors in microwave communications systems. 

Los Alamos National Laboratory is a multidisciplinary research organization that applies science and technology to problems of national security ranging from defense to energy research. It is operated by the University of California for the Department of Energy.

 Article 12 *******************    


New technique increases current-carrying ability of high-temperature superconducting crystals 

887 words 
7 August 1991
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1991, Business Wire) 

YORKTOWN HEIGHTS, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Researchers have significantly improved the current-carrying ability of single crystals of the high-temperature superconducting material known as yttrium-barium-copper oxide. 

The advance gives scientists new insight into improving the curent-carrying capability of high-temperature superconducting materials, knowledge that one day may help them use the materials to make powerful and compact superconducting motors, generators and magnets. 

The demonstration of the current-improving technique is the collaborative work of scientists at the IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, (IBM), Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Oak Ridge, Tenn. (ORNL), Argonne National Laboratory in Argonne, Ill. (ANL), and Ames Laboratory and the Iowa State University in Ames, Iowa (Ames). 

The technique consists of the deliberate, controlled introduction of defects into crystals of the superconducting material by bombarding them with a beam of very energetic, electrically charged atoms of the element tin. 

These particles, called ions, produce damage in the crystals in the form of very thin columns (20 atoms wide) that are no longer superconducting. The defects are aligned with the direction of the bombarding ions and extend most of the way through the smallest dimension of the crystals, platelets that typically measure 1 mm by 1 mm by 0.02 mm. 

The energetic tin ions were produced at ORNL's Holifield Heavy Ion Facility, in a very-high-voltage Van de Graaff accelerator ordinarily used in nuclear physics research. They were accelerated to an energy of 580 million electron volts. Defects cause an increase in the maximum current a superconductor can sustain, particularly in external magnetic fields. They do so by ``pinning''-- preventing the motion of magnetic field lines that would otherwise produce electrical resistance and the loss of usefulness of the material. Defects produced by heavy ions at the energies used in this work are just what theory predicts to be perfect pinning sites. 

The researchers found that the presence of these defects resulted in values of the critical current density (a measure of the maximum current the superconductor can sustain) that are the highest ever observed for yttrium-barium-copper oxide bulk material at high temperature and high magnetic field. The pinning was found to be strongest when the magnetic field is aligned in the direction of the damage columns. 

At liquid-nitrogen temperature, 77 K, or 320 Fahrenheit degreees below zero, the critical current density was 450,000 amps per square centimeter in a magetic field of 1 Tesla (which is the strength of a typical strong permanent magnet, or approximately 20,000 times greater than the magnetic field of the earth). This critical currnet density is comparable to that achieved with an already well known technique that uses proton bombardment to create defects of a different type. But for much larger magnetic fields, only the heavy-ion banbardment resulted in crystals able to sustain still useful amounts of current. The strength of the pinning and the resulting values of the critical current density for those crystals are the largest ever observed in in bulk yttrium-barium-copper oxide material at liquid-nitrogen temperatures in high magnetic fields. Significantly, the researchers found that as the dosage of heavy-ion bombardment increased, the critical current density also continued to increase. 

Thin films of yttrium-barium-copper oxide already have very high critical currents and active research efforts are underway at many institutions to identify the sources of the pinning that must be taking place. For example, researchers at the IBM Zurich Research Laboratory in Switzerland and at the Los Alamos National Laboratory in Los Alamos, N.M., recently showed, with scanning tunneling microscope images, that so-called screw dislocations are present in thin films of the material and might also play a role in pinning. Those defects are also long and thin, like the columns produced by heavy ions, but they form while the thin films are being fabricated and are difficult to control. By comparison, bulk crystals grow with relatively few defects, but the new technique provides a way to produce ideal defects in a totally controlled way: the defects can be engineered into the material. 

The most important pratical application of bulk material would be in superconducting wire. Such wire would have the bulk material in the form of polycrystals. While this work has shown that it is possible to engineer defects into single crystals to make their current-carrying properties good enough for applications, problems remain with yttrium-barium-copper oxide in polycrystalline form: the boundaries between crystals can sustain only small amounts of current before electrical resistance appears. 

These research results were published in the July 29 issue of the technical journal Physical Review Letters. Its authors are Leonardo Civale, Alan D. Marwick, Thomas K. Worthington, Lia Krusin-Elbaum, and Frederic H. Holtzberg (IBM); James R. Thompson and Yangren Sun (ORNL); Mark Kirk (ANL); and John R. Clem (Ames). The ORNL and ANL work was supported through the DOE High Temperature Superconductivity Pilot Center program. 

The researchers will next explore bombardmant at higher doses as a possible way to further improve pinning. They also plan on using other species of ions.

Most importantly, Job says, the technology is available for immediate use by industry...without the normal two to five year implementation lag.

 Article 14 *******************    


Scientists ``see'' molecules of heredity 

610 words 
3 February 1992
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1992, Business Wire) 

LIVERMORE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Slowly but surely, working with sophisticated new types of microscopes that ``see'' with electrons and force fields, scientists are moving closer to the ability to visualize the individual molecules whose patterns determine human heredity. 

Using a special kind of microscope known as a scanning tunneling microscope, researchers at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory can now distinguish between two of the four base molecules that encode all genetic information in the well-known double-helix of DNA. The two are adenine and thymine, whose structures can be clearly identified under the microscope's sensitive tip. 

Their work has been done under simpler-than-life conditions, with the molecules detached from the DNA and laid out on graphite for ease of identification. 

But the accomplishment nevertheless raises the hope that bioscientists will someday be able to place complex genetic molecules under a microscope and identify their components directly. This in turn could help make it possible to pinpoint and correct genetic defects responsible for diseases like cancer and diabetes. 

Rod Balhorn, LLNL bioscientist, said: ``A direct method of visualizing base molecules assembled in complete strands of DNA is sort of a Holy Grail to biologists. It's a goal we can't reach right now, but demonstrating that we can discriminate between adenine and thymine is a step in the right direction. But there are many more steps left to take.'' 

The primary structure of the DNA molecule consists of repetitions of pairs of bases, adenine-thymine and guanine-cytosine, within a winding helical structure. 

Today's standard method of analyzing DNA is very indirect. DNA is cut apart chemically into segments of varying lengths. The cuts occur at the location of specific bases (for example, at the adenines). 

The segments are separated by size and analyzed, and the resulting data are fed into a computer. Then the process is repeated, but the cutting is done at a different base -- say, the thymines. Eventually, the computer restructures the DNA mathematically using sophisticated computer programs. 

The scanning tunneling microscope, which can record structural details of surfaces as small as a single atom, gave Livermore researchers the first three-dimensional images of the DNA double-helix more than two years ago. 

``Following our initial DNA studies we developed techniques for obtaining high-resolution, reproducible images of the bases,'' Balhorn said. ``We obtained the best results when small amounts of the bases, dissolved in distilled water, are placed on a heated graphite surface.'' 

A good electrical conductor, graphite provides a flat surface and is chemically inert. 

``The adenine and thymine molecules stick to the graphite surface and form a crystal lattice which is easy to work with,'' Balhorn said. ``Because the molecular structure of thymine contains a single hexagonal ring and the adenine molecule has a double ring structure, we can tell them apart.'' 

A report on identifying adenine and thymine, accomplished in late 1990 and early 1991, has just been published in the journal Scanning Microscopy. The researchers continue to explore methods of imaging the final two bases, guanine and cytosine. Guanine is hard to distinguish from adenine. Cytosine is more difficult still because it forms amorphous arrays of molecules that lack distinctive features. 

Similar research is going on at centers around the world. For example, last year the University of Munich in Germany reported identifying DNA base molecules in a project assisted by a visiting Livermore researcher. 

Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory is managed by the University of California for the U.S. Department of Energy.

IBM scientists report first observation of a virus exiting a living cell 

809 words 
5 February 1992
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1992, Business Wire) 

YORKTOWN HEIGHTS, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Scientists in the Munich Group of the IBM Zurich Research Laboratory believe they have witnessed a never-before-seen biological process - the escape of a virus from a living cell. 

This first observation of a virus exiting a living cell should open the door to studying a broad variety of processes occurring in living organisms. 

The observation was made possible by a scanning force microscope (SFM), an instrument that can image biological materials and resolve details in them as small as 10 nanometers, or 10 billionths of a meter. Such resolution is unobtainable with even the best optical microscopes, but is possible with electron microscopes. 

However, electron microscopy requires that biological materials be placed in vacuum and be specially prepared with contrast enhancing techniques such as staining and fixation processes that kill them. Consequently, only scanning force microscopy is capable of such extremely high-resolution imaging of live samples, in this case cells in the size range of tens of millionths of a meter. 

The experiments were performed with the SFM tip submerged in a nutrient solution containing cultured cells. Four to ten images can be produced every minute with the SFM, allowing image sequences to be recorded throughout the entire observation period of up to 48 hours. Three prominent processes were observed in the course of the experiments. 

Several seconds after the researchers infected the cells in the solution by introducing a strain of pox virus that is harmless to humans, the SFM began producing images with considerably lower contrast than usual, showing a softening of the cell membrane. That condition, previously unknown, continued for the next several minutes, until the cell membrane became rigid again. Although the researchers did not observe endocytosis -- the penetration of viruses into cells -- they believe the viruses cause the cell softening, thereby facilitating their penetration. 

About 2 hours after infection, SFM images revealed the growth of protrusions up to 100 nanometers in size that disappeared abruptly after a few minutes. The IBM scientists believe that this phenomenon is exocytosis, or the exiting through the cell membrane, of by-products of the reproduction process of the viruses within the cell. Such a process would be consistent with the knowledge that the early stage of virus reproduction occurs within two to three hours after infection. 

After more than eight hours of incubation, a particularly dramatic process is observed: protrusions as large as 300 nanometers begin growing and disappearing at the end of one of the microvilli, which are long fingerlike structures that form on the cell surface. Other scientists have already determined that between four and eight hours after infection, the first progeny virus will have appeared within the cell. Based on the timing of the events, the sizes of the objects, and electron microscopy experiments that sometimes find viruses in such microvilli, the researchers believe the protrusions are progeny viruses exiting the living cell. 

The work was performed by IBM researchers Walter Haeberle, Frank Ohnesorge, and Douglas Smith, together with Heinrich Hoerber of the Max Planck Institute for Medical Research in Heidelberg and Claus Czerny of the University of Munich, and was led by IBM Nobel laureate Gerd Binnig, all working in the laboratories of the IBM Physics group in Munich, Germany. A preliminary report of this work was presented at the International Conference on Scanning Tunneling Microscopy, ``STM '91'' held in Interlaken, Switzerland, in August of 1991. 

The scanning force microscope is an offspring of the scanning tunneling microscope (STM). For the invention of the latter, IBM scientists Binnig and Heinrich Rohrer received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1986. The SFM was developed in 1985 by Binnig, Christoph Gerber, also an IBM Zurich researcher, and Calvin Quate of Stanford University. 

The heart of the instrument is a minute tip mounted on a cantilever that is scanned linearly over the sample. The tip touches the sample with only one ten-millionth of the pressure of a phonograph stylus. Thus, it is possible to scan the surface profile without altering the surface itself. 

The tip movement is measured with a laser beam reflected off the cantilever. The data obtained after consecutive scans in this way yield a three-dimensional map of a small area (only a few micrometers) of the sample surface. The image can then by computer enhanced. 

The scientists use a high-resolution optical microscope to locate a single cell that is captured by being drawn by suction onto the tip of a micropipette whose diameter is smaller than that of the cell. Still in the nutrient solution, the cell is then moved towards the cantilever and the SFM tip, all submerged in the solution, at which time the scanning proceeds.

Tencor Instruments announces strategic alliance with Park Scientific Instruments

Business Wire

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Tencor Instruments and Park Scientific Instruments, (PSI) have announced a five-year agreement under which they will introduce a scanning force microscope (SFM) designed specifically for use in a semiconductor manufacturing environment. 

The product will be developed and manufactured by PSI and will be marketed exclusively by Tencor Instruments to the worldwide semiconductor industry. 

Scanning force microscopy provides three-dimensional imaging and measurement of surface topography on an atomic-scale. Existing laboratory versions of SFMs have demonstrated lateral image resolution beyond the capabilities of optical microscopes, and vertical resolution beyond the capabilities of electron microscopes. 

``The alliance between PSI and Tencor unites PSI's technical expertise is scanning force microscopy with Tencor's worldwide surface metrology base in the semiconductor industry,'' said Jon Tompkins, president and chief executive officer of Tencor Instruments. 

Sang-il Park, chairman and chief executive officer of Park Scientific Instruments, added, ``These combined strengths should bring new ultra-high resolution imaging and measurement capabilities to semiconductor processes at a time when inspection and control of smaller feature dimensions has become a critical issue throughout the industry.'' 

According to Tompkins, a major design objective of the new microscope for semi-conductor applications is to inspect intact 200mm wafers. The targeted introduction date is summer 1992. 

Scanning force microscopy is based on the scanning tunneling microscopy technology for which the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded. 

A SFM produces images using a micro-fabricated cantilever and tip which is placed in contact with, or a few nanometers above, a surface. A sensor detects cantilever deflections as the tip rides over surface undulations. In some applications the SFM can resolve individual atoms. 

The SFM technique has proven useful for semiconductor research applications because it is effective on conducting or insulating samples. Even soft materials, such as photoresist, can be imaged non-destructively. In addition, topographic images from the SFM are digitally stored three-dimensional images which allow very precise calculation of surface roughness, step height, and other surface characteristics. 

These capabilities make scanning force microscopy particularly suitable for highly precise topographical characterization and measurement of surfaces, thin films and defects. 

Park Scientific Instruments is an innovative technology leader in the design and development of scanning force microscopes. Founded in 1988, the company's products are used extensively in advanced research laboratories around the world. Headquarters are located at 1171 Borregas Ave., Sunnyvale. Project Manager at PSI is Ian Smith. 

Tencor Instruments designs, manufactures, markets, and services surface contamination inspection and metrology systems for use in semiconductor manufacturing and other industries. Sales in 1991 exceeded $53 million.

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Tencor Instruments has announced the acquisition of FleXus Inc., a 5-year-old privately held company which manufactures a family of products for measuring stress in thin films. 

Terms of the agreement, which was finalized this week, were not disclosed. 

Jon Tompkins, president and chief executive officer of Tencor Instruments, said that the entire staff of FleXus will be relocated to Tencor's headquarters in Mountain View, including key executives, Ilan Blech, president, and Dov Hirsch, vice president. Blech will continue to manage the Tencor FleXus group, reporting directly to Tompkins. 

``The FleXus team has developed very impressive technology for measuring thin film stress, both at room temperature and the elevated temperatures which are frequently encountered during semiconductor manufacturing,'' Tompkins stated. 

``Their high temperature capability adds to Tencor's existing products for thin film measurement.'' 

The acquisition of FleXus marks the third strategic business move by Tencor in as many weeks. Two weeks ago, it announced a strategic alliance with Park Scientific Instruments (PSI), which gives Tencor exclusive rights to market a new scanning force microscope, under development by PSI, to the worldwide semiconductor industry. 

Last week, Tencor and Prometrix Corp. jointly announced an alliance to market a defect data analysis system utilizing Tencor's wafer defect inspection expertise and Prometrix's strengths in the area of data analysis. 

Tompkins, who was named president and chief executive officer of the company a year ago, said that all three moves are good examples of the ``partnering'' trend in the semiconductor equipment industry in which companies are working together on advanced technology instead of funding duplicate and costly research and development efforts. 

``The FleXus acquisition, like the PSI and Prometrix alliances, fits well with our goal of providing customers in the semiconductor industry with the metrology and wafer defect inspection systems they need to precisely control their manufacturing processes.'' 

Measurement of film stress is particularly critical in semiconductor production where it can identify process conditions likely to result in unreliable and defective integrated circuits. 

Semiconductor films are exposed to high temperatures both during processing and in the environment where the integrated circuit operates. Therefore, analysis at high temperatures provides a superior understanding of the film properties. 

The Tencor P-2 stylus surface profiler, a current Tencor product, can be used to measure thin film stress at room temperature, but does not measure under the high temperatures where FleXus technology excels. 

The FleXus family of products provides highly specialized features for film stress measurement at room temperatures, as well as at temperatures up to 900 degrees Celsius. 

Stress can be measured on nitride, oxide, metal, silicide and polyimide films on wafers up to 200mm in diameter. In addition, proprietary FleXus technology overcomes the destructive interference effects that may occur with silicon nitride films on silicon. The systems will be marketed worldwide by Tencor Instruments under the Tencor FleXus name. 

Tencor Instruments is a technology leader in the design and manufacture of wafer defect inspection and metrology systems for semiconductor manufacturing and other industries.  Article 19 *******************    


Major advance in DNA imaging reported 

675 words 
26 May 1992
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1992, Business Wire) 

SANTA BARBARA, Calif.--(HealthWire)--A team of scientists from UC Santa Barbara, the University of Oregon and Digital Instruments Inc. has reported an important advance in the use of a revolutionary new type of microscope for the study and manipulation of DNA. 

In the May 22 issue of the journal, Science, the researchers report that using an Atomic Force Microscope they have obtained the first reproducible images of DNA that show features the size of the double helix -- a characteristic of the long-chained molecule that controls most living processes by means of the genetic code. 

They also reported that this unusual instrument can be used to cut strands of DNA with considerable precision. 

The images represent a major advance in efforts to extend the use of this experimental microscope from inorganic substances, where it has provided the first atomic-scale pictures of a number of surfaces, to biological materials. The letters of the genetic code, chemical bases contained in DNA, are much too small to see with conventional microscopes. 

So, the ability to identify them directly would provide biologists and genetic engineers with a powerful new tool. The possibility that the AFM might be able to do just that has attracted considerable scientific interest. 

``It took 30 years before the electron microscope could image DNA. Similarly, a major effort will be required to permit the AFM to achieve its full potential for imaging DNA. This is an important step down that road,'' said team member Robert L. Sinsheimer, professor emeritus of biological sciences at UCSB. 

Although considerably more work remains to be done to achieve the AFM's full potential, the scientists have now demonstrated that the new instrument can make images of DNA comparable to those produced by electron microscopy. The electron microscope, however, requires that molecules be coated with protein and metal, which deactivates them. The AFM images, by contrast, were obtained of biologically active DNA. 

``We now have the capability of obtaining before-and-after images of DNA involved in a number of basic biological processes,'' said Helen G. Hansma, the assistant research biologist at UC Santa Barbara who is lead author on the paper. 

To achieve these results, the scientists had to overcome a number of technical problems that result from the AFM's unique mode of operation. Unlike conventional microscopes, it generates detailed images of surfaces by scanning them with an ultra-sharp tip while precisely recording the tip's motion. 

As a result, the moving tip tends to brush aside small targets like DNA unless they are firmly attached to the atomically smooth mica surface used as a substrate. University of Oregon scientists -- James Vesenka, Christina Siegerist and Carlos Bustamante -- discovered that magnesium acetate could be used to hold the spaghetti-like DNA molecules in place. 

With firmly attached strands of DNA, the scientists also demonstrated that it is possible to use the AFM tip to sever DNA molecules with considerable precision at any location. The ability to cut and splice DNA plays an important role in genetic engineering. Currently, scientists use special enzymes to cut DNA, which only operate at a limited number of sites. 

In order to obtain the significantly improved level of resolution, the UCSB researchers introduced two additional innovations. They established that immersing the DNA in propanol provided substantial improvements. In addition, the best images were obtained using special ``super-tips'' made by undergraduate students Greg Kelderman and Hal Morrett. 

They started with conventional AFM tips and then, using a variety of micro-fabrication techniques, sharpened them substantially. 

Paul K. Hansma, professor of physics at UCSB, who has played a significant role in the development of the microscope since it was invented by IBM scientists, and Virgil Elings, head of Digital Instruments, which made the AFM that was used, also contributed to the research. 

NOTE TO EDITORS: Photos available upon request from UCSB.

IBM experimental transistors are world's smallest 

624 words 
28 May 1992
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1992, Business Wire) 

ORLANDO, Fla.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--IBM Research scientists are reporting in Orlando Thursday that they have made the world's smallest transistors. 

The experimental devices are so small that the active area of a single one is just 1/75,000th of the cross-section of a human hair. That's a size that in the future will permit memory-chip fabrication in the realm of four gigabits (Gb) and beyond. Previously, the smallest transistor in existence was 20 times larger in area, and according to the researchers, these new transistors can readily be further reduced in size by another factor of two. 

Memory chips containing at least four billion transistors, one for each bit of information to be placed in memory, would dramatically contribute to the continuing reduction in the cost of computing we have been experiencing for the past 40 years. Currently, the largest memory chip available has a capacity of 16-megabits (Mb, or million bits). 

The new transistors, operating at room temperature and fully scaled down in size with an ultra-compact design, establish a new milestone for the technology in which the sizes of nearly all physical features of the devices are as small as a tenth of a millionth of a meter. 

Of the type known as metal-oxide semiconductor field-effect transistor, or MOSFET, such ultra-compact devices could lead to 4-Gb memory chips (actually dynamic random access memory chips, or DRAMs) within the first decade of the 21st century. But the electron-beam nanolithography fabrication techniques used in this experimental effort are not necessarily appropriate for the mass production of chips. Such production probably will require advances in manufacturing technology. 

Interestingly, these transistors are in the size range in which electronic devices in general would be expected to exhibit unique physical properties predicted by quantum theory. Indeed, scientists are now beginning to acquire knowledge to exploit those properties in "quantum devices" that might be useful in practical applications. The behavior of the ultra-compact transistors, on the other hand, is still entirely conventional and well understood. 

Further work aimed at optimizing the device characteristics will include testing in high-speed circuits and in prototype logic and memory circuits. 

The achievement is being reported in detail at the 36th International Symposium on Electron, Ion, and Photon Beams being held in Orlando, May 26-29, by Clive M. Reeves, Shalom J. Wind, and Fritz J. Hohn. They performed their work at the IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, N.Y., with the additional participation of James J. Bucchignano, Johann Keller, David P. Klaus, Yeong T. Lii, Thomas H. Newman, Brian M. Tebin, and Richard P. Volant. 

Technical 

The researchers demonstrated that device scaling is fully extendable down to 100 nanometers, and provided the device structures for this silicon n-channel MOSFET with several unique features: shallow trench isolation with butted gate electrodes leaving no overlap between the gate and the trench; fully overlapped source and drain contacts; and direct over-the-gate contacts. 

The active area of the device measures only 700 nm by 150 nm and is enclosed by an isolation trench of 150 nm wide. Within this structure is a gate electrode of length 100 nm and width 150 nm. Source, drain and gate contacts measure 150 nm by 200 nm. The spacing between 200-nm-wide metal tracks is a minimum of 100 nm. Level-to-level fabrication, tolerance, or overlay, was required to be better than 25 nm for all levels. 

The IBM group is working toward producing a CMOS implementation of the device.

``The work being done at M.I.T. will allow Hampshire to demonstrate the effectiveness of X-ray technology to provide specific advantages and process results in manufacturing nanostructures for commercial applications. The company is actively involved if SEMI/SEMATECH and has been a prime contractor to the U.S. Government's Microelectronics and Defense Advanced Lithography Programs.

New Microscope Technique promises savings in millions for semiconductor manufacturers. 

426 words 
9 November 1992
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1992, Business Wire) 

Yorktown Heights, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--IBM researchers have developed a technique for inspecting, measuring and imaging regions of semiconductor integrated circuit chips that for the first time are accessible by nondestructive means. 

The advance is expected to have significant impact on semiconductor manufacturing. 

According to Kumar Wickramasinghe, manufacturing research scientist at the IBM Thomas J. Watson Research Center and principal developer, with IBM researcher Yves Martin, of the new technique, ``the advance has the potential of saving the semiconductor industry many millions of dollars a year.'' 

The technique is a variation of scanning force microscopy, in which the attractive force between a fine tip and the nearby surface of the material being studied is sensed as the tip is scanned across the surface. It can produce images of surfaces with resolution down to one nanometer, a billionth of a meter. 

The variation employs a new type of tip with an unconventional shape and novel schemes for sensing the sample surface and for scanning the tip along the surface. As a result, the technique overcomes the limitations of standard scanning force microscopy: it can inspect, characterize, and profile accurately and simultaneously both the width and depth of microcircuit features, in a noncontacting, nondestructive fashion. And it can do so on a scale previously difficult or impossible to attain. 

The specially shaped probe tip was developed by a team led by Johann Greschner at the IBM German Manufacturing Technology Center in Sindelfingen. 

The technique might find its way to widespread use outside IBM in two different ways. IBM will make it available to companies producing metrology equipment through licensing arrangements. Also, IBM will offer it as an option for a scanned-probe-microscope tool (the IBM SXM scanning probe microscope) already being manufactured by IBM for internal use in semiconductor fabrication and now being marketed commercially. 

Adequate inspection of critical dimensions of integrated circuits has been a major impediment to process-control improvement in the manufacture of semiconductors. Previously, the only available method for imaging the smallest features of chips was scanning electron microscopy. But wafers filled with chips could sustain contamination and electron-beam-induced damage. Further, with such microscopy, inspection of certain microcircuit features -- vertical sidewalls, for example -- suffered the drawback of requiring the wafers on which they were fabricated to be broken so as to expose the profile. Consequently, needlessly high expenses were being incurred.

Atomic Force Microscopy is a variation of a technique called Scanning Tunnelling Microscopy, which was invented by two IBM scientists who shared the Nobel Prize in Physics for their invention of the Scanning Tunnelling Microscope. 

The SXM model is capable of non-contact, non-destructive, nanometer scale measurement of sub-micron structures. This automatic, in-line manufacturing inspection tool is capable of measuring next generation semiconductor features on a 200mm diameter wafer. 

A unique Critical Dimension (CD) option permits the user to profile vertical sidewalls, measure sidewall angles and obtain true width measurements of sub-micron lines or trenches without damaging or breaking the wafer. The SXM workstation also can perform horizontal and vertical measurements on micron-size features to a precision of two nanometers (a nanometer is equal to one billionth of a meter). Even with its technical sophistication, the workstation is typically installed in one day. 

According to Edward H. Braun, President and CEO of Veeco Instruments Inc., "The SXM provides extraordinary sub-micron '3D' images and critical dimension measurements in a production line environment. No other metrology system offers this level of precision without damaging or breaking the wafer."

Veeco Instruments is a worldwide supplier of thin film measurement instruments, precision ion etching equipment and helium leak test stations for semiconductor, material science and industrial applications. The SXM Scanning AFM Microscope Workstation is a significant extension of the Dektak stylus profiler instrument line currently offered by Veeco's Sloan Technology Division. 

The SXM workstation was created through a joint product development program involving the MTC, IBM Manufacturing Research in Yorktown, N.Y., and IBM's German Manufacturing Technology Center in Sindelfingen, Germany. 

Veeco provides customer application and product support from its two U.S. manufacturing sites, as well as distribution centers in France, Germany, England, Japan and the Pacific Rim.

 Article 25 *******************    


New "buckyballs" stop crucial AIDS virus enzyme 

748 words 
29 July 1993
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1993, Business Wire) 

SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--During his search for drugs targeted against HIV, the AIDS virus, a friend's "What will they try next?" remark led a young UC San Francisco researcher to discover the anti-HIV potential of "buckyballs," recently created molecules nicknamed because their shape resembles the late Buckminster Fuller's multi-sided geodesic domes. 

In what appears to be the first potential biological application of buckyballs, spherical lattices of 60 carbon atoms, a team of UC researchers has found that the soccer-ball-shaped molecules fit into a cylindrical pocket of a crucial HIV enzyme protein, thereby stopping the enzyme from carrying out a chemical reaction vital to the virus' survival. 

The team reports its findings in the current "Journal of the American Chemical Society." 

According to George Kenyon, Ph.D., professor and chair of pharmaceutical chemistry and interim dean of the UCSF School of Pharmacy, "This work represents a novel approach to the fight against the HIV. Combining ideas from three distinct areas of research -- AIDS, buckyballs, and computer-assisted, structure-based drug design -- has resulted in the development of a molecule that may, when modified, lead to a useful drug." 

Simon Friedman, a graduate student who works in Kenyon's laboratory, took seriously the question posed by his friend Diane Roe -- "What next, buckyballs?" -- and realized that buckyballs might fit into the space normally used by the HIV protease enzyme to attach to protein and break it apart. 

This function is required for HIV to reproduce itself, and the HIV protease enzyme has recently become a target of intensive drug development efforts following its purification and determination of its structure. 

Kenyon leads the structure-based drug design program at UCSF, targeted against HIV viral structures, including the protease, and funded by the National Institutes of Health. 

Working with postdoctoral fellow Diane DeCamp, Friedman tested his idea with a computer program, DOCK 3, developed at UCSF for calculating and displaying in stereoscopic three-dimensional form the attachment of potential drugs to their target molecules. The program predicted that the buckyball would fit into the center of the protease pocket. 

Friedman knew that the distribution of electrical charge on the buckyball also would influence the strength of its attachment to the protease pocket. An unmodified buckyball, with no strong electrical charges, would for the most part be complementary to the protein building blocks -- called amino acids -- lining the pocket. 

However, the research team also wanted to create a buckyball with regions where electrical charges would be great enough to cause the buckyball to dissolve in water, the milieu within living organisms, and to more easily travel through the bloodstream to HIV-infected cells. 

Friedman presented the challenge to Fred Wudl, a pioneer and expert in the design and construction of buckyballs, more formally known as fullerenes. 

Wudl, professor of chemistry at UC Santa Barbara, working with postdoctoral fellow Rint Sijbesma and Gordana Srdanov, a research assistant, succeeded in adding to the buckyball a molecule derived from a chemical called diphenyldiazomethane, which made the resulting molecule soluble in water. UC Riverside chemists Charles Wilkins and John Castoro verified the structure of the buckyball after it was made. 

In test-tube experiments, the UCSF researchers found that this derivative, called a "fulleroid," fit into the protease pocket and prevented the enzyme from cutting protein. 

Because they are the first of their kind, the water-soluble buckyballs have not yet been tested for safety in animals. However, an Emory University research team led by Raymond Shinazi and Craig Hill has found that the derivative made in Wudl's laboratory can stop HIV from reproducing in white blood cells in culture at concentrations that do not appear to kill healthy cells. 

At UCSF, Friedman now is trying to make a more refined buckyball to stop the AIDS virus, one which will target two electrically charged arms deep within the HIV protease pocket. 

The arms extend from two negatively charged molecules of aspartate, an amino acid, and are used by the enzyme to grasp protein and bring it together with water molecules so that the protein may be split apart through a chemical reaction called hydrolysis. 

A buckyball with strategically spaced, positively charged amino groups that would be electrically attracted to the aspartates may better outcompete protein in the struggle to attach to the protease pocket, according to Friedman and Kenyon.

English
(Copyright (c) 1994, Business Wire) 

ZURICH, Switzerland--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Feb. 24, 1994--IBM scientists have developed the world's most sensitive heat-measuring instrument. 

Called a calorimeter, it is a thousand times more sensitive than any similar instrument available today: it can measure the heat generated in chemical reactions with a sensitivity to temperature changes as small as a hundred-thousandth of a degree. 

The calorimeter was microfabricated with integrated-circuit technology and is relatively inexpensive. It should prove useful in a large variety of chemical observation, detection, measurement, and analysis applications such as drug design, forensics, and catalysis. When specially configured, the calorimeter can function as a supersensitive "nose on a chip," capable of "smelling" extremely minute quantities of a wide range of substances. 

Developed at the IBM Research Division's Zurich Research Laboratory, the technique employs a micromechanical silicon lever that is coated with aluminum. 

When heated the lever bends because the two materials expand by different amounts. The amount of bending directly indicates how much heat has been absorbed by the lever. The effect is similar to what happens in an ordinary thermometer: when it absorbs heat, the liquid mercury in it expands. Whereas markings on the thermometer show how much the mercury expands, the IBM researchers use a laser to measure how much the lever bends; and they can measure bends as small as one hundredth of the diamter of an atom. 

In a particular demonstration, a thin layer of platinum was applied to the aluminum-coated silicon lever. In the presence of a mixture of oxygen and hydrogen, the platinum functioned as a catalyst that promoted the combining of oxygen and hydrogen to form ordinary water. In the process, the platinum layer generated heat that was then absorbed by the lever, causing it to bend. By carefully monitoring and measuring that bend, the researchers were able to show that the hydrogen and oxygen do not combine at a uniform rate. The rate actually oscillates with time, a phenomenon previously known to occur but never before sensed with a calorimeter. 

The lever in this new calorimeter has a thickness only abouth a fiftieth of the diameter of a human hair -- actually 1.5 microns -- and a length of 400 microns. (A micron is one millionth of a meter, or 1/25,000th of an inch.) An array of hundreds or even thousands of such levers could be integrated on a chip. If each lever were coated and thereby sensitized for the detection of a specific chemical, the resulting combination would function as a "supernose". Even coatings such as reaction-specific enzymes and bacteria could be used, and because the calorimeter is so sensitive, chemical reactions involving only a few molecules could be detected. 

A typical person can discern several hundred odors, and a trained expert might be able to identify several thousand. While computers have been given the ability to see, hear and touch, they are as yet unable to emulate the olfactory organ -- they can't smell. This may soon change. The IBM scientists believe that the apparatus for this technique could be incorporated into a portable package, with the "nose on a chip" and a laptop computer, to provide an instrument capable of detecting gases and pollutants such as ozone and carbon monoxide and even odors such as that of fish. 

The researchers believe that through the use of micromechanics and nanotechnology, their calorimeter, already the most sensitive in the world, can be made many thousands of time even more sensitive. They are already working on that| 

A detailed report on the work, written by James Gimzewski, Christoph Gerber and Reto Schlittler of the IBM Zurich Research Laboratory, together with Ernst Meyer, on sabbatical from the University of Basel, Switzerland, was published recently in the Jan. 28, 1994 issue of the journal Chemical Physics Letters.

Renowned Cornell University Ph.D. joins Applied Laser Systems as chairman of its scientific advisory board
