MEDFORD, Ore.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--March 1, 1994--Applied Laser Systems (ALS)(NASDAQ:LZZRA) announced Tuesday that it has retained Dr. Lester Eastman, Ph.D., as the chairman of its new Scientific Advisory Board, which is designed to provide research and scientific support to all ALS subsidiary companies. 

Eastman received his Ph.D. from Cornell University in 1957 and has since been a faculty member of Electrical Engineering at Cornell University where he has supervised over 85 Ph.D. graduates. During this time, Eastman has served as a member of the graduate field of Applied Physics at Cornell; founded the National Research and Resource Facility for Submicron Structures (now National Nanofabrication Facility); served as a member of the Kuratorium (Visiting Senior Advisory Board) of the Fraunhofer Applied Physics Institute; and is a member of the National Academy of Engineering. 

Eastman is the founder and former chairman of Northeast Semiconductors Inc., a New York company, which has done research on compound semiconductor materials, high speed devices and circuits, and helped develop one of the smallest producible high power laser diode systems. 

Applied Laser Systems of Oregon ("ALSO") recently acquired all of the assets and technology of Northeast Semiconductor Inc. and signed consulting agreements with Eastman and Richard Shealy, Ph.D., also of Cornell University. This technology will position ALSO among the world leaders in semiconductor-based high power laser technologies, which have applications in the medical, industrial and fiber optics fields. This technology is expected to replace the present, universally used, gas-based laser systems. 

Applied Laser Systems' wholly owned subsidiary develops and manufactures proprietary laser diode products. ALS recently announced the acquisition of Simco/Ramic Corp., a computer aided vision (CAV) company and signed non-binding letters of intent to acquire both North American Scientific Inc. and Quadrax Corp.

BEAVERTON, Ore.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--March 14, 1994--CAChe Scientific and IBM Monday announced a major partnership agreement that gives CAChe access to the IBM Research Division's world-class computational chemistry technology and exclusive worldwide distribution rights to related products developed by its Chemical Services and Applications (CSA) unit. 

"We needed a partner who could help us in two areas, user interface and marketing," said Michael Hehenberger, CSA Program Director at the IBM Almaden Research Center in San Jose, Calif. "We spoke with computational chemists, R&D directors and experimental chemists. And CAChe Scientific emerged as having the leading user interface on the market for the experimental chemist. Through that interface, we'll provide tools that perform difficult computing tasks requiring high levels of theory and a depth of knowledge in computer-aided chemistry. This will satisfy the advanced user and give new users easy access to some powerful capabilities." 

"CAChe and CSA are very well positioned to take computer-aided chemistry into the mainstream," said George Fabel, president of CAChe Scientific. "The IBM Research Division's reputation for innovation in computational chemistry is very strong and their scientists are world renowned," he added. Dr. Fabel said he expected the first products to emerge from the partnership later this year. 

The partnership provides a marketing channel for CSA's on-going development of application software in computational chemistry. It strengthens CAChe Scientific's ability to deliver a steady stream of powerful new chemistry applications. In addition, the partners envision a full range of application support, consulting, education and training services to ensure successful integration of computer-aided chemistry into a customer's R&D operations. 

"CAChe and CSA will deliver real competitive advantage to chemical and pharmaceutical companies by providing complete solutions for a range of chemical applications. Our combined tool sets, application expertise, and support services ensure that computer-aided chemistry will have a significant and positive impact on the success of a customer's organization," said Lyle Ochs, CAChe vice president of Marketing. 

CAChe's user interface has been enthusiastically received by experimental chemists. Its ProjectLeader, an application that simplifies project planning, experiment setup, program execution and documentation, makes it easy to achieve chemically significant results. CAChe's powerfully simple graphical user interface and its new ProjectLeader application run on popular desktop platforms backed up by compute servers that include IBM RISC System/6000, Silicon Graphics and Macintosh. 

Applications and services will draw upon the Research Division's expertise in computational chemistry, data base technology, polymers, materials science, and nanoscale technology. The products will be sold through CAChe Scientific's worldwide network of distributors and direct sales and supported with training, consulting and applications services from both parties. 

IBM Research formed CSA to provide services and application software for the chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical and biotechnology markets. Based in San Jose, Calif., but also drawing on technologies from other IBM research laboratories in Yorktown Heights, N.Y., and Zurich, Switzerland, CSA will solve chemical problems by combining both experimental and computational skills. Initial application software development focuses on computational chemistry and chemical/biological database technology. 

Contact Information

The company develops and markets a full suite of chemistry software for popular desktop and compute server platforms and stereoscopic displays for 3D visualization. CAChe products are used routinely by educators and experimental chemists in leading corporations in the petrochemical, pharmaceutical, plastics, dyes and inks, soaps and detergents, and other industries worldwide.

Nanogen Inc. completes $3.5 million round of venture capital; Berger Nova, Evans and Heller join senior management 

1,016 words 
15 March 1994
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1994, Business Wire) 

SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--March 15, 1994--Nanogen Inc. has completed a $3.5 million round of venture capital financing to fund the development of a powerful new level of DNA-based diagnostic tests using a revolutionary proprietary combination of computer science and biotechnology, according to Howard C. Birndorf, chairman and chief executive officer. 

Birndorf also said a veteran biotechnology company executive and two leading scientific researchers have become part of the company's senior management. Joining Nanogen are Tina Berger Nova, Ph.D., as president and chief operating officer; Glen A. Evans, M.D., Ph.D., as vice president, molecular biology and medical director; and Michael J. Heller, Ph.D., as chief scientist. 

Nanogen is one of the first companies to combine molecular genetics, microelectronics and nanotechnology to develop medical diagnostics and biopharmaceutical assays. The company's initial effort will focus on the development of cost-effective diagnostic tests capable of instantly and simultaneously analyzing up to thousands of genetic and infectious diseases. 

"The microchip has totally revolutionized the electronics industry and now it is doing the same for biology," said Birndorf. "We will be replacing an entire diagnostic laboratory with a single computer chip." 

Nanogen's technology uses ultraminiaturized silicon chips inlaid with artificial DNA to detect specific gene sequences. Birndorf said the technology should significantly increase the speed and accuracy of currently available diagnostic tests. Nanogen's proprietary technology also has broad applications for a number of fields, including DNA sequencing, gene discovery, drug evaluation and discovery and basic research. 

He said today's existing DNA-based diagnostic tests are expensive, time consuming and labor intensive. 

"Our testing unit will reduce the many steps of processing and handling a specimen to one," Birndorf said. "Within seconds, a computer will provide test results that today would take hours -- even days -- to complete. And we will provide this with a significant reduction in costs. 

"While others have been working in this field, no one has yet been able to match the sophistication of Nanogen's technology." 

Investors in Nanogen's current round of financing include Enterprise Partners, Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers and Howard C. Birndorf. The investors have committed to additional funding as the company reaches certain milestones. 

"This recent funding will enable Nanogen to continue its rapid research progress, including the development of a prototype product within the next 12-18 months," Birndorf said. "We also are pleased to have started to put in place our senior management team as the next step in building a successful biotechnology company." 

Birndorf, who founded Nanogen, is also president of Birndorf Biotechnology Development, which is actively engaged in the formation of new companies. He has co-founded several successful San Diego-based biotechnology companies, including Ligand Pharmaceuticals, Gen-Probe Inc., Hybritech Inc. and IDEC Pharmaceuticals. He was also involved in the formation of Gensia Pharmaceuticals. 

Birndorf is currently a director of the Cancer Center of the University of California, San Diego, and is a presidential appointee to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Biotechnology Technical Advisory Committee. 

As Nanogen's president and chief operating officer, Berger Nova brings to the company a combination of scientific and management skills, having participated in the successful start up of several biotechnology companies. Prior to joining Nanogen, she was vice president and chief operating officer for San Diego-based PRIZM Pharmaceuticals, where she helped set up the company and raise over $20 million in capital. 

Previously, as executive director of development at Ligand Pharmaceuticals, she developed the automated high-throughput screening assay utilized for the company's drug discovery efforts. She began her scientific career at Hybritech, where she was responsible for the development of several diagnostic products commonly used in clinical laboratories today. 

Berger Nova received her doctoral degree in biochemistry from the University of California, Riverside, followed by a postdoctoral fellowship in dermatology and pharmacology at New York University Medical School. She has been published in numerous scientific journals and has issued patents in the area of assay development. 

Evans, vice president, molecular biology and medical director, is a world-renowned molecular biologist with years of expertise in the areas of molecular biology and genetics. He recently began a 12-to-18-month sabbatical from the Salk Institute, where he served as an associate professor in the Department of Molecular Genetics and director of the Molecular Genetics Laboratory. 

Also serving as the director of the Human Genome Project while at Salk, Evans managed a multimillion-dollar grant for the physical mapping and sequencing of the human genome. He is a member of the Human Genome Organization and was recently elected to the American Academy of Microbiology. 

Evans received his medical and doctoral degrees from the University of California, San Diego. He did an internship in internal medicine at Stanford University Medical Center followed by a postdoctoral fellowship in molecular genetics at the National Institutes of Health. Evans has more than 125 publications in some of the world's most prestigious scientific journals. 

As chief scientist, Heller is considered a leading expert in the area of florescent energy transfer. Prior to joining Nanogen, he was president and founder of Integrated DNA Technologies in Iowa City, Iowa. He has also served as director of molecular biology at Molecular Biosystems Inc. in San Diego. 

Heller received his doctoral degree in biochemistry from Colorado State University and completed a postdoctoral fellowship at Northwestern University under the direction of Robert Letsinger. 

Heller has an extensive publication record and 13 patents and applications. 

"Tina, Glen and Michael are all leaders in their fields and have tremendous depth of experience that will greatly assist Nanogen in reaching the company's goals," Birndorf said. 

He said Nanogen, founded in 1992, currently has seven employees. The company will add about 10 employees over the next few months and expects to employ 30 people by the end of the year.

Los Angeles Times and Voice of America feature stories on new Internet-based electronic magazine 

889 words 
23 March 1994
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1994, Business Wire) 

LOS ANGELES--(BUSINESS WIRE)--March 23, 1994--The Los Angeles Times ran as its "lead" story, in the Wednesday, March 2, Orange County Edition business section, a feature on the HOTT Internet-based magazine. (Other editions of The Times ran a condensed version of the story.) 

On Monday, March 7, The Voice of America aired a segment on HOTT titled, "Information Highway Magazine." Related articles have appeared in IEEE Spectrum (the flagship publication of the IEEE) and Computer (the flagship publication of the IEEE Computer Society). 

HOTT -- Hot Off The Tree -- is a FREE monthly (10/year) electronic magazine featuring article summaries on new-generation computer, communications and electronics technologies from over 200 trade magazines and research journals as well as key U.S. and international daily newspapers, news weeklies and business magazines. 

Each issue provides article summaries on new and emerging technologies, including VR (virtual reality), neural networks, PDAs (personal digital assistants), intelligent agents, genetic and evolutionary programming, wireless communications, video phones, nanotechnology and interactive multimedia. 

Plus, HOTT includes exclusive interviews with technology pioneers. The first several issues feature interviews with Mark Weiser (head of Xerox PARC's Computer Science Lab), Nobel laureate Joshua Lederberg, MCC CEO (and former DARPA director) Craig Fields, and Caltech's Carver Mead. 

The first issue of the reinvented HOTT e-magazine is scheduled for transmission in April. 

In the last few months HOTT has grown from 2,000 to over 40,000 individual subscribers; this already makes HOTT the largest circulation "e-zine" on the Internet. And this figure does NOT include mail exploders or BBSes (bulletin board systems) in the United States, such as the 2,700-member Arizona Macintosh Users Group (AMUG). 

An additional 15,000 readers are being reached through mail exploders and BBSes in over a dozen countries. And HOTT is making an extensive effort to reach non-U.S. Internet providers and FidoNet-based BBSes. 

The goal is to make HOTT the first mass distribution AND truly global periodical on the Information Superhighway.

LOS ANGELES TIMES BUSINESS SECTION "LEAD" ARTICLE ON HOTT 

TITLE: Paper-Less Publisher: Irvine `infomaniac's' `e-magazine' 

exists only in cyberspace. 

Source: Los Angeles Times (LT) -- WEDNESDAY, March 2, 1994 

By: DEAN TAKAHASHI; TIMES STAFF WRITER 

Section: Business Page 1 Pt. D Col. 2 

Full-Text Word Count: 1,518 

IRVINE--David Scott Lewis calls himself an "infomaniac." 

In 1975, when he was 17, he built a personal computer from the first available Altair kits. He became a "hacker" and served as a consultant to "WarGames," a 1983 film about a teen- age computer nerd who nearly triggers a nuclear war. 

Today, the 35-year-old Lewis cruises the Internet, the global electronic supernetwork known simply as "the Net" that links 20,000 computer networks and boasts 20 million users. He spends an hour or more a day perusing more than 200 groups of on-line information. He even acquired an Internet address -- a sort of ID number -- for his 19-week-old daughter on the day she was born. 

So naturally, this walking encyclopedia and information junkie is a fitting editor and publisher of an Internet magazine, Hot Off The Tree, which summarizes more than 100 printed publications and explores our technological world. 

His "publication" circulates electronically -- only in cyber-space -- and is a sign of the coming grass-roots explosion in the electronic publishing world. 

"What Mr. Lewis is doing with HOTT is exciting in itself and also as a demonstration of how to reach a large audience on-line," said Daniel Dern, author of the Internet Guide for New Users and outgoing editor of Internet World magazine in Newton Center, Mass. Lewis believes his magazine will become must reading among the 2.5 million serious 'Net users like himself. 

Larry Lasker, who co-wrote the screenplay for "WarGames," said Lewis has a talent for making technological subjects understandable to novices. "As a hacker, you could tell he knew his way around," Lasker said. "He was an incredibly fast reader. He was always motivated to find information if he didn't have it." 

Edward Roberts, a professor of management at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, said Lewis clearly has the energy to be successful with HOTT. "He has a craze for scanning information and cramming it into his head and putting it together into tidbits." Copyright (c) 1994, Times Mirror Co.

New Product Preview From CAChe Scientific-IBM Partnership; POWERFUL, EASY-TO-USE PROGRAM HELPS BENCH CHEMISTS SOLVE PRACTICAL PROBLEMS INVOLVING LARGE MOLECULES 

765 words 
22 August 1994
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1994, Business Wire) 

WASHINGTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 22, 1994--CAChe Scientific today previewed a powerful, versatile, easy-to-use quantum chemistry software program developed by scientists at IBM's Almaden Research Center in San Jose, Calif. 

The product enables chemists to solve practical problems involving large, complex molecules with little effort. CAChe demonstrated the software at the American Chemical Society Conference here in Washington. 

Two factors contribute to the software's ease of use. The first is CAChe Scientific's award-winning graphical user interface that makes prediction and visualization of molecular properties simple, even for first-time users. The other is a collection of "robust" algorithms that don't break down under complex calculations. 

The speed of the application software's ab initio calculations is the result of novel solution techniques, state-of-the-art numerical algorithms, and its ability to be used in the parallel computing mode. Both workstation clusters and parallel processors are supported. Users can simply "tell" the software the names of the machines on which it is to run. 

"The new application is an excellent complement to CAChe's product family," said George Fabel, CAChe Scientific president. "The software enables our customers to use more advanced techniques to generate even more accurate estimates of chemical structures, providing a better starting point for property estimates and calibration of experiments. Moreover, first row transition metals can now be studied with even greater accuracy." 

"The goal of the IBM - CAChe Scientific partnership has been to make powerful, reliable computational chemistry software widely available and easy to use for both experimental and computational chemists," said Dr. A. Currie Munce, manager of scientific and technical application software at the Almaden lab. "With this effort, we've taken an important first step towards our goal. Practical chemical problems involving more than 100 atoms will now be solvable in standard industrial computing environments in less time than was ever before possible." 

For example, the charge density of valinomycin, an antibiotic molecule consisting of 171 atoms, can be calculated on a IBM RS/6000 Model 590 in under 100 minutes. Running this calculation in parallel on three computers would reduce the run time to less than 40 minutes. Speed is also derived by taking advantage of molecular symmetry. For example, it only takes six minutes to calculate the charge density of Buckminster Fullerene. Without symmetry, the calculation would take about eight times longer. 

The software features an open architecture, which allows chemists to integrate their own or other programs at any step of the process and still take advantage the software's speed and ability to handle large molecules. This feature greatly benefits chemists whose applications require a combination of their proprietary quantum chemistry programs and the new routines. The quantum chemistry program also offers versatility by providing users four methods for studying molecular property, reactivity and structure: molecular mechanics, semi-empirical quantum chemistry, ab initio quantum chemistry and the newer density functional theory. Chemists can choose the most effective method to solve their particular problem. 

This development was made possible by 30 years of experience in computational chemistry by IBM researchers in San Jose. The Scientific and Technical Application Software area at the Almaden Research Center provides services and products for the chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical and biotechnology markets. The research also draws on IBM Research Division resources in Yorktown Heights, N.Y., and Zurich, Switzerland.

First practical applications of "buckyballs" seen resulting from Lawrence Livermore research 

258 words 
4 October 1994
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1994, Business Wire) 

LIVERMORE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 4, 1994--The first practical applications of "buckyballs" in the manufacture of silicon carbide microchips, electro-mechanical devices and sensors -- appears possible as a result of research at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. 

Buckyballs are soccer-ball shaped carbon molecules more formally known as buckminsterfullerenes. 

The research was sponsored by the U.S. Department of Energy. Livermore engineers found that when they bombarded heated silicon wafers with a stream of buckyballs, the round carbon molecules "open up like tulips" to form silicon carbide in intricate, controllable patterns. 

The researchers are mechanical engineer Mehdi Balooch and chemical engineer Alex Hamza of the Laboratory's Chemistry and Materials Science Department. 

"This technology is going to open up tremendous applications," Hamza said. "This may allow us to do many things with silicon carbide that we now do with silicon." 

"We really believe this is a breakthrough," Balooch said. "The beauty of it is that it's so simple." 

Silicon carbide is a tough, hard, high-performance material that can withstand extreme operating conditions. 

"Silicon carbide is a very promising material for semiconducting applications," Hamza said. "Prototype devices have been made, but it's extremely difficult to work with. The material is so inert, it's difficult to etch." 

The Livermore engineers' method bypasses this difficulty. "Our technique for patterning chips means that we don't need etching," Balooch said.

EAST BRUNSWICK, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 13, 1994--CAChe Scientific today announced Mulliken, a powerful, versatile, easy-to-use quantum chemistry software program, developed by scientists at IBM's Almaden Research Center in San Jose, Calif. The product enables chemists to solve practical problems involving large, complex molecules with little effort. CAChe demonstrated the software at the Molecular Modeling Conference here in East Brunswick. 

Two factors contribute to the Mulliken's novel ease of use. The first is CAChe Scientific's award-winning graphical user interface that makes prediction and visualization of molecular properties simple, even for first-time users. The other is a collection of "robust" algorithms that don't break down under complex calculations. 

The speed of Mulliken's ab initio calculations is the result of novel solution techniques, state-of-the-art numerical algorithms, and its ability to be used in the parallel computing mode. Both workstation clusters and parallel processors are supported. Users can simply "tell" the software the names of the machines on which it is to run. Mulliken is the first program of its kind to bring ab initio calculations to the desktop. 

"In the past, ab initio quantum chemistry was confined to small, simple molecules," said Lyle Ochs, CAChe Scientific vice president of marketing. "Mulliken enables the bench chemist to solve problems of practical interest because of its speed and the wide variety of computational methods that can be used." 

"The goal of IBM's partnership with CAChe Scientific has been to make powerful, reliable computational chemistry software widely available and easy to use for both experimental and computational chemists," said Dr. A. Currie Munce, manager of scientific and technical application software at the Almaden lab. "With this effort, we've taken an important first step towards our goal. Practical chemical problems involving more than 100 atoms will now be solvable in standard industrial computing environments in less time than was ever before possible." 

For example, Mulliken calculates the charge density of valinomycin, an antibiotic molecule consisting of 171 atoms, on an IBM RISC System/6000 Model 590 in about 90 minutes. Running this calculation on three parallel computers would reduce the run time to less than 40 minutes. Speed is also derived by taking advantage of molecular symmetry. For example, it only takes six minutes to calculate the charge density of Buckminster Fullerenes. Without symmetry, the calculation would take about eight times longer. 

Mulliken features an open architecture, which allows chemists to integrate their own or other programs at any step of the process and still take advantage the software's speed and ability to handle large molecules. This feature is especially valuable for expert users who may want to use it in conjunction with their other quantum chemistry programs. 

Mulliken also offers versatility by providing users four methods for studying molecular property, reactivity and structure: molecular mechanics, semi-empirical quantum chemistry, ab initio quantum chemistry and the newer density functional theory. Chemists can choose the most effective method to solve their particular problem. 

This development was made possible by 30 years of experience in computational chemistry by IBM researchers in San Jose. Among the projects in the scientific and technical application software area at the Almaden Research Center is an effort to provide services and products for the chemical, petrochemical, pharmaceutical and biotechnology market. The project also draws on IBM Research Division resources in Yorktown Heights, New York, and Zurich, Switzerland.

Mulliken's price is $25,000 with special pricing available for educational institutions. The price includes CAChe's ProjectLeader application and the CAChe Satellite user interface. 

Software Named in Honor of Nobel Prize Winner

Mulliken is named after the late Dr. Robert P. Mulliken, a 1966 Nobel Prize winner in chemistry. Dr. Mulliken is considered by many to be the father of modern theories of structural chemistry. His work helped lay the foundation for computer-based molecular modeling.

The investment by Harris & Harris Group was part of a $2.35 million private placement through which Nanophase issued 2.35 million shares of Series D Convertible Preferred Stock largely to its original equity investors led by Arch Venture Partners.

By controlling both particle size and the spacing between particles, Nanophase is able to produce materials with a rich variety of physical properties. Since its formation in 1989, Nanophase has raised over $5.7 million in equity capital and successfully developed a laboratory process into customer-driven production and sales of nanometric-sized crystals. 

The proceeds of this financing will allow Nanophase to relocate from its office/laboratory space into a production facility capable of producing over 40 tons per year of nanometric-sized materials. Nanophase is currently producing trial quantities of nanometric-sized iron oxide and titanium dioxide for use in cosmetics as a transparent sunscreen. Other potential applications of the company's products include sensors for environmental pollutants and affordable net-shaped, ceramic components for applications in engine components, electronics and manufacturing. These applications are being jointly developed with partial funding by independent industrial collaborators and government funding. 

Harris & Harris Group is a closed-end, non-diversified investment company with 9,136,747 common shares issued and outstanding.

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 7, 1994-- Hewlett-Packard Company today announced that Supriyo Datta, professor of electrical engineering at Purdue University, has received the Frederick Emmons Terman Award for 1994. The Terman Award was established by HP in 1969 to recognize outstanding young electrical-engineering educators. 

Robert W. Ritchie, HP's director of University Affairs, presented the award to Datta on Nov. 5 at the annual Frontiers in Education meeting in San Jose, Calif. The meeting is sponsored by the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) Education Society, the American Society for Engineering Education (ASEE) Education and Methods Division, and the IEEE Computer Society. 

The award includes $4,000 and an engraved medal. The recipient must be an electrical-engineering educator who is the principal author of an electrical-engineering textbook published before her or his 40th birthday. The book must be considered an outstanding original contribution to the field of electrical engineering, and the recipient also must have displayed achievements in teaching, research and service. 

Datta was honored for his contributions to engineering education and research in the fields of surface acoustic-wave devices, novel quantum wells and superlattices, and nanoelectronics and, in particular, for his book "Surface Acoustic Devices" (Prentice-Hall, 1986). The text develops quantitative models for basic surface acoustic-wave devices without complex mathematics. It has become the authoritative text in this area, and is widely used by practitioners in the field. 

"Professor Datta is a truly outstanding young faculty member," said Richard J. Schwartz, professor and head of the School of Electrical Engineering at Purdue. "His research has received international recognition. The electrical engineering students here at Purdue chose him to receive our annual award for outstanding teacher in the school. One of the keys to Professor Datta's success is his uncanny ability to take complex concepts and explain them in the simplest of terms." 

Frederick Emmons Terman, known as the "father of Silicon Valley," has been credited with the idea of establishing near a university an industrial community that emphasized research and development. He was instrumental in starting the Stanford Industrial Park in 1951, which fostered closer cooperation between industry and academia and led to the creation of Silicon Valley. During Terman's 40-year career at Stanford University, he served as dean of engineering and provost. Terman is a member of the ASEE Hall of Fame and was the recipient of the 1970 Herbert Hoover Medal for Distinguished Service to Stanford University. In 1976, Terman was presented with the national Medal of Science by President Gerald Ford. 

Hewlett-Packard Company is an international manufacturer of measurement and computation products and systems recognized for excellence in quality and support. The company's products and services are used in industry, business, engineering, science, medicine and education in approximately 110 countries. HP has 97,900 employees and had revenue of $20.3 billion in its 1993 fiscal year.

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 18, 1994-- Catalytica Inc. (Nasdaq:CTAL), announced Friday that it has been awarded a $2 million grant from the Advanced Technology Program (ATP) of the U.S. Department of Commerce's National Institute of Standards and Technology. 

The award was granted to Catalytica and Microfluidics International Corp. (Nasdaq:MFIC) to develop and demonstrate the manufacturability of nanoscale (one-billionth of a meter) catalysts with enhanced performance for use in the chemical and petroleum refining industries. Nanotechnology has the potential to significantly lower manufacturing costs and reduce byproduct waste by improving catalyst activity and selectivity. 

The $2 million award will fund about half the cost of the three-year project. The first year of the project will demonstrate technical aspects such as synthesis techniques and catalyst performance, followed by catalyst development in year two and scale-up for prototype batches and customer evaluation in year three. 

The project will target three types of nanoscale catalysts: nanocrystalline zeolites, colloidal catalysts, and mixed metal oxides. Zeolites are used for petroleum upgrading and petrochemical production. Colloidal catalysts are an emerging market for the processing of residual feedstocks in the petroleum refining industry. Metal oxide catalysts are used for partial oxidations in chemical manufacturing. 

The ATP is designed to fund research and development on enabling technologies with the potential for new and improved products, manufacturing processes and services. Grant awards are expected to leverage an equal expenditure by industry. The Commerce Department has reported that they will commit up to $137 million over five years on new projects. 

The Catalytica-Microfluidics project is one of 32 projects in the areas of industrial chemistry, electronics, materials, manufacturing, biotechnology, medicine and software selected from 397 proposals received in the ATP's 1994 general competition. The ATP will fund approximately $85 million for these 32 projects. 

Catalytica and Microfluidics are seeking other companies to work with to facilitate the development and commercialization of the nanoscale materials. The two companies began collaborating in November 1993 to develop and commercialize technology using the patented Microfluidizer(TM) device. 

In April 1994, Catalytica signed a cooperative research and development agreement with the Naval Research Laboratory in Washington, D.C., to synthesize and evaluate nanoscale materials for a wide range of applications such as superconductivity, piezoelectric materials, ceramics and metals. 

Microfluidics, located in Newton, Mass., provides patented, proprietary Microfluidizer fluid processing systems for high-energy mixing applications in the chemical processing, pharmaceutical, biotechnology, cosmetic and food industries. 

Catalytica is focused on catalytic products and processes for the economical prevention of pollution. The company's nanotechnology program has the potential to significantly lower manufacturing costs and reduce byproduct waste. The program could also provide novel catalysts for the company's activities in the refining, combustion, and fine chemicals industries.

Three Stanford scientists receive NSF Young Investigator Awards 

646 words 
30 November 1994
18:01 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1994, Business Wire) 

STANFORD, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 30, 1994--Three Stanford scientists were among the 197 scientists and engineers selected by the National Science Foundation this year to receive NSF Young Investigator Awards, a program designed to recognize outstanding young faculty and enhance their careers. 

The three researchers are John H. Griffin, assistant professor of chemistry; Chaitan S. Khosla, assistant professor of chemical engineering; and Charles M. Marcus, assistant professor of physics. The young investigator awards provide up to $100,000 per year of public and private funds for five years. Each year, NSF provides $25,000 in base support and up to $37,500 to match support that the researcher receives from private or nonprofit sources. 

Awards were made based on a merit review of the 1,435 nominations that NSF received. The review emphasized an individual's accomplishment to date and potential to make substantial contributions to the overall academic enterprise. 

This is the last year that these awards will be made. According to the agency, they are being "subsumed" by a new Faculty Early Career Development (CAREER) program that will be tailored to specific science and engineering disciplines. 

Griffin's research lies at the boundary between chemistry and biology. His primary interests are the methods by which molecules recognize each other and the process of catalysis. (A catalyst is a compound that speeds up a chemical reaction without undergoing any permanent change.) 

One of his current research efforts involves the creation and study of "catalytic antibiotics." Normally, antibiotics fight foreign bacteria and fungi by attacking specific enzymes or compounds attached to the intruders' outer membrane. Normally, they destroy themselves in the process, so it takes a large number of antibiotic molecules to neutralize one bacterium. 

Starting with two commonly used antibiotics, vancomycin and bacitracin, the chemist is searching for derivative compounds that can attack bacteria without destroying themselves. If this effort is successful, it could lead to more powerful antibiotics. 

Khosla uses genetic engineering to imitate the way in which nature makes an important class of biological molecules, called polyketides, that are found in a number of antibiotic, immunosuppressant and anti-cancer drugs. When drug companies begin looking for a new drug and have no place to start, they begin by screening thousands of natural products looking for a "lead" molecule that exhibits some of the desired activity. 

Khosla's approach is an alternative to the traditional method that could develop into a better way to identify some kinds of lead molecules. He has used it successfully to create a number of novel polyketides that have not been seen in nature. Recently, he has started a new project that attempts to apply this basic approach to the discovery of new enzymes. 

How randomness of nature appears out of atomic perfection is the focus of Marcus' research. At the level of the single atom, nature is perfectly ordered and each atom of the same element is identical. By contrast, at the macroscopic level of everyday life, disorder, randomness and unrepeatability appear. 

By fabricating ultraminiature semiconductor structures known as quantum dots that lie midway in size between atomic and bulk scales, Marcus has shown that even structures free of disorder can exhibit random behavior due to the quantum mechanical signatures of chaos. Quantum dots are tiny spots of electrical conductor, a ten-thousandth of a centimeter across, that are given a precise shape using advanced nanofabrication techniques. 

Although the quantum dot is free of disorder, one of its electrical properties -- its impedance to electron flow -- varies randomly when it is subjected to an external magnetic field, Marcus has found. This is one example of the research that he is pursuing at the "mesoscopic" realm that lies midway between the atomic and macroscopic scales.

President Clinton to Honor IBM Scientists with National Medal of Technology 

884 words 
27 September 1995
14:53 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1995, Business Wire) 

WASHINGTON, D.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sept. 27, 1995--President Clinton will present the National Medal of Technology, the nation's highest award for technological innovation, to three IBM scientists for their discovery of the special magnetic materials that made possible today's $2 billion rewritable-optical-disk data storage industry, U.S. Secretary of Commerce Ron Brown announced today. 

The IBM researchers who will receive the medal October 18 in ceremonies at The White House are: Praveen Chaudhari, Jerome J. Cuomo (retired) and Richard J. Gambino (retired). The trio were working together at IBM's Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, N.Y., in the 1970s when they discovered a combination of elements that possessed unusual magnetic and optical properties that made them suitable media for optical data storage. Since the 1980s, films of these materials only a millionth-of-an-inch thick have been used to hold data on rewritable "magneto-optic" (MO) disks. 

Virtually all of today's rewritable optical disks worldwide still use these IBM-invented materials. MO disks are used most often by businesses, governments and universities to store, retrieve and update vast amounts of information on economical and easily portable cartridges. By contrast, data on read-only CD-ROMs cannot be updated. 

"We are proud that our scientists have been honored with the nation's highest technology award," said Jim McGroddy, IBM senior vice president, research. "Their invention has spawned a worldwide $2 billion market that is having a major impact on American business and economy. IBM will continue to be the foundry for much of the intellectual capital created in our industry. Our first imperative is to leverage that technology in the marketplace." 

With this year's award, IBM scientists have won the National Medal of Technology more often than those of any other company. Previous IBM recipients are: 

-- N. Joseph Woodland for bar code technology and contributions to the Universal Product Code (1992); 

-- John Cocke for reduced instruction set computers (RISC) (1991); 

-- Robert H. Dennard for the one-device memory cell, the basis for industry-standard dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) (1988); 

-- Reynold B. Johnson for the 305 RAMAC, the first magnetic hard disk system for data storage (1986), and 

-- Frederick P. Brooks Jr., Erich Bloch and Bob O. Evans for the System/360 mainframe computer (1985). 

IBM scientists have also won the Nobel Prize for physics twice -- in 1986 for the scanning tunneling microscope and in 1987 for high-temperature superconducting materials -- and the National Medal of Science, in 1976 for the development of the FORTRAN computer language. Moreover, during each of the past two years, IBM employees have been awarded more U.S. patents than those of any other company, including a record 1,298 U.S. patents in 1994. 

The National Medal of Technology was established by Congress and has been awarded annually since 1985. Any U.S. citizen, team or U.S.-owned company is eligible to win. 

Chaudhari has been a key figure in some of the company's most advanced science and technology developments. He has received numerous awards and has served on national and presidential advisory councils. Chaudhari holds a doctoral degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. 

Cuomo received many awards for his inventions during a 30-year career at IBM. He was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1993 and has served on the National Research Council Committee. He is now a Chaired Professor in the Materials Science and Engineering Department at North Carolina State University. Cuomo received his B.S. from Manhattan College (1958), M.S. from St. John's University (1960) and his Ph.D. from Odense University in Denmark (1979). 

Gambino, who retired from IBM in 1993, is now a professor in the Materials Science and Engineering Department at the State University of New York at Stony Brook. He received his M.S. degree from the Polytechnic Institute of New York in 1976. While at IBM, Gambino received numerous awards for his research. He has also been recognized by engineering and research societies. 

IBM Research operates in seven locations worldwide: the Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, N.Y.; the Almaden Research Center in San Jose, Calif.; the Zurich Research Laboratory in Ruschlikon, Switzerland; the Tokyo Research Laboratory in Yamato, Japan; the Haifa Research Group in Haifa, Israel; the China Research Laboratory in Beijing, China; and the Austin Laboratory in Austin, Tex. The major areas of research are computer systems, computer applications and solutions, systems technology, physical sciences, mathematical sciences, data storage and communications. 

The IBM home page can be found on the Internet at: http://www.ibm.com More details about the technological achievements of IBM Research scientists can be found on the IBM Research home page at: http://www.research.ibm.com

Technical background: 

Magneto-optic materials are so called because magnetic fields can alter the way light passes through them. Briefly heating the material with a pulse of focused laser light in the presence of an external magnetic field can create a cylindrical domain having the magnetic orientation of the external magnetic field. Data is recorded as a coded pattern of domains with detectably different magnetic orientations. 

The materials discovered by Chaudhari, Cuomo and Gambino consist of combinations of "rare-earth" and transition-metal" elements that form amorphous, not crystalline, alloys. Their amorphous structure enables the formation of very small and well-defined domains within the material that can still yield strong and low-noise MO signals. Various members of this IBM-invented family of materials also occupy a "sweet spot" of other desirable properties for optical storage media: They require modest magnetic fields and laser powers for erasing and writing that are suitable for practical implementation and are also sensitive to a broad range of laser wavelengths. Indeed, IBM's 1993 demonstration of a world-record optical data storage density of 2.5 billion bits per square inch on a removable disk used a blue laser and an amorphous MO alloy (terbium-iron-cobalt) media only slightly different from that used in today's rewritable disk drives having infrared lasers. 

From the very beginnings of the optical data storage industry, IBM has been a leader in research and technology. Today, IBM and other companies provide a broad family of optical storage solutions, ranging from desktop storage systems of a few hundred megabytes (a few hundred million bytes) to large automated optical disk library systems handling terabytes (trillions of bytes) of accessible storage. The high density and portability of optical disks are major advantages. To illustrate this technology's impact, one terabyte of data is equivalent to the text on 500 million double-spaced pages, enough to fill more than 30,000 four-drawer filing cabinets. 

Optical products are projected to grow 60 percent this year, faster than any other segment of the data storage industry (such as, magnetic hard disks or tape products), said industry consultants Robert C. Abraham and Raymond C. Freeman in their "Optical Data Storage Outlook 1995" report. They expect rewritable MO systems to be the second fastest-growing optical segment, after compact disc/read-only memory (CD-ROM) products. Breakthrough technology vaporizes metals to produce unique materials with diverse commercial usages 

1,353 words 
9 November 1995
14:27 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1995, Business Wire) 

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 9, 1995--Leading international scientists begin assembling here today to discuss the future of what could be called the ultimate in miniaturization. 

This is the world of "molecular nanotechnology," where manufactured products are made from atoms and the ruler for measurement is scaled in nanometers, which are one-billionth of a meter. It is a world that envisions an entire encyclopedia printed in an area no larger than the head of a pin...or computers the size of matchbooks...and medical diagnostic devices which a physician might inject into a patient's bloodstream. It will be a world subject to debate and conjecture, as the scientists attending the Fourth Foresight Conference on Molecular Nanotechnology, scheduled here from November 9 through 11, 1995, assess the state of this seemingly arcane field. 

Yet as the scientists gathered in Palo Alto ask "what if...?," other scientists and their business colleagues two thousand miles away in the Chicago suburb of Burr Ridge are asking "how much...?" as they begin to ship materials based on their own proprietary application of nanotechnology. In so doing they are validating their claim to be the first company worldwide to bring nanotechnology from laboratory curiosity to commercial reality. 

The company, Nanophase Technologies Corporation, employs a proprietary breakthrough technology which literally turns solid metal into vapor, much as water boils off as steam. That technology is promising a broad array of new consumer and industrial products with characteristics far superior to those they replace, in commercial applications ranging from chemical-free sunscreens to fade-resistant fabrics and high-stress engine parts. 

To produce the raw materials for such products, Nanophase technicians feed common metals such as iron, aluminum or titanium into specially designed chambers in which the metal is vaporized within seconds and then combined with oxygen. The molecular vapor then condenses in a cooling apparatus (like moisture collects on a mirror during a hot shower) where it converts to powder form as nanocrystalline particles with a typical average size of 30 nanometers The resultant particles, which are a fraction of the diameter of a human hair, are ultra-pure (99.96 percent purity level) metal oxides, and have uniform size, quality and reproducibility. These attributes provide superior performance over similar materials produced by other means. 

Sole Global Leadership 

According to Robert W. Cross, NTC President and Chief Executive Officer, his company is the only one in the world capable of producing high-purity nanocrystalline materials on a commercial scale. 

"Physicists and other scientists have conjectured about molecularly engineering materials probably since Einstein's days," Cross noted. "In the last dozen years, however, the potential of nanocrystalline materials began to attract worldwide attention and has led to research initiatives in this country, Europe, Japan, China and India. 

"With the exception of NTC," Cross continued, "none of those initiatives has been able to move these unique high-purity materials from the lab bench to commercial viability. We're the sole global leader in what we feel will be an industry with broad benefits to the consumer." 

As an example of one benefit consumers soon should be enjoying, Cross cited the company's production of titania (titanium dioxide) for use in chemical-free sunscreens. "If a consumer has heard of titania, he or she would recognize it as the ingredient that makes white paint white," said Cross. "Unfortunately, the titania traditionally used in sunscreens also looks white on the skin's surface. Our nanocrystalline titania, which we've trademarked NanoGard(TM), is so small in particle size that it becomes transparent against the skin, yet remains remarkably effective in protecting against the damaging effects of exposure to the sun." 

Cross pointed out that NTC has arranged for distribution of the protective sunscreen material to more than 300 targeted cosmetics markets worldwide. He said consumers should begin to see sunscreens that incorporate NanoGard(TM) titania as the primary effective and chemical-free ingredient at retailers in 1996. 

The ability of NTC's titania to protect skin from the damaging effects of the sun's ultraviolet rays while remaining transparent also makes the material excellent for use in coating fabrics to guard against fading, Cross notes. "Drapery and upholstery fabrics exposed to the sun will retain their colors considerably longer when protected with our titania. It helps keep the sun out and the color in," he said. 

Consumers also may see NTC's iron oxide soon in women's cover and blush cosmetics, where it offers deep, rich colors without caking problems. The company has been working with a major cosmetic manufacturer to tap that market. 

Ceramics Hold Substantial Promise 

Although consumer applications of NTC's materials represent strong market potential for the company, Cross sees commercial usage, particularly in various forms of ceramics, as holding even greater promise in terms of market demand. "Automotive engineers have long recognized that ceramic engine components far surpass their metal counterparts in their ability to withstand high temperatures and resist wear," he said. "The barrier to using ceramics has always been cost, not in raw materials, but in their fabrication." 

As Cross explained, fabricating a ceramic part traditionally has required the molding or casting of a ceramic blank. The blank then needed to be machined to its final high tolerance shape, a process that typically took hours because of the material's resistance to even diamond cutting tools. "Those hours of machine and labor time are what have kept ceramic components on the drawing boards instead of inside the diesel or gasoline engine," Cross pointed out. 

In contrast, the super-small size of NTC's ceramic powders enable the manufacture of high-tolerance components through a relatively simple molding process. The molded part is as dimensionally accurate as its machined counterpart, but can be produced in a matter of minutes rather than multiple hours. Cross said that NTC is working with Lockheed Corporation, as well as leading engine manufacturers, to refine this technology and believes it will lead to numerous commercial applications before the end of this decade. 

Cross also stated that the company's ceramics are being tested for a wide range of other applications, and sees electronic component manufacturers as a promising outlet for NTC ceramic production thanks to the material's heat resistance. "The trend in electronics is that small is better, so component manufacturers are constantly trying to squeeze more things into less space," he notes. "That crowding produces heat, and too much heat will cause the substrate to warp and the product to malfunction. A molded ceramic substrate wouldn't have that problem." 

Nanophase's scientists are also exploring applications for other materials their technology can create. Since the company's founding in 1989 as an offshoot from research at Argonne National Laboratory, it has produced nanocrystalline powders from a diverse range of raw materials, including gold, silver, chromium, yttrium, silicon, cobalt, nickel and copper. 

Future Is Bright 

As CEO Cross points out, the company's future indeed looks bright. "We see sunscreen and cosmetics applications as being at least a $50 million revenue source for us within a very few years," he said. "Ceramics will at least equal, and probably exceed, that amount, and we have yet to gauge the potential of materials still in the research and development stage. 

"I'm confident that we're in the process of spawning an entirely new industry category," he continued. "All of us at Nanophase Technologies are excited about that future, because we have the technology that not only gives us a position of industry leadership today on a worldwide basis, but the momentum to stay in the forefront as the industry expands." 

Cross' enthusiasm is tacitly shared by others from the scientific community. Research and Development magazine bestowed its "R&D 100" award to the company in September, 1995, an honor granted to what the publication views as one of the world's 100 most significant technological developments for the year.

 Article 64 *******************    


UCSF Scientists View Smallest Motors, Vital For Life 

1,066 words 
11 April 1996
04:50 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1996, Business Wire) 

SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--April 10, 1996--Life depends on the smallest motors known. They're inside cells, they're less than one-millionth of an inch in size, and UC San Francisco scientists are now dissecting how these small machines work. 

By applying the most advanced laboratory techniques, the researchers working on these tiny biological motors have finally been able to see how they are built and to observe directly their movements along the tracks on which they ride, discoveries highlighted on the cover of the latest issue of the prestigious journal Nature. 

"The most tiny motors are not man-made gadgets made via engineering feats in the field of nanotechnology," says Ron Vale, PhD. "Instead, they arise within living organisms and are themselves indispensable for life." 

The motors are zippy proteins that ferry cargo around on microscopic "railroad" tracks. They are responsible for muscle contraction, and enable a sperm cell to swim toward an egg. And as a fertilized egg divides, the motors ensure the accurate partitioning of genetic material among daughter cells. The motors continue to fulfill this role among the progeny of every dividing cell during the course of development and throughout the lifetime of a mature organism, Vale explains. 

The drug taxol, used to treat breast and ovarian cancer, works by interfering with the intracellular tracks on which the motors move, thereby wreaking havoc on dividing tumor cells, he adds. 

The custom-engineering of motor proteins to move microscopic materials, including non-biological materials, is not too far-fetched, nor is the idea of directly interfering with motor proteins as a way to fight cancer, according to Vale, the first scientist to discover a member of the smallest motor protein family, kinesin, in 1985. However, Vale says, both applications require first knowing the detailed structure of the motor, just as fixing a car requires knowledge of all of its parts. 

Vale, professor of pharmacology and biochemistry and pharmacology and associate investigator with the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, along with Robert Fletterick, PhD, professor of biochemistry and biophysics at UCSF, and their colleagues at UCSF now report major progress in motor protein research in two papers in the April 11 issue of Nature. 

Graduate student F. Jon Kull and post-doctoral fellow Elena P. Sablin used a technique called x-ray crystallography to determine the structures of kinesin, the motor first discovered by Vale, which hauls cargo in cells, and of NCD, which helps divide genetic material during cell division. Kull and Sablin were guided in their studies by Vale and Fletterick. 

The new information is also valuable for understanding how 40-or-so cargo-ferrying proteins in the kinesin family all move within human cells along a special gauge of railroad track, a long-stranded polymer called a microtubule. "These motors evolved early and they are everywhere," Vale says. "They play a role in fruit-fly development and in yeast cell-division." 

In a third article appearing in the April 4 issue of Nature, Vale and colleagues from Osaka University in Japan report using a new microscopic technique called "internal reflection fluorescence microscopy" to trace the movement of a single kinesin protein along a microtubule by spotlighting the protein with fluorescent dye. This work shows that kinesin may move in a hand-over-hand manner similar to a person climbing a rope. 

The kinesin motors are more than twice as efficient as automobiles, Vale says. They are powered not by gasoline, but by ATP, the energy currency of living cells. For their size, the kinesin motors are about four times faster than a speeding sports car, moving at about 100 lengths-per-second, compared to 25 lengths-per-second for the racer, according to Vale. 

The structure of one end of the motor protein specifies the cellular cargo it will attach to and haul. The opposite end serves as the motor, mechanically moving the protein in ways that are still unclear. 

"One of the oldest questions in biology is how do things move? The molecular answer to that question is still unknown, but the details may unfold in the next few years," Vale says. 

Kinesin motor proteins consist of two entwined strands. As ATP is consumed inside the motor, the two strands somehow act as feet to propel the protein along the microtubule in very quick steps, eight nanometers long. Vale believes that the protein acts as a complicated spring, in which a small change in protein shape at the site of ATP attachment is amplified like a Rube Goldberg device, ultimately causing the protein's feet to move along the track. 

Clues to how the protein moves came from the unexpected surprise that the "carburetor," or ATP-burning region of the two kinesin family proteins described in Nature, is highly similar to that of the slightly larger cellular motors involved in muscle contraction, called the myosins, the researchers discovered. 

The UCSF team also discovered a striking structural similarity between this ATP-burning region and a comparable part of an important class of biological molecules called G proteins. G proteins use the chemical energy stored in another fuel, GTP, to communicate signals within individual cells. 

The similarity between the G proteins and the motor proteins was previously unsuspected and raises new questions about energy conversion by proteins, Vale says. 

The UCSF researchers also found that the two kinesin family motors, NCD and kinesin itself, have remarkably similar structures. Yet, the small differences that are present somehow cause the two motors to move in opposite directions on microtubules, another mystery the UCSF team hopes to solve. 

Crystallographers Fletterick and Kull have paid a visit to geologists at the California Academy of Sciences in San Francisco to obtain mineral samples that they hope will shed more light on how mechanical movement results from interactions between fuel-driven kinesin family proteins and the tracks they ride on. 

While microtubule polymers are well-ordered repeating structures, the crystal structures of the minerals are even better known at the level of individual atoms. In theory, it should be possible for kinesin family motor proteins to interact with the mineral surfaces and perhaps to move across them, according to Fletterick. "We're going to tickle kinesin's feet and see what happens," he says.

SOUTH SAN FRANCISCO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--April 29, 1996-- Gryphon Sciences announced today the signing of a collaboration with SmithKline Beecham (NYSE:SBH). 

The agreement focuses on Gryphon's Dextroceutical(TM) technology for the discovery of mirror image proteins (proteins made entirely or partially of D-amino acids) as potential pharmaceuticals. Under the terms of the agreement, Gryphon will synthesize certain D-proteins and SmithKline Beecham will assess the biological characteristics of the target molecules. Both companies will share in joint inventions from the project. Other terms of the agreement were not disclosed. 

"We are very happy to be able to work with SmithKline Beecham to explore the pharmaceutical potential of D-proteins," said Janice M. LeCocq, Gryphon's chief executive officer. "If we are successful, we could be on the leading edge of a powerful new class of pharmaceuticals, ones which can address the complexity of protein-protein interactions with the extended half-life and lower immunogenicity more characteristic of small molecule drugs. It is an exciting frontier and we're pleased to have such a strong partner in this exploration." 

Gryphon Sciences possesses proprietary chemical synthesis technologies which the company is applying to: 1) creation of a new class of pharmaceuticals based on the use of mirror image proteins (Dextraceutical(TM) technology), and 2) the synthesis of large, complex multifunctional molecules for next generation vaccines and gene therapy (Nanoceutical(TM) products), and 3) chemical synthesis of new proteins and protein analogues for enhancing productivity of new molecule discovery programs. Gryphon can precisely synthesize large, complex protein and protein-like molecules with a speed, efficiency and purity not available through conventional peptide synthesis technology. Gryphon's chemistries are not limited to "biological" components, enabling synthesis of structures which are impossible to clone and express through bioengineering. As a result, Gryphon technologies provide access to new frontiers in pharmaceutical discovery, and an entree to emerging fields in nanotechnology. 

SmithKline Beecham -- one of the world's leading healthcare companies -- discovers, develops, manufactures and markets pharmaceuticals, vaccines, over-the-counter medicines and health-related consumer products and provides healthcare services including clinical laboratory testing, disease management and pharmaceutical benefit management.

NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--May 7, 1996--Harris & Harris Group, Inc. announced today that its affiliate, Nanophase Technologies Corp., has placed privately $7.45 million of Series E Convertible Preferred Stock, which is convertible into Nanophase common stock at $2.25 per share. 

Harris & Harris Group owns 1,162,204 shares of Nanophase Series D Convertible Preferred Stock, which is convertible into Nanophase common stock at $1.00 per share, for which Harris & Harris Group paid a total of $1,162,204 in two separate transactions, in October, 1994 and November, 1995. Harris & Harris Group's fully-diluted equity interest in Nanophase is now 7.6 percent.

All valuations are subject to quarterly review by the Investment and Valuation Committee of Harris & Harris Group's Board of Directors. 

Nanophase is a privately held company that has developed a unique process, based on patented technology licensed from Argonne National Laboratory, to synthesize crystals of nanometric dimensions. A nanometer is one billionth of a meter or 10,000 times smaller than the diameter of a human hair. By controlling both particle size and the spacing between particles, Nanophase is able to produce materials with a rich variety of physical properties. Since its formation in 1989, Nanophase has successfully scaled up its technology from a laboratory process to a production facility capable of producing tonnage quantities of nanometric size crystals.

National Institutes Of Health Awards Curagen $4.8 Million For Next Generation Of Instruments For Human Genome Project 

855 words 
7 May 1996

Business Wire

(Copyright (c) 1996, Business Wire) 

BRANFORD, Conn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--May 7, 1996--In one of the largest technology development grants ever, the National Center for Human Genome Research has awarded $4.8 million to CuraGen Corporation of Branford, CT to develop the next generation of instruments to decipher the human genome. 

CuraGen's collaborators in the grant are MIT's Whitehead Institute and Soane BioSciences. This grant complements CuraGen's participation with MIT's Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research in a separate award announced in mid-April, which ensures the use of CuraGen's instruments in pilot projects to sequence the human genome. Dr. Gregory T. Went, CuraGen's Senior V.P., is a co-investigator with Dr. Eric Lander of the Whitehead Institute on the pilot project. The joint participation on these two awards is synergistic: CuraGen provides access to the most advanced hardware and software available for decoding genetic information, while the Whitehead Institute contributes expertise in the large scale workflow and informatics which it previously successfully applied to complete the genetic maps that index the genome. Corporate collaborators include co-investigator Dr. Herbert Hooper, V.P. of Soane BioSciences of Hayward, California, leaders in advanced separation materials for electrophoresis. 

Dr. Francis Collins, Director of the National Center for Human Genome Research, part of the National Institutes of Health, stated, "CuraGen's research project is part of the new technology that will push us down the path to much better sequencing technology, and help ensure the timely and cost-effective completion of the Human Genome Project's most ambitious goal." 

In the Project's final phase, the 1990's equivalent of the quest to reach the moon, the National Center for Human Genome Research has set out to determine the precise order of the string of three billion chemical units that contain the 100,000 genes arranged on each of our 23 chromosomes. Technology to decode the human genome will identify hereditary information responsible for the life processes that take us from conception to death, and help reveal the secrets that may lead to cures for complex diseases such as cancer, heart disease, diabetes, mental illness and over 3500 other known devastating disorders. This blueprint for a human being will serve as the foundation of pharmaceutical and biotechnology research for the 21st century. 

The $4.8 million award will be used to develop instrumentation that will be tested at CuraGen and put into operation at the Whitehead Institute, one of the largest federally funded genome centers. CuraGen will lead this effort with the support of Dr. Lincoln Stein, Director of Informatics, and Dr. Trevor Hawkins, Director of Sequencing and Automation, at the Whitehead Institute. Starting as early as 1999, sequencing platforms will be distributed to pilot centers chosen to complete the human genome sequence. 

This award will enable a 10-fold increase in speed in CuraGen instrumentation that is already 10 times faster than commercially available systems. "This NIH award puts us in a unique position, not only to continue development of the most effective systems for gene sequencing and disease gene discovery, but also to witness the power of these systems in operation at both MIT and CuraGen," observed Dr. Jonathan M. Rothberg, CuraGen's CEO. Dr. Trevor Hawkins, Director of Whitehead's Sequencing and Automation, said, "Our collaboration with CuraGen will enhance profoundly the efficiency with which the human genome project can be completed, and the rate at which genomic information can be created." In addition to DNA sequencing, CuraGen's instrumentation enables all major DNA analysis techniques required for disease gene discovery, including genotyping and gene expression analysis. This flexibility is made possible through a unique combination of advanced imaging technology, microfabricated channels, and adaptive pattern recognition software. 

This is the second time CuraGen has landed two prestigious back-to-back awards. In 1994 CuraGen became the first small company to win two coveted ATP awards from the National Institute of Standards and Technology in a single year. These represented projects in excess of $10 million. "Together with the recent NIH awards, CuraGen has assumed what is arguably the most potent and sustainable proprietary position on technology with application to genomics," stated Dr. Went. 

CuraGen Corp., a leading genomic biotechnology firm, continues to develop new generations of tools to aid the rapid discovery of disease-specific genes for pharmaceutical development. The instrumentation developed at CuraGen serves as the backbone of a full-service genomics program using proprietary informatics, data mining tools, and workflow to integrate expression analysis, positional cloning, and large-scale sequencing efforts. The company is leveraging its role in the Human Genome Project to enable and coordinate large-scale genomic assaults on disease through its Internet-based GeneScape(TM) system. In addition to MIT's Whitehead Institute and Soane BioSciences, current collaborators include Yale's Comprehensive Cancer Center, Cornell's National Nanofabrication Facility, and Wyeth-Ayerst Research, a division of American Home Products.

Aurora Biosciences And Packard Instrument Company Form Strategic Alliance: Will Build Ultra-High-Throughput Screening Systems To Accelerate Drug Discovery 

843 words 
20 May 1996

Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1996, Business Wire) 

LA JOLLA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--May 20, 1996--Aurora Biosciences Corporation and Packard Instrument Company today announced a strategic alliance to develop and market miniaturized instrumentation systems for ultra-high-throughput drug screening. 

The systems will employ Packard's leading-edge instrumentation technology, optimized for Aurora's novel fluorescent screens. As part of the agreement, Packard received an exclusive sublicense to market certain of Aurora's fluorescence assay reagents to not-for-profit research institutions. Packard also made a $1 million investment in Aurora series B preferred stock. 

The co-development project between Packard and Aurora will focus in three areas. First, the companies will develop very high-density assay plates, called "Nano-Platesx," suitable for use with Aurora's mammalian cell-based fluorescence assays. 

Second, they will develop computer-controlled robotic arrays of miniature pipettes for aspirating and dispensing reagents and samples in nanoliter (one millionth of a milliliter) volumes. 

Finally, the companies will develop optical imagers that can quantify and analyze thousands of fluorescence assays within a few minutes. 

Following the development of these products, Aurora will have up to three years' exclusive rights to market them for use in ultra-high-throughput screening and in automated synthetic chemistry. After that time, Aurora and Packard will share co-exclusive rights for these markets. 

Packard holds exclusive rights to market products developed through the collaboration in other areas including the diagnostics, cellular/biomolecular research, and DNA sequencing markets. 

"We are delighted and privileged to become partners with the acknowledged leader in screening instrumentation," said Timothy J. Rink, MD, ScD, chairman, president and chief executive officer of Aurora. "Packard's outstanding track record of innovation, service and quality, combined with our platform of new assay technologies is a winning formula to provide uniquely flexible and cost-efficient solutions for our customers." 

"These new systems will provide the basis for a quantum leap in sensitivity, throughput, versatility and cost-effectiveness to meet the unprecedented need in the pharmaceutical and biotech industries for extremely rapid screening," said Harry Stylli, Ph.D., senior director of screen technology at Aurora. 

"Current screening bottlenecks result from the need to test large numbers of novel biomolecular targets emerging form genomics with the millions of candidate drugs available from combinatorial chemistry, natural product sources and existing `file' compounds." 

Richard McKernan, president of Packard noted that he views the alliance with Aurora as cornerstone development towards more productive screening systems. 

"Aurora's chemistries developed by the renowned Dr. Roger Tsien at the University of California present Packard with the opportunity to fully exploit the potential of its new imaging and liquid handling technologies. "Jointly, we can develop systems that will deliver significant productivity increases to laboratories involved in drug discovery." 

Staf C. van Cauter, vice president of business development at Packard confirmed that the combination of both companies' core competencies may lead to nanotechnology breakthroughs in various fields. 

"The ultra-high sensitivity of Aurora's fluorescence assays, combined with Packard's single-photon imaging and nanoliter liquid handling capabilities will permit researchers in cellular and molecular biology to do more tests, more quickly, at significantly reduced costs. We believe that this is a major step forward toward the implementation of nanotechnology in routine instrumentation." 

Aurora Biosciences Corporation's primary mission is to advance the drug discovery process by commercializing novel, automated systems for ultra-high-throughput screening. The company's systems primarily use fluorescence-based screens in mammalian cells, but are also adaptable for enzyme or receptor-ligand assays. 

Internal research and development efforts will focus on developing novel screens, and establishing screening systems at Aurora and in customers' facilities. The company will partner with industry leaders in adapting and developing robotics, informatics, compound and liquid handling systems, and miniaturized assay and detection devices. 

Aurora expects to set the new standard for drug screening and to enable multiple pharmaceutical and biotech customers to speed up the discovery of innovative medicines in return for research fees, milestone payments and product royalties. 

Aurora recently raised over $16.5 million in equity financing, and announced a collaboration with Sequana Therapeutics Inc. for functional analysis and screening of gene targets. 

Packard Instrument Company is a fast growing, privately owned company focused on the drug discovery market. With annual sales of $110 million, Packard's current scintillation and luminescence microplate readers and robotic liquid handling equipment are used by over 300 pharmaceutical and biotech companies worldwide. 

Over the last years, Packard has invested heavily in nanotechnology. In collaboration with Cambridge Imaging Ltd. (U.K.) and Microdrop AG (Germany), Packard has developed photon counting imaging and nanoliter liquid handling technology that will be implemented in next generation drug discovery systems.
