21:43 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1996, Business Wire) 

SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--June 21, 1996--Five San Jose State University professors have received awards from Research Corp., a foundation for the advancement of science. 

Two awards are Partners in Science Awards, which give qualified high school science teachers an opportunity to work with university scientists in research during summers. Two other awards are Cottrell College Science Awards, which support basic scientific research by professors. And the third award, a General Award, supports projects that will enhance science research or that bear on the infrastructure of science. 


Partners in Science Awards


The Partners in Science Program provides opportunities for high school science teachers to participate in college and university research under the guidance of faculty scientists. Such collaboration provides opportunities for professional growth and develops a broader understanding of the relationship between high school and college science education. 

Stephen E. Branz, professor of chemistry, and Brien R. Sparling of Live Oak High School will collaborate on a project titled, "Investigations of Fullerene Solubilities." The award has been cosponsored by the Bristol-Meyers Squibb Co. through funds contributed to Research Corp. 

Joseph F. Becker, professor of physics, and Eric E. Smith of Aptos High School will collaborate on a project titled, "Miniaturized Laser Spectrometer Measurements of Stable Carbon and Oxygen Isotopes." 


General Award


As part of the Partners in Science Program a three-year award also has been made to Roy K. Okuda, associate professor of chemistry. The General Awards Program supports projects, within specific fields of activity, that fall outside the regular programs. 


Cottrell College Science Awards


Two professors also have received Cottrell College Science Awards. The Cottrell College Science Awards Program supports basic research in chemistry, physics, and astronomy at public and private, predominately undergraduate colleges. 

The award will allow Paul S. Wagenknecht, assistant professor of chemistry, to research his project, "An Investigation of the Role that Lewis Acids and Constrained Geometries Play in Small Molecule Redox Transformations." 

Brenda Kesler, assistant professor of chemistry, will conduct her research on a project titled, "Asymmetric Functionalization of Isolated Double Bonds Via Chiral Selenium Reagents." 

Research Corp. is one of the first U.S. foundations and the only one wholly devoted to the advancement of science and technology. Research Corp. makes between 200 and 300 awards annually.

Veeco Surface Metrology Receives $3M Order From Siemens; Siemens Buys Multiple Surface Profilers And Atomic Force Microscopes

428 words 
11 July 1996
17:26 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1996, Business Wire) 

PLAINVIEW, N.Y. and SEMICON WEST, BOOTH 502--(BUSINESS WIRE)--July 11, 1996--Veeco Surface Metrology has received an order in excess of $3M from Siemens Microelectronics Center GmbH & Co. OHG in Dresden, Germany. 

The order, which includes four Dektak(R) SXM atomic force microscopes and three Dektak 8200 automated surface profilers, will be used for DRAM manufacturing at Siemens' semiconductor fabs in Germany, France and England. 

"We are pleased to have been chosen as a full-service provider of surface metrology equipment by Siemens," said Dr. Timothy Stultz, vice president and general manager of Veeco Surface Metrology. "This multi-fab order reflects confidence in our global service and support, and the synergy between our automated surface profilers and atomic force microscopes." 

The Dektak SXM atomic force microscope (AFM) is used to monitor semiconductor manufacturing processes by providing critical dimension (CD) measurements of lines and spaces as small as 0.25 micron. It gives repeatable measurements in three dimensions with an accuracy comparable to transmission electron microscopy (TEM). This reduces the need for time-consuming and costly wafer cross-sectional inspection, which is often used to measure depth and sidewall angles of submicron features. The Dektak SXM is an automated, in-line production metrology tool that provides non-contact, non-destructive nanometer scale measurements. Exclusive scanning and probe tip technologies enable the system to profile vertical sidewalls and even re-entrant sidewalls. 

The Dektak 8200 automated surface profiler enables semiconductor manufacturers to continually monitor and perfect key aspects of process performance including deposition uniformity, etch rate and chemical mechanical polishing (CMP) planarity. This automated surface profiler is capable of repeatedly measuring wafer topography and the vertical heights of semiconductor thin films to within 10 angstroms. At its heart is Veeco's new SoftScan II low-inertia sensor, which enables non-destructive measurements on product wafers, even on very soft films such as photoresist. 

Veeco Instruments Inc. (NASDAQ: VECO), headquartered in Plainview, N.Y., is a worldwide leader in precision ion etching deposition and surface metrology equipment for high growth microelectronics applications such as semiconductors, thin-film magnetic heads and flat panel displays, as well as a broad range of industrial applications. Veeco Surface Metrology, based in Santa Barbara, Calif., is a wholly owned subsidiary of Veeco Instruments Inc. Global sales and service offices are located in the U.S., Europe and the Asia-Pacific market.

Business Wire

(Copyright (c) 1996, Business Wire) 

SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--July 16, 1996--OnTrak Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:ONTK), a leading provider of semiconductor capital equipment for chemical mechanical planarization (CMP), today announced that it has significantly expanded capabilities and cleanroom space at its research and development (R&D) facility in Milpitas, Calif. In addition to housing additional R&D space for both the company's cleaning and polishing product lines and a dedicated metrology lab, the 4,900-square-foot cleanroom also offers increased customer demonstration capability. 

According to OnTrak's Executive Vice President and Chief Technical Officer Dr. Wilbur Krusell, the expanded facility will enhance OnTrak's ability to support its worldwide customer base. "OnTrak's customers recognize the value of our cleaning technology to the overall CMP process, which is continuing to be adopted for IC manufacturing worldwide. Our cleanroom expansion will enable us to accommodate customer requests for demonstrations more efficiently, as well as provide complete in-house demonstration capability from the process stage through characterization," Krusell added. 

Originally 350 square feet, the Class 10 demonstration lab has been expanded to 600 square feet and includes two DSS-200 cleaning systems, which are devoted to process development and customer demonstrations. The R&D facility also includes a 2,000-square-foot Class 10,000 cleaning R&D lab, which will provide OnTrak with more space to house new products under development. An additional 2,000-square-foot Class 10,000 pre-production and sub-component testing area is dedicated to the Aurora polisher. 

OnTrak's on-site metrology capability, which previously included a surface particle counter in the Class 10 cleaning lab and a large-stage atomic force microscope, has been augmented significantly with the addition of a 300 square-foot Class 100 CMP metrology lab. This new lab features more than 10 metrology tools, enabling OnTrak technicians to perform thin film measurement, surface profiling, resistivity measurement and feature size measurement after demonstration wafers have been polished and subsequently cleaned. With the added capability, OnTrak reports that the company can efficiently polish, clean and characterize wafers on-site, offering added value and convenience to its local and international customers. 

OnTrak Systems, Inc. is a leading provider of semiconductor capital equipment for CMP. Its primary product, the DSS-200, is a double-sided, single-wafer cleaning system used in a variety of advanced applications. OnTrak is headquartered in San Jose, Calif., and has sales, service and manufacturer's representative offices in strategic locations worldwide. The company's common stock is traded on The Nasdaq Stock Market under the symbol ONTK.

PLAINVIEW, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--July 25, 1996--Veeco Instruments Inc. (NASD: VECO) announced today record sales, operating and net income for the second quarter and six months ended June 30, 1996. 

For the second quarter of 1996, net sales increased 43% to $25.1 million, from $17.5 million for the corresponding quarter of 1995. Operating income rose 61% to $3,251,000 from $2,020,000. Net income increased 42% to $2,106,000 from $1,482,000 for the second quarter of 1995. The increase in sales reflects significant growth in Ion Beam System sales driven by continued use of Veeco Microetch(TM) in manufacturing high density hard drive memory products. 

For the six months ended June 30, 1996, net sales increased 45% to a record $45.7 million from $31.6 million for the same period in 1995. Operating income rose 75% to $5,936,000 from $3,397,000. Net income increased 52% to $3,916,000 from $2,578,000 for the first half of 1995. The sales growth was led by Ion Beam Systems (+71%) followed by Surface Metrology (+34%) and Industrial Measurement (+15%). 

Earnings per share were $.35 for the second quarter of 1996 as compared to $.29 for the second quarter of 1995, and $.66 for the first six months of 1996 as compared to $.51 for the first six months of 1995. These increases were achieved despite an effective tax rate of 37.8% for the first six months of 1996 as compared to 24.4% in 1995 due to utilization of NOL benefits in 1995. Weighted average shares outstanding were 5,958,000 for the 1996 second quarter as compared to 5,123,000 in the second quarter of 1995. For the first six months of 1996, weighted shares outstanding were 5,925,000 as compared to 5,100,000 for the corresponding period in 1995. 

Bookings increased 13% for the second quarter of 1996 to $25.1 million as compared to $22.2 million for the second quarter of 1995. Bookings for the first six months of 1996 were a record $50.5 million, an increase of 29% over bookings of $39.3 million for the corresponding period in 1995. The book/bill ratio was 1.0 for the second quarter of 1996 and 1.10 for the first six months of 1996. 

"We are pleased by Veeco's strong second quarter performance," said Edward H. Braun, chairman, CEO and president. "Our record sales demonstrate the worldwide acceptance of and demand for our products, particularly for next-generation hard drive and advanced semiconductor applications. Most of our sales growth this past six months was attributable to Veeco's advanced ion beam systems used in the manufacture of thin film magnetic heads, and our SXM Atomic Force Microscope used in .35 micron semiconductor device metrology."

Speaking on the 30th of August to the International Symposium on the Physics and Chemistry of Ice, attended by 200 other leading international chemists and physicists, Dr. Lo detailed information on what ATG has termed the Ie crystal structure described as "the manipulation and isolation of molecular electrical forces inherent in microscopic particles." The crystal structures were illustrated with color pictures taken with electron beam and atomic force microscopes and by laser autocorrelation measurements. Stable at room temperature and pressure, bottled samples of the material were presented to symposium participants. 

The first product to be developed with these crystal structures is a combustion catalyst proven effective by Dr. Selim Senkan, UCLA Professor of Chemical Engineering, called "The Force." The Force, an airborne fuel combustion additive, utilizes environmentally benign, highly charged particles made from solid, micron-sized, hydrogen and oxygen ice-like particles. which, when mixed with the incoming combustion air, causes a cleaner, more efficient burning of fuel in the engine. Completed tests conducted at Dr. Senkan's laboratory show reductions in methane emissions by as much as 50% and increases in LPG (propane) combustion efficiency by 27%. Tests conducted by Environmental Testing Corporation of Orange, California, an EPA accepted laboratory, show increases of 3 to 4% in fuel economy with reductions in harmful emissions. These tests results are consistent with previous tests conducted by the German DEKRA laboratory, Czech Republic Institute for Research of Motor Vehicles, Engine Division and by the Environmental Protection Department of Hungary. 

Controlled field tests by Bob Sikorsky, nationally syndicated automotive columnist, and others, showed comparable or better results in fuel economy. Sikorsky has written referring to The Force "It's a great new product that really works at delivering more power and fuel economy, not to mention a much cleaner engine with reduced emissions. I have personally used the product for over one year now, with excellent results."

Nanocor previously announced plans to spend approximately $3 million on research activities and business development during 1996. Maul said the Aberdeen study would not have a meaningful impact on those expenditures.

Continued Expansion of Position Sensor Market Predicted in Europe 

1,013 words 
3 December 1996
18:27 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1996, Business Wire) 

LONDON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Dec. 3, 1996--The market for position sensors in Europe is projected to be worth $1.41 billion in 1996, equivalent to 23.5 million units. Although recession has slowed growth considerably, it has not wiped it out, and the market is forecast to be worth $1.78 billion in 2002. 

These data come in an instrumentation and controls study from international marketing consultant Frost & Sullivan, which analyzes and forecasts the market for nine types of sensors in eight national or regional markets to the year 2002. 

It also includes analysis of the major technology trends and the core issues' future success in the marketplace. 

Generally speaking, the sensor market is forecast to expand over the coming years, as the need for accurate sensing in the manufacturing process is increasing. In fact, the recession has led to a greater awareness of the benefits of precise sensing during the production process, which has resulted in continuous growth for the sensor industry, albeit at lower rates than seen prior to the recession. 

Technologies with a higher degree of accuracy and versatility are forecast to show higher growth rates than the simple types of sensors. 

According to the report, the single most important type of position sensor is the proximity sensor, accounting for 36.8 percent of market revenues in 1995. The second most important group of sensors is a mixed bag of "other" sensors, including potentiometers, optoelectronic sensors, fibreoptic sensors, integral sensors, inductosyns and limit switches. Together, these account for around one-fifth of revenues. 

Hall effect sensors, LVDTs, RVDTs and resolvers are forecast to lose their importance to other sensor technologies in the coming years. 

Frost & Sullivan's research has established that Germany is by far the largest market for position sensors, contributing some 48 percent of revenues in 1995. France comes some way behind at just over 11 percent, and the UK is a close third. The importance of the German market is expected to increase slightly during the forecast period. 

In its analysis of the major technological trends impacting the market, the study notes that computer integrated manufacturing (CIM) systems are growing in importance. CIM systems are based on a link established between the actual execution of a sensing process, the electronic control element and a central computer software system, and permit the central control of all key elements on the factory floor. 

Also, the growth of smart sensors is highlighted. Smart sensors are devices which carry an incorporated basic electronic circuit that can conduct highly complex data processing and control functions. Due to their design, they allow an immediate interference with the data-gathering and sensing process and thus provide an easy way to apply changes and adjustments, such as regulation of the sensing distance or angle. 

On the subject of the competitive structure of the market, Frost & Sullivan says that the vast majority of companies are medium to small in size, and most are active throughout Europe. Transnational companies have the advantage of being able to use their existing distribution network which already serve other industries, allowing them to access markets without overcoming the same hurdles as smaller suppliers. 

Competition is dominated by technological requirements and the ability of suppliers to satisfy customers' needs by offering an acceptable level of service and support as well as competitive prices. 

Three factors are identified which are expected to influence the future development of the position sensors market in Europe. The leading of these is the growing demand -- enhanced by the recession -- to cut costs of energy, raw materials, lead-times, personnel and warehousing even further. Also significant are the growing necessity for effective safety and environment protective measurements, and the industry's ability and flexibility to provide individual and custom-made systems solutions. 

Companies participating in this market include: Allegro Microsystems Inc., Allen-Bradley, AMP Deutschland GmbH, Amroh Electronics GmbH, Amtec GmbH, Analog Devices, ASM Automation, Baumer Electric AG, Bernstein-Senso Plus GmbH, Brodersen Teknik AS, Burgess Micro Switch Company Ltd, Control Techniques, EG&G Heimann Optoelectronics GmbH, Erwin Sick GmbH, Festo Holding Company, Fogale Nanotech, FOS Messtechnik GmbH, Hamamatsu Photonics, Hans Turck GmbH & Co KG, Heidenhain GmbH, Heimann Optoelectronics GmbH, Hengstler GmbH, HL-Planar Technik GmbH, Hohner Elektrotechnik KG, Honeywell Ltd, I C Msures, Idec Elektrotechnik GmbH, Ident, IFM Electronic GmbH, Inducoder GmbH, Interlink Electronics Europe SARL, International Electronics & Engineering (IEE), Internet BV, Keyence UK Ltd, Laser 2000, Laser Components GmbH, Leane International SRL, Lucas Schaevitz, MCB Industrie, Meder Electronic GmbH, Micro-Epsilon Messtechnik GmbH & Co., Microtel Tecnologie Elettroniche Srl, Muirhead Vactric Components, Multiprox NV, Murata Elektronik, Novotechnik Stiftung GmbH, Omron Electronics Ltd, Osmor Technologies Ltd, Penny & Giles Position Sensors Ltd, Pepperl & Fuchs GmbH, Philips Semiconductors, Photonetics GmbH, PIL-Sensoren GmbH, Polytech GmbH, Pulsotronic GmbH & Co., RAP-Sensoric GmbH, Sagem (Socit d'Application Gnrales d'Electricit et de Mcanique), Saia Industrial Electronics and Components AG, Seikosha Europe GmbH, Selcom, Sensorex, Sextant Avionique, Siemens AG, Sonotec, Steeg & Reuter Przisionsoptik GmbH, TdP (Technique de Pointe) SA, Telemecanique, Temic Mikrosysteme, Tetra, Transducer Systems Inc., Turck, TWK-Elektronik GmbH, Vacuumschmelze GmbH, and Wenglor Sensoric Electronische Gerte GmbH.

Tencor Instruments introduces breakthrough metrology system for disk drive industry; New Tencor HRP-100 High Resolution Profiler's advanced capabilities significantly enhance Tencor's product presence in the disk drive industry 

793 words 
23 January 1997
21:30 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

MILPITAS, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jan. 23, 1997-Tencor Instruments (Nasdaq:TNCR) today introduced a breakthrough metrology system for monitoring critical processes in the manufacture of magnetoresistive (MR) and inductive heads, as well as magnetic and optical disks. 

The Tencor HRP-100 combines the proven measurement repeatability, ease-of-use and long-scan capability of Tencor's family of surface profilers with the micro-analysis and imaging capability previously offered only by laboratory-oriented products, such as atomic force microscopes (AFMs). 

According to Tencor, the HRP-100 is the first metrology system to offer disk drive manufacturers the combined monitoring capability traditionally achieved by two process tools-an in-line profilometer and an off-line AFM tool. The Tencor HRP-100 will help enable manufacturers to bring the high-resolution surface analysis and characterization necessary for MR head and laser texture disk development to in-line process monitoring. By addressing this dual need, the HRP-100 significantly broadens Tencor's metrology product line for the rapidly evolving disk drive industry. 

Dennis Fortino, Tencor vice president and Metrology division general manager, affirmed that the Tencor HRP-100 provides the disk drive industry with advanced monitoring capabilities. "The disk drive industry is currently experiencing the process challenges associated with next-generation products and performance levels. This is creating a need for advanced surface monitoring to accommodate both MR head and disk media development," said Fortino. "We worked extensively with our customers to develop a unique system that will help the disk drive industry meet the challenges of developing more new products with increasingly higher performance levels." He added that sales to the disk drive industry represented approximately seven percent of Tencor's overall sales in the first three quarters of 1996, and anticipates the HRP-100 will contribute to this figure in 1997. 

Due to its increased sensitivity, MR head technology has become the standard over inductive heads in addressing the decrease in bit-area associated with increasing areal densities. Additionally, disk media have become increasingly smooth to accommodate higher storage densities. These advancing technologies are creating new process monitoring challenges. These increasingly complex process requirements, combined with ever-shrinking geometries, have created the need for a new metrology system such as the Tencor HRP-100 that combines high-resolution surface analysis with in-line ruggedness. 

Phil Devin, vice president and chief analyst of independent market research firm Dataquest (San Jose, Calif.), explained that laser texture disk and MR head technologies are both critical to the advancement of the disk drive industry. "In 2000, areal density of production drives is projected to be 8-Gbit/in2, and demand in this industry is expected to reach 215 million units per year," noted Devin. "This progressive increase in storage density and demand will require next-generation, multi-functional process technologies for MR head and disk media development to be on the production floor in the near future," added Devin. 

The Tencor HRP-100 utilizes Tencor's proprietary Dual Stage Imaging (DSI) technology, enabling the system to provide macro-to-micro imaging (i.e., features from 50mm down to 0.25m) with scan lengths up to 200mm and lateral resolution down to 1nm. This combination of macro- and micro-imaging, unavailable on any other surface profiling system, allows the HRP-100 to capture more surface detail-necessary for optimizing the development and production of MR heads and disks. The Tencor HRP-100 also incorporates Tencor's UltraLite sensor, allowing it to scan surfaces with a constant force as low as 0.05 mg with no damage to the disk or head surface-critical to manufacturing strategies that only process production disks and heads. 

Currently in beta test with several key customers, the HRP-100 is scheduled to begin production shipments in the second quarter 1997. 

About Tencor: Tencor Instruments, founded in 1976, is a recognized leader in the design and manufacture of innovative wafer defect inspection, software-based yield management, film measurement and metrology systems used in semiconductor manufacturing and related industries. 

The company reported record revenues of $97.0 million for the quarter ended September 30, 1996. Corporate offices are located in Milpitas, Calif., with sales and service offices worldwide. Tencor's World Wide Web site is located at http://www.tencor.com

Sea Grant News and Notes From Around the Nation 

964 words 
25 February 1997

Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

WASHINGTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Feb. 25, 1997--The following was released today by the National Sea Grant College Program: 

SEA GRANT NEWS AND NOTES FROM AROUND THE NATION -- FEB. 25, 1997 


GENETIC DETECTIVES IDENTIFY DISEASE-CAUSING MICROBES


Modern genetic technology is paving the way to faster, more reliable tests for detecting seafood-borne pathogens that can cause illnesses ranging from minor gastrointestinal complaints to fatal consequences. 

Mississippi-Alabama Sea Grant Researcher, Asim K. Bej, is using polymerase chain reaction (PCR) DNA amplification as the basis for a new method to detect pathogens such as Vibrio vulnificus, V. cholerae, V. parahaemolyticus, and Salmonella spp. in oysters. Using PCR, researchers can make millions of copies of a specific gene or gene segment unique to each of these pathogens in a relatively short period of time. 

Bej's approach of PCR technique tests for a number of specific pathogens simultaneously in a single amplification reaction. Other attractive features of the procedure are accuracy, dependability, and the reduction of processing time of samples from seven days or more -- required by current microbiological and biochemical methods -- to under two days. A number of biotechnology companies are exploring commercial development of the procedure. 

Bej and his colleagues at the Food and Drug Administration Seafood Laboratory in Dauphin Island, AL are also using PCR to develop a database of DNA "PCR-fingerprints" of clinical and environmental strains of V. vulnificus that can be used to identify the potential pathogenic strain and the reef from which the diseased oysters originated. 

Researchers hope that these new methods for monitoring pathogens in shellfish and seafood will decrease the disease outbreaks, thereby increasing the public's confidence in the safety of seafood. 


   CONTACT: Asim. K. Bej, Mississippi-Alabama Sea Grant Researcher,
205/934-9857; E-Mail: abcj(At)uab.edu
SAFETY IN NUMBERS: CHANGING TROUT STOCKS MAY LOWER PCB RISK


The potential human heath risk posed by the toxic contaminant PCB in Lake Michigan fish could be significantly reduced by changing the mix of species stocked into the lake according to University of Wisconsin Sea Grant Researcher, Stephen Carpenter. 

Carpenter reports that if fisheries managers stocked steelhead instead of lake trout, anglers who catch and eat Lake Michigan trout would be exposed to far fewer PCBs. This is because steelhead, also known as rainbow trout, accumulate only about one-eighth of the PCBs in their flesh as do lake trout. Although the manufacture of PCBs was banned in 1976, the contaminant breaks down slowly in the environment and can still be found in the Great Lakes. It is one in a group of chemical compounds suspected of causing reproductive health problems in humans. 

Carpenter's suggestion to change fish stocking practices would not hasten an overall PCB decline, but rather would target contaminant levels in fish, since fish consumption is one obvious way that humans come in contact with PCBs. Because most Lake Michigan sport fish are bred in hatcheries and stocked into the lake, fisheries managers have a great deal of control over the species mix anglers catch and people end up eating, Carpenter said. Carpenter's plan poses a problem, however. 

Lake trout nearly disappeared from their native Lake Michigan in the 1950s and rigorous efforts to restore their population have been the focus of many individual and organizations in the Great Lakes region. 

According to Carpenter, "It's certainly possible to continue working on lake trout restoration while stocking a lot of steelhead. Anglers can be encouraged to concentrate on steelhead and leave lake trout stocks alone." 


   CONTACT: Stephen Carpenter, University of Wisconsin Sea Grant
Researcher, 608/262-8690; E-Mail: srcarpen(At)facstaff.wisc.edu
MOLECULAR ENGINEERING TOOLS AID IN INDUSTRIAL WASTE CLEAN UP


Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) Sea Grant Researcher, Alan Hatton is working on a new, efficient way of cleaning industrial waste streams and aquifers contaminated with harmful hydrocarbons and other organic contaminants. 

For the past five years, Hatton and his coworkers have been focusing on the "micelle" -- a structure comprised of molecules whose two ends have differing properties: one end "hates" water and the other "loves" it. When in water, the two ends form a "water-hating" core surrounded by the remaining "water-loving" molecules. The result is a water-based solvent, with a core capable of absorbing large amounts of organic contaminants. 

Once micellar solution and wastewater mix, however, removing the contaminant-laden micelles from the treated water is a problem. Hatton and his team developed a technique in which the fresh micellar solution is pushed through hollow tubes whose walls serve as ultra-fine filters. The contaminated stream flows in the opposite direction in the space surrounding the hollow filter. 

The relatively large micelles cannot flow through the walls of the tubes, but the organic contaminants can, and will join the cores of the micelles. What results is a clean stream of treated water and a highly concentrated solution of contaminant-bearing micelles. One series of tests showed that a two percent micelle solution removed 80 percent of the contaminant toluene from a feed stream. 

Hatton and his colleagues are performing further experiments and hope to develop a method for cleaning and recycling used micelles.

Dr. Philip Chang and Hoseob Kim Join Etec


Dr. Philip Chang, a senior scientist at IBM, has joined Etec, reporting directly to Dr. Mark Gesley, Vice President of Technology Development. Dr. Chang brings a wealth of experience from IBM where he has worked since 1971 and has extensive experience in electron beam lithography and nanostructure fabrication. He has coordinated a wide range of research projects, and most recently pioneered IBM's microcolumn program. In addition to his extensive research, he has published and delivered a number of papers on the possible benefits of the technologies Etec has purchased from IBM. 

Dr. Hoseob Kim joined IBM in 1992 and has worked in microcolumn systems in a variety of capacities. Prior to IBM he worked at the University of Missouri on STM/AFM and performed a number of applications-to-surface studies. We are excited to have them join Etec's world-class technology development team. Their addition confirms our commitment to remaining the leader in pattern generation technology and to hiring the world's best and brightest technologists." 

Both men have relocated to work in Etec's Hayward Technology Development Group. 


Microcolumn Architecture


In addition to hiring two of the researchers responsible for its development, Etec has also acquired a variety of equipment and intellectual property rights surrounding IBM research on electron-beam microcolumns. This research offers many potential applications in future Etec products and could help in the development of systems capable of writing sub-100 nanometer (0.1 micron) device rules. 

Microcolumn architecture offers a number of possible long-term advantages for Etec, including high resolution, miniaturization and new source technology possibilities. In general, microcolumn technology refers to the design and fabrication of electron-optical focused electron-beam devices with column lengths of several millimeters as opposed to current technologies, which are much larger. Gesley explains, "Microcolumn architecture brings some interesting possibilities, and obtaining the work of these gentlemen and others at IBM puts us years ahead in terms of research and development in this area. It is a significant step along our product roadmap and towards continuing to meet the industry's future requirements."

IMEC Receives Two Federal SBIR Awards for All-Metal Electronics, Unified Memory Architecture 

520 words 
4 June 1997
17:08 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

BERKELEY, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--June 4, 1997--IMEC, a Berkeley, California startup in the memory chip field, has received two major SBIR awards from Federal agencies for work in all-metal memory and storage technology. 

The first, a $743,000 award from the Department of Energy, is to develop all-metal electronics based on the company's proprietary "transpinnor" technology. This is a Phase II award resulting from a DOE solicitation in 1996 for nanoscale electronics to simplify the circuitry of microelectromechanical systems (MEMS). The second award, a Phase I contract from the Department of Defense, BMDO, is to design a unified memory architecture based on its all-metal memory/storage chip, PRAM. In this project a single technology would replace the semiconductor and rotating disk technologies now necessary for memory and storage in computers. 

MEMS are "machines on a chip," miniature, single-chip systems that combine electronics and micromachined mechanical systems for sensing and activating in a range of devices. Just two MEMS applications -- air bags and disposable blood-pressure test kits -- account for a $2.2 billion industry. In this award, IMEC will go well beyond MEMS applications by demonstrating that its all-metal electronics is a technology that can challenge semiconductor electronics across a broad range of applications. 

The IMEC transpinnor essentially duplicates functions of the transistor: amplification, logic, or switching. The transpinnor can also function as a transformer; there is no transformer in semiconductor bipolar technology. The transpinnor is also easier to fabricate, with potential reduction in feature sizes down to nanoscale dimensions. In full production, all-metal electronics based on the transpinnor will compete in performance and cost with both digital and analog semiconductor electronics. 

IMEC's award from BMDO focuses on the memory/storage capabilities of all-metal electronics. IMEC envisions a single memory device -- PRAM -- taking over the functions presently filled by SRAM, DRAM, Flash, and rotating disk in computers. PRAM is the acronym for "permanent random access storage." Permanence, or nonvolatility, is typically associated with magnetic storage on disks, whereas random access is associated with semiconductor chips. PRAM bridges that chasm. The only other technology with these characteristics, Flash, has limited cycles, slow write, and only partial random access. In a unified memory/storage architecture, costs would plummet not only because a single technology would replace three or four, but because these devices could be fabricated for many other applications from the same facility. 

All-metal, transpinnor technology is based on a phenomenon known as giant magnetoresistance (GMR). The use of GMR by IMEC in its patented designs has created a new era for magnetic memories. Up to now, GMR has been exploited mostly in mechanical storage (disks), and solid-state memories based on GMR have had limited read/write cycles. IMEC's most recent patent protects the technology that gives PRAM unlimited read-write cycles. IMEC's R&D is conducted in Minneapolis, Minnesota. The company was incorporated in 1987 and is privately held.

National Inventors Hall of Fame Selects Three IBM Scientists 

846 words 
16 June 1997
16:55 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

WASHINGTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--June 16, 1997--Three IBM inventors -- Robert H. Dennard, Mark E. Dean, and Dennis L. Moeller -- were selected today to be inducted into The National Inventor's Hall of Fame. The three IBM engineers were individually recognized for their innovation and impact on the computer age. 

The National Inventor's Hall of Fame was formed by the US Patent and Trademark Office in 1973 to celebrate the creative genius of those inventors who conceive great technological advances. The annual induction ceremony will take place on September 13, 1997, at Inventure Place in Akron, Ohio. 

Today's new inductees join the ranks of Thomas Edison, Henry Ford, Louis Pasteur, George Eastman, and Charles Goodyear. Only 134 other men and women, including IBM Research Nobel prize winners Heinrich Rohrer and Gerd Karl Binnig, who invented the scanning tunneling microscope in 1981, are honored in the Inventor's Hall of Fame. 

"The recognition of these outstanding inventors affirms IBM's long-term commitment to experimental and exploratory science and research," said Paul Horn, senior vice president, IBM Research. "These individuals challenged the status quo and pushed the limits of technology, which resulted not only in outstanding science but a dramatic impact on industry and society." 


Dr. Robert H. Dennard
           Dr. Robert H. Dennard, a Fellow at the IBM Thomas J.  Watson
Research Center and the inventor of the one-transistor Dynamic Random
Access Memory (commonly known as DRAM or simply RAM), was honored
today for creating the system which has supplied the memory needs for
most computers since the mid-1970s.  With computers now common in
millions of homes and offices, Dennard's invention is one of the most
pervasively used in the world.
           DRAM was patented in 1968 and first appeared in commercial products
in the early 1970s.  Today DRAM is a $25 billion business.  In 1996
alone, 2.5 billion units of RAM were sold at approximately $9 per
per megabyte (MB).
           Before Dennard's invention, RAM was implemented with cumbersome and
costly wired arrays of magnetic components which were far too large
and heavy for mass use.  Dennard's invention of DRAM was a core
development in the launch of today's computer industry, setting the
stage for development of increasingly dense and cost-effective RAM
that continues even today with every succeeding generation of
computers.
           Dennard created his invention in 1966 at T.J. Watson Research
Center where he was a member of a project team that was working on
early development of field-effect transistors and integrated
circuits.  His inspiration emanated from a presentation by in-house
competitors describing the things they planned to do with thin-film
magnetic memory.
           "I went home that evening discouraged because their approach looked
very simple compared to the complex six transistor memory cell which
my team was using for each bit of data," says Dennard.  "That
evening I started exploring the possibility of storing data in a
simpler way as a charge level on a capacitor.  Within a few hours I
had gotten the basic ideas for the creation of DRAM ironed-out in my
mind.  "
           Over a period of several months, Dennard refined the ideas for his
simpler memory cell which uses only a single transistor and a small
capacitor.  Within a year, IBM and Dennard were granted a patent on
this cornerstone technology of the computer age.
Mark E. Dean and Dennis L. Moeller


Also being honored today are IBM engineers Mark E. Dean and Dennis L. Moeller who developed the improvements in computer architecture that allow IBM and compatible PCs to use high performance software and to work in tandem with peripheral devices. 

The work of Dean and Moeller has truly enhanced the agility of the PC by enabling components to communicate with each other in a high-speed and efficient manner. The first commercial use of this development was marketed in 1984 in the IBM PC/AT, and it is currently being used in more than 40 million personal computers produced each year. 

"We never looked at it as a revolutionary invention," said Dean, now vice president in IBM's RS/6000 Division. "We wanted a useful tool that would make designing reliable systems easier. As engineers, we recognized a need in the PC industry from which our customers would benefit." 

IBM Research operates in seven locations worldwide: the Thomas J. Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, N.Y.; the Almaden Research Center in San Jose, Calif.; the Zurich Research Laboratory in Ruschlikon, Switzerland; the Tokyo Research Laboratory in Yamato, Japan; the Haifa Research Laboratory in Haifa, Israel; the China Research Laboratory in Beijing, China; and the Austin Research Laboratory in Austin, Texas. The major areas of research are computer systems, computer applications and solutions, systems technology, physical sciences, mathematical sciences, storage and communications. More details about the technological achievements of IBM Research scientists can be found at: www.research.ibm.com

PLAINVIEW, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--July 25, 1997--Veeco Instruments Inc. (NASDAQ: VECO), announced today that it has completed a merger with Wyko Corp. of Tucson, Ariz., a leading supplier of optical interferometric measurement systems for the data storage and semiconductor industries. The merger was approved at a Special Meeting of Stockholders of Veeco held on July 25, 1997. This merger extends Veeco's current Surface Metrology product line to include automated, non-contact optical testing systems. 

Commenting on the completed acquisition of Wyko Corp., Edward Braun, chairman, president and chief executive officer of Veeco, said, "The combination of Wyko's non-contact, optical measurement products with Veeco's line of atomic force microscopes, Dektak surface profilers and laser scatterometers provides our data storage and semiconductor customers with a complete range of measurement technologies for yield improvement and integrated test programs." 

Under the merger, Wyko shareholders received 2,863,810 shares of Veeco common stock, and holders of options to acquire Wyko common stock received options to acquire an aggregate of 136,190 shares of Veeco common stock. The merger will be accounted for as a pooling of interests transaction. 

Wyko, which was privately held, had sales of $8.2 million and operating income of $2.4 million for the three months ended March 31, 1997. 

Wyko instruments are used to improve product yield and product quality by generating precise, consistent quantitative data throughout the the manufacturing cycle. In the manufacturing process for computer hard drives, Wyko systems produce precise measurements of magnetic head shape and height, suspension arm height and angle, and disk texture and flatness. Semiconductor manufacturers use Wyko equipment for measuring flip chips and wafer roughness. 

New products introduced by Wyko in 1997 include an automatic inspection and test system for advanced microelectronic packaging applications which provides 3D measurement of flip chip solder bumps of 1,000 microns and below, and up to 64,000 bumps on a single die. In addition, a new in-line laser inspection system precisely adjusts the static attitude of disk drive suspension arms and is ideal for next generation miniaturized (pico size) automated thin film head fabrication. 

Veeco Instruments Inc. is a worldwide leader in precision ion beam systems, physical vapor deposition systems and surface metrology equipment for high-growth microelectronic markets such as thin film magnetic heads and advanced semiconductor devices as well as for a broad range of industrial applications. Manufacturing and engineering facilities are located in Plainview, Orangeburg and Congers, N.Y.; Tucson, Ariz. and Santa Barbara, Calif. Spectra-Physics Solid State Pulsed Laser Used to Create New Form of Carbon; Scientists Win 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for Discovery 

458 words 
28 August 1997

Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 28, 1997-- Spectra-Physics Lasers, Inc., today announced that its Quanta-Ray solid state pulsed laser was used by the winners of the 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry to help create fullerenes. 

Fullerenes are a revolutionary new form of carbon with potential uses in the aerospace, electronics and industrial markets. 

Richard E. Smalley, Ph.D., the Gene and Norman Hackerman Professor of Chemistry and Professor of Physics at Rice University, in conjunction with two other scientists, received the Nobel Prize for the 1985 discovery. Directing an intense beam of laser light from the Quanta-Ray at a carbon surface, the team generated gaseous carbon. The carbon was mixed with helium gas to create atom clusters, then cooled, resulting in fullerenes. 

Spectra-Physics Lasers' Quanta-Ray is a market leader in Nd:YAG solid state pulsed lasers. These consist of a cylindrical rod of yttrium-aluminum-garnet (YAG) doped with neodymium (Nd). Pulsed lasers are used in a variety of scientific and industrial applications, including atmospheric pollution sensing and monitoring, nuclear contamination monitoring, holography and pump sources for dye lasers. When the Quanta-Ray laser was first introduced in the mid-1970s, it immediately became the industry standard. The newest member of the product line is the Quanta-Ray Pro 200/300 Series, which was introduced in May 1997. 

Currently, Dr. Smalley is using Quanta-Ray lasers 24 hours per day in his lab to produce fullerenes. "Chemical research requires reliability and performance in a laser to ensure accurate and predictable results," said Smalley. "The Quanta-Ray has a long history of leading the market in both of these areas." 

Because of their unique properties, including superior thermal and electrical conductivity and high tensile strength, fullerenes are expected to influence a wide range of areas related to carbon, including the creation of new polymers, catalysts, materials and sensors. The subsequent discovery of nanotubes -- thin tubes with closed ends one-billionth the size of a human hair -- also has far-reaching applications in space travel and medical equipment. 


The Company


Founded in 1961, Spectra-Physics Lasers, Inc., is a leading designer and supplier of lasers for industrial, scientific, medical and entertainment markets. The company offers a diverse range of laser products backed by a sales, service and support organization located in more than 35 countries. Veeco Process Metrology Receives $4.5M In Orders For Critical Dimension Atomic Force Microscopes

454 words 
22 October 1997

Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

PLAINVIEW, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 22, 1997--Multiple systems to be delivered to major semiconductor manufacturers in United States, Europe, and Asia Pacific 

Veeco Process Metrology recently received over $4.5 million in orders for the DEKTAK(R) SXM Critical Dimension Atomic Force Microscope (CD-AFM) from several major semiconductor manufacturers worldwide. The advanced metrology systems will be installed at wafer fabs located in the United States, Korea, Taiwan and Great Britain, with scheduled delivery in Q4 '97. 

The sales included three orders for the new DEKTAK SXM- 320 automated AFM for semiconductor wafers up to 300mm, first introduced at Semicon/West 97. The DEKTAK SXM-320 is the first CD-AFM to meet the needs of advanced, 300mm, 0.18- micron wafer fabs for in-line topographical and critical dimension (CD) metrology solutions. The fully automated tool characterizes processing of wafers up to 300mm in diameter by performing non-destructive measurements such as surface roughness, trench widths, depths, sidewall slopes, linewidths and vias down to .18-microns and below. 

"These orders for the Dektak SXM-320 validate the need for automated, critical dimension metrology as semiconductor manufacturers move toward next-generation 300mm substrates and 0.18-micron linewidths", said Phil Roberts, Director of Sales and Marketing for Veeco Process Metrology , Santa Barbara. 

Three scanning modes make the Dektak SXM-320 the industry's most flexible surface metrology system, enabling it to measure a wide variety of surface features without requiring time-consuming sample preparation. The standard, non-contact mode provides highly precise measurements of line and trench widths. The CD operating mode uses a unique flared tip to measure sidewall angles, trenches and linewidths as small as 0.18-microns and below without destructive cross-sectioning. As a third option, the high definition (HD) mode uses an intermittent contact method to produce surface characterization with measurements down to 1 Angstrom resolution. 

New graphical user interface software provides an easy to learn and operate environment for setting up measurement recipes, as well as easy connectivity to statistical process control (SPC) systems and database programs. 

Veeco Process Metrology Group, located in Santa Barbara, California and Tucson, Arizona, is a division of Veeco Instruments Inc. (NASD: VECO). Headquartered in Plainview, New York, Veeco is a worldwide leader in etch and deposition Process Equipment for data storage, Process Metrology tools for the data storage, semiconductor and flat panel display industries. Manufacturing and engineering facilities are located in New York, California and Arizona. Global sales and service offices are located throughout the United States, Europe, Japan and Asia-Pacific.

 Article 115 *******************    


Bell Labs Researchers Build World's Smallest Practical Transistor; Paving Way for More Powerful Integrated Circuits 

583 words 
19 November 1997
17:28 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

MURRAY HILL, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 19, 1997--Researchers at Bell Laboratories, the research and development arm of Lucent Technologies, have fabricated the world's smallest practical transistor that is four times smaller, five times faster and draws 60 to 160 times less power than today's transistors. 

While Bell Labs and others have built extremely small transistors before, no one has built a transistor this small with all the components scaled to deliver the kind of performance needed for a practical microchip, the company said. The achievement paves the way for powerful new integrated circuits that pack many billions of transistors on a single silicon chip, as opposed to the millions on today's chips. 

"As we celebrate the 50th anniversary of inventing the transistor at Bell Labs, we are ushering in the age of 'nanoelectronics' by developing the technology to produce future generations of microchips," said Mark Pinto, chief technical officer of Lucent Technologies' Microelectronics Group. In microelectronics, chip features are measured in microns, or millionths of a meter; in nanoelectronics, chip features will be measured in nanometers, or billionths of a meter. 

The experimental "nanotransistor" exceeds today's transistors in such key measures as how much current flows through a transistor and much a transistor boosts a signal. Future chips based on this technology would consume far less energy, a boon for users of portable communications and computing devices. 

"This new technology could go a long way toward satisfying consumers' demands for longer battery life, less weight, and additional capabilities in wireless telephones and portable computers," said Pinto. "Cutting power demand could lead to portable multimedia terminals that run for weeks on a single battery and include features such as automated adaptability to wireless standards around the world." 

The technology could prove especially attractive in digital signal processors, a class of chips used in cellular phones and other communications devices. Lucent Technologies is one of the world's leading producers of digital signal processors. 

Pinto noted that the work on these nanotransistors was possible because of Bell Labs' expertise in several leading-edge research fields, such as electron-beam lithography, materials science and precision etching. 

"The nanotransistor puts us way in front of the industry curve," said Pinto. "It is what the semiconductor industry predicts will become state-of-the-art 12 years from now." 

Bell Labs scientist and project team leader Greg Timp will describe the achievement on Dec. 8 at the International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM), a leading venue for reporting microelectronic device developments. IEDM is being held in Washington, D.C., at the Washington Hilton Hotel. 

Lucent Technologies, headquartered in Murray Hill, N.J., designs, builds and delivers a wide range of public and private networks, communications systems and software, data networking systems, business telephone systems and microelectronic components.  Article 119 *******************    


Bell Labs Researchers Create Images of Ultrasmall Transistor Using Sensitive Microscopy Technique 

692 words 
10 December 1997
14:48 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 1997, Business Wire) 

MURRAY HILL, N.J.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Dec. 10, 1997-- Researchers at Bell Laboratories, the research and development arm of Lucent Technologies, have made the first direct images of the core of an ultrasmall transistor, an achievement that will provide crucial information for building smaller, more efficient integrated circuits. 

Using a technique called scanning capacitance microscopy (SCM), the researchers were able to measure the length of an electrical channel - the path through which signals travel - as small as 0.12 micron in an experimental transistor structure. Chip manufacturers are particularly interested in this measurement because the channel length affects the speed and switching ability of the transistor. 

The SCM imaging work supports efforts by Lucent Technologies to decrease the size and power consumption of transistors. Bell Labs, which invented the transistor 50 years ago this month, recently announced the fabrication of the world's smallest practical metal oxide semiconductor transistor, paving the way for integrated circuits that pack many billions of components on a single chip. 

"As we celebrate the 50th anniversary of inventing the transistor, we are ushering in the age of nanoelectronics by developing the technology to produce future generations of chips," said Mark Pinto, chief technical officer of Lucent Technologies' Microelectronics Group. 

"There are very sophisticated models for designing transistors and there are very sophisticated processes for making them," said Rafael Kleiman, a scientist and team leader in the company's Semiconductor Physics Research Department. "Now we've closed the loop. With SCM, we can actually see what we've made." 

The scanning capacitance microscope works by scanning a tiny tip over the surface of the device being imaged, while simultaneously measuring the electrical properties of the material, even through an oxide layer. 

"A lot of standard types of microscope probes give you structural information, but don't give enough information about the electronic properties," Kleiman explained. "You need a probe that's sensitive to the electronic properties of the material and the electric charge distribution inside ultrasmall devices." 

Using SCM, researchers were also able to chart the impurity atoms, or dopants, in a silicon chip faster than they could using scanning tunnelling microscopy. The number and position of dopant atoms create the structure that gives transistors their switching capability. Since the electrical properties of silicon depend on the number of dopant atoms, researchers can create detailed dopant profiles of transistors by measuring the electrical properties of the silicon in each part of the transistor. 

"This work demonstrates the value of fundamental scientific research to advanced technology," said Federico Capasso, head of the Semiconductor Physics Research Department. "We have been using scanned-probe microscope techniques for over ten years for our scientific studies, and now we're applying them to developing future generations of semiconductor devices." 

Earlier this year, Bell Labs scientists reported a related imaging technique - the single-electron transistor scanning electrometer (SETSE). It is very sensitive to electric fields emanating from nearby electric charges, and can easily detect as little as one percent of an electron's electric field. Like the SCM, the SETSE can also be used to locate charged dopant atoms in a semiconductor material. 

Kleiman will describe the SCM's application to imaging electrical channels in transistor structures on Dec. 10 at the International Electron Devices Meeting (IEDM), a leading venue for reporting microelectronic device developments. IEDM is being held in Washington, D.C., at the Washington Hilton Hotel. 


Lucent Technologies, headquartered in Murray Hill, N.J., designs, builds and
delivers a wide range of public and private networks, communications systems
and software, data networking systems, business telephone systems and
microelectronic components. Bell Labs is the research and development arm for
the company. For more information on Lucent Technologies, visit our web site
at
http://www.lucent.com.

at http://www.lucent.com/press/.

JACKSON, Miss.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Jan. 2, 1998--ChemFirst Inc. (NYSE: CEM) announces the acquisition through its wholly owned subsidiary EKC Technology, Inc. of chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) assets for semiconductor production from Baikowski Chimie, a subsidiary of Groupe PSB Industries, S.A., (French Compeant Exchange) and from Moyco Technologies, Inc. (NASDAQ: MOYC). 

EKC, a global market leader of advanced cleaners for semiconductor production and a supplier of post-CMP cleaners, will develop, produce and market slurries and ancillary products for the CMP market. CMP is a key enabling technology in the manufacture of semiconductors with sub-0.35 micron feature size and high circuit density. The process involves mechanical polishing of silicon wafers using a slurry of abrasives and chemicals to produce a flatter surface for shorter wave length lithography. 

"These technologies and products complement and enhance our current electronic and performance chemicals business, and give ChemFirst a leading position in CMP, a small but rapidly growing market," said J. Kelley Williams, ChemFirst's chairman and chief executive officer. "The additional investment in semiconductor CMP research and development activities initially will be slightly dilutive to earnings. However, we expect this investment to create additional growth in revenues and earnings longer term and to help maintain our leading position in electronic chemicals." 

The transaction with Baikowski involves the acquisition by EKC of Baikowski's semiconductor CMP business, including technology, customers, slurry manufacturing equipment and an applications laboratory, and a supply agreement for proprietary powders used in the production of CMP slurries. In addition, EKC and Baikowski have formed a strategic alliance that utilizes Baikowski's broad expertise in the development and production of precision polishing materials to conduct future research for new CMP applications. EKC and Baikowski each will acquire a minor interest in the other and each will hold a seat on the other's board of directors. 

Under the transaction with Moyco, EKC will receive Moyco's CMP technologies, products, customer positions and slurry manufacturing equipment, and will assume Moyco's supply agreement with Nanophase Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: NANX) for unique, patented nanometer-sized particles used in the production of CMP slurries. In addition, EKC and Nanophase have entered into a technical support agreement for CMP applications. 

ChemFirst Inc. companies produce electronic and performance chemicals, specialty chemicals and chemical intermediates for industry and agriculture, and provide engineered products and services to chemical and other industries. ChemFirst's wholly owned subsidiary EKC Technology, Inc. is the world leader in the manufacture, service and distribution of advanced wafer cleaning chemicals used to support the manufacture of advanced microprocessors, memory devices and flat panel displays. 

Baikowski Chimie is the world's leading supplier of fine and pure alumina powders and has built a strong position in the lighting industry. It also has a global reputation for designing fine inorganic materials for advanced technology markets, including leading edge semiconductor applications. 

Moyco Technologies, Inc. manufactures precision abrasives and professional dental supplies. 

Nanophase Technologies Corporation is the world's leader in the production and marketing of nanocrystalline materials for a wide range of critical commercial applications.

PLAINVIEW, N.Y.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Feb. 9, 1998--Veeco Instruments Inc. (NASDAQ: VECO), today reported financial results for the fourth quarter and 12 months ended December 31, 1997. The Company indicated that it achieved record bookings, sales and earnings for the year. Historical financial results have been restated to reflect the merger of Veeco and Wyko Corporation, which closed on July 25, 1997, using the pooling of interests accounting method. Separately, Veeco announced today plans to merge with Digital Instruments, the world leader in scanning probe/atomic force microscopy; as well as the receipt of a record $10 million in metrology orders for in-line production tools from two leading U.S. data storage customers. 

For the year ended December 31, 1997, record sales of $165.4 million reflect a 44% increase over the prior year's sales of $115.0 million. Operating income increased 54%, excluding the previously announced one-time merger-related charge of $2.25 million and the one-time in-process R&D charge of approximately $4.2 million, to $25.6 million as compared to $16.7 million for 1996. Bookings increased 21% to $164.0 million, resulting in a book to bill ratio of .99 to 1.0 for the year. Net income for 1997 increased to a record $12.3 million or $1.32 per share (diluted), as compared to net income in 1996 of $10.9 million or $1.22 per share (diluted). Excluding the one-time charges, Veeco's 1997 earnings per share increased 43% to $1.75 (diluted). 

Veeco's 1997 fourth quarter fell short of a previously announced earnings estimate due to data storage customer postponements of shipments and new orders. Sales increased 33% to $42.9 million from $32.3 million in 1996, while operating income decreased 2% to $4.3 million from $4.4 million. Fourth quarter bookings decreased 25% to $36.7 million from $49.2 million in 1996, resulting in a book to bill ratio for the quarter of .86 to 1.0. Net income for the 1997 fourth quarter was $2.8 million or $0.30 per share (diluted) compared with $2.8 million or $.32 per share (diluted) for the fourth quarter of 1996. 

"Veeco delivered record results for 1997 despite the industry's fourth quarter weakness," noted Chairman and CEO Edward H. Braun. "1997 was a year of dramatic successes for Veeco: we completed two acquisitions - one in each of our core business areas; strengthened Veeco's leadership positions in our major product lines through investment in R&D that yielded eight significant new products; strengthened our international sales force and established a worldwide customer support group. All of these successes were the direct result of our strategic focus on Veeco's two core business areas, Process Equipment and Process Metrology, and our ability to capitalize on opportunities for each of these businesses." 

1997 sales increased in Veeco's two core product areas, with Process Equipment up 59% and Process Metrology up 46% from the prior year, driven by the continued data storage industry transition to next generation MR/GMR technologies for high density thin film magnetic heads, and semiconductor process development investment in smaller linewidth .25 micron devices. 

Commenting on the fourth quarter, Mr. Braun stated, "Veeco's fourth quarter earnings were influenced more than originally anticipated by the hard drive industry's inventory oversupply and the poor operating results of major head manufacturers. We experienced a product mix heavily weighted with new product introductions in ion beam deposition and metrology tools which impacted gross margins. In addition, operating expenses increased versus the third quarter, resulting from Veeco's investment in a worldwide direct sales organization and customer field support as well as increased investment in R&D for new product development." 

"At the present time, our data storage customers are anticipating a weak first half of 1998. As a result of this short-term outlook, the Company has taken steps to reduce operating costs, while maintaining investment in customer service and critical technology for new products. We expect second half improvement based on a more rapid phase out of inductive heads, and an acceleration of MR/GMR production likely to increase the use of Veeco in-line metrology and ion beam deposition products. Long-term opportunities continue to look favorable for the Company based on continued 15% unit PC growth, continued hard drive unit growth, and investment in sub half-micron technology from our semiconductor customers." 

Veeco Instruments Inc., headquartered in Plainview, New York, is a worldwide leader in etch and deposition Process Equipment for data storage, and Process Metrology tools for the data storage, semiconductor and flat panel display industries. Manufacturing and engineering facilities are located in New York, California and Arizona. Global sales and service offices are located throughout the United States, Europe, Japan and Asia-Pacific. In addition, An-Con will also receive two manufacturing reactors and $1 million in cash. Dylyn(TM) is exclusively licensed worldwide by Advanced Refractory Technologies Inc. (ART), an advanced materials company in Buffalo, N.Y. Pursuant to a separate agreement, ART will be responsible for managing and operating the equipment for An-Con. 

Moshe Citronowicz, chief operating officer of An-Con, stated, "This license which will be directed at the coating of medical products, including electrosurgery, clearly places the company in new and expanding markets characterized by attractive profit margins. Furthermore, this transaction is a good example of management's commitment to pursuing a selective acquisition program." According to ART's management the advanced Dylyn(TM) coating technology has the potential to revolutionize a number of industrial processes and products for a broad range of biomedical applications. Dylyn(TM) is the trade name for DLN, Diamond Like Nanocomposite, a complex three dimensional "film" with unique tailorable properties. 

Production for distribution is scheduled for August 1998 through Aaron Medical Industries Inc. (Aaron), An-Con's wholly owned subsidiary. 

As a result of the then impending acquisition of the new Dylyn(TM) advanced coating, An-Con, on advice of counsel, caused Aaron to settle the two year old patent infringement case brought by Megadyne against Aaron. Management concluded that the legal costs relating to this matter and any potential liability assessed could far exceed the cash portion of the settlement agreement. As part of the settlement, Aaron also agreed to refrain from marketing any non-infringing coated electrosurgical blades for six months. Andrew Makrides, president of the company, stated, "With our new licensing arrangement on the Dylyn(TM) technology it made no business sense to continue a legal cause of action involving a coating technology that the company was no longer going to use and only contributed six percent to 1997 revenues." 

In related news, An-Con Genetics has retained the services of Messrs. Norman Fuchs and Eric Bashford of the Merchant Banking Group of the thirty-year old investment firm, M.H. Meyerson & Co., Inc. Messrs. Fuchs and Bashford specialize in mergers and acquisitions for small-cap technology companies. 

An-Con Genetics Inc., through its wholly owned subsidiary Aaron Medical Industries Inc, is engaged in the manufacturing and marketing of a diverse line of medical devices.

The text of Syntroleum's February 17, 1998 press release is as follows: 

"Tulsa, OK - Syntroleum(R) Corporation announced that it will participate in funding Catalytica Advanced Technologies' research project to develop an advanced process for directly converting natural gas into liquid fuels, such as methanol and gasoline. 

Catalytica Advanced Technologies, a subsidiary of Catalytica, Inc. (NASDAQ: CTAL), is developing a new class of catalysts for direct oxidation of methane into methanol or other liquid hydrocarbons which could be complementary to and potentially less expensive than some current Fischer-Tropsch technologies. Because liquids can be transported and marketed more efficiently than gas, continuing development and refinement of such gas-to-liquids technologies will benefit energy producers by expanding their ability to economically develop and monetize more natural gas which would otherwise be stranded in remote areas. 

In 1997, Catalytica received a $2 million, three-year grant for its methane conversion research from the Advanced Technology Program of the U.S. Department of Commerce. Syntroleum will supplement this funding in each of the next three years, subject to Catalytica meeting mutually established milestones. Subject to certain benchmarks, follow-on efforts will include additional funding by Syntroleum for continuing development through the pilot plant stage in return for exclusive rights to market the technology worldwide. Mitsubishi Oil and Petro-Canada, which provided funding for previous development work, are also parties to the agreement. 

Mark Agee, Syntroleum President and Chief Operating Officer, commented that, `We believe Catalytica's methane oxidation process has promise and long-term potential. Successfully commercialized, Catalytica's process could complement Syntroleum's gas-to-liquids process and provide Syntroleum licensees with additional options for monetizing more of their natural gas reserves. Teaming with Catalytica underscores Syntroleum's commitment to provide our licensees with the best available technologies.' 

`We share a strong common interest with Syntroleum in the application of innovative technology to make hydrocarbons more useful and more accessible,' said Norman R. Smith, President and Chief Executive Officer of Catalytica Advanced Technologies. `We are looking forward to working together to develop and commercialize our new process for converting natural gas to liquid.' 

Syntroleum Corporation, based in Tulsa, Oklahoma, licenses its proprietary process for converting natural gas into synthetic crude oil and transportation fuels. The process can be applied to plant sizes ranging from 2,000 barrels per day to 50,000 barrels per day and larger. Licensees of the process include Texaco, Marathon, ARCO, YPF and Kerr-McGee. 

Catalytica Advanced Technologies, applies Catalytica's broad knowledge of catalysis and catalytic systems to spawn promising commercial products. In addition to methane conversion, significant projects are under way in the fields of metallocenes, specialty catalysts used to enhance the properties of plastics, and nanoscale catalysts, which have the potential to improve selected manufactured products while reducing costs and waste."

MOUNTAIN VIEW, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Feb. 17, 1998-- Catalytica Advanced Technologies, Inc., a subsidiary of Catalytica, Inc. (NASDAQ:CTAL), and Syntroleum Corporation today announced that Syntroleum has agreed to provide funding in support of a Catalytica Advanced Technologies research project aimed at developing an advanced process for the direct conversion of natural gas to liquid fuels such as methanol and gasoline. 

Catalytica Advanced Technologies is developing a new class of catalysts for the direct oxidation of methane into methanol or other liquid hydrocarbons -- a process which could be complementary to and potentially less expensive than some current Fischer-Tropsch technologies. Because liquids can be transported more efficiently than gas, development of gas to liquid technologies for methane conversion would make it more economical for energy producers to recover natural gas in remote areas. 

In March, 1997, Catalytica received a $2 million, three-year grant for its methane conversion project from the Advanced Technology Program of the U.S. Department of Commerce. That funding will be supplemented by Syntroleum funding in each of the next three years, subject to Catalytica's meeting mutually established milestones. Contingent upon certain benchmarks, follow-on efforts will include funding by Syntroleum for complete development of the technology through the pilot plant stage. In return, Syntroleum will have exclusive rights to market the technology, for which Catalytica and its original partners will receive royalties. Mitsubishi Oil and Petro-Canada are the original partners which provided funding for the preceding development of this technology. 

Mark Agee, president and chief operating officer at Syntroleum, commented that "We believe Catalytica's methane oxidation process shows promise and has long-term potential. If successfully commercialized, Catalytica's process could complement Syntroleum's gas-to-liquids process and provides Syntroleum licensees with additional options for monetizing more of their gas reserves. Teaming with Catalytica underscores Syntroleum's commitment to provide our licensees with the best available technologies." 

"We share a strong common interest with Syntroleum in the application of innovative technology to make hydrocarbons more useful and more accessible," said Norman R. Smith, president and CEO of Catalytica Advanced Technologies. "We are looking forward to working together to develop and commercialize our new process for converting natural gas to liquid. This is one of several projects in which Catalytica Advanced Technologies is developing advanced catalytic technology with long-term commercial potential and environmentally sound new products and processes." 

Syntroleum Corporation, based in Tulsa, Oklahoma, licenses its proprietary process for converting natural gas into synthetic crude oil and transportation fuels. The process can be applied in plant sizes ranging from 2,000 barrels per day to 50,000 barrels per day and larger. Licensees of the process include Texaco, Marathon, ARCO, YPF and Kerr-McGee. 

Catalytica Advanced Technologies, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Catalytica, Inc., applies Catalytica's broad knowledge of catalysis and catalytic systems to generate promising commercial products. In addition to methane conversion, significant projects are under way in the fields of metallocenes (specialty catalysts used to enhance the properties of plastics) and nanoscale catalysts, which have the potential to improve selected manufactured products while reducing costs and waste. 

Catalytica, Inc., through its subsidiaries, provides catalytic technologies and advanced products which improve manufacturing processes and solve environmental problems economically. The three subsidiaries are Catalytica Pharmaceuticals, Inc., which is a full-service provider to the healthcare industry; Catalytica Combustion Systems, Inc., which produces XONON for the energy market; and Catalytica Advanced Technologies, Inc., which creates new catalytic technologies. Find Catalytica on the world wide web at www.catalytica-inc.com.

AlliedSignal Advanced Microelectronic Materials Strengthens Position in Advanced Low K Dielectrics with Acquisition of Nanoglass LLC 

597 words 
4 April 1998

Business Wire 
English
(c) 1998 Business Wire

SUNNYVALE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--April 3, 1998--AlliedSignal Advanced Microelectronic Materials (AMM), a division of AlliedSignal Electronic Materials, strengthened its position in providing low k dielectric materials solutions to the global integrated circuit (IC) industry today by acquiring its partner's stake in Nanoglass(TM) LLC, a joint venture formed in 1996 to develop and market xerogel-type dielectrics for use in advanced integrated circuits. 

NanoPore Inc. the former partner in the joint venture, will continue to work closely with AMM to refine and commercialize Nanoglass, as the product is now known. 

The IC industry has been working to incorporate low k dielectric insulators in next-generation ICs in order to minimize circuit delays and other chip performance problems. AlliedSignal's consolidation of the Nanoglass technology within its AMM business unit strengthens the company's focus on low k materials solutions. 

"Although 'xerogel' is an historical designation for porous silica," commented Dr. Neil Hendricks, director of strategic technologies for AlliedSignal Electronic Materials, "Nanoglass is unique in terms of its ease of processing and mechanical strength. It is likely the 'ultimate' dielectric, in that it's extendable. It can be made increasingly more porous as better insulation is needed for shrinking designs of next-generation chips. This class of dielectric insulator appears in the roadmaps of practically all IC companies. Moreover, the IC industry prefers it, because chemically it's glass, the traditional IC insulator." 

According to Hendricks, Texas Instruments has been instrumental in the development of Nanoglass and recently published several technical papers demonstrating the viability of Nanoglass as an IC dielectric, including use in highly advanced copper-containing ICs. 

Industry interest in low k intermetal dielectric technology as a critical technology and market driver has increased significantly as chipmakers make the move to 0.18-, 0.13- and even 0.08-micron IC manufacturing, so much so that it is expected to challenge current technologies and processes such as chemical vapor deposition (CVD). AlliedSignal AMM has been at the forefront of low k materials research for many years, enabling it to differentiate itself from its competitors by offering the industry the broadest range of low k solutions with dielectric constants ranging from k = 4.0 to k = 1.8. 

AlliedSignal Electronic Materials, a strategic business unit of AlliedSignal Inc., provides materials solutions to the global semiconductor and electronics industries and employs 3,000 people worldwide. Based in Los Gatos, Calif., it has sales, marketing and manufacturing facilities in California, Wisconsin, Arizona, New York, South Carolina, Indiana, Taiwan, China, Singapore, Germany and India. Its businesses include Advanced Microelectronic Materials (AMM), AlliedSignal Substrate Technology & Interconnects (ASTI), Amorphous Metals, Laminate Systems, Oak-Mitsui and Optical Devices. 

With corporate headquarters in Morristown, N.J., AlliedSignal Inc. is a $14.5 billion advanced technology and manufacturing company with 70,500 employees at more than 300 facilities in 40 countries. It serves customers worldwide with advanced materials, aerospace and automotive parts, chemicals, fibers and plastics. It is among the largest 100 companies on the Fortune 500 and is one of 30 companies included in the Dow Jones Industrial Average.
