MIDDLEFIELD, Conn.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--June 11, 1999-- 

Advanced Metrology for Semiconductor and Mask Manufacturing 

At the semiconductor equipment manufacturer's annual tradeshow, Semicon West, San Francisco, California, Zygo Corporation introduces their new line of scanning probe atomic force microscopes. The Zygo SXM product family delivers the most advanced metrology capability for measuring critical dimensions (CD) for the leading edge semiconductor and photomask technology. The system's production proven performance has been qualified on features down to 0.13 um and routinely demonstrated on smaller features. The fully automated systems with their patented measuring techniques have been released to production in semiconductor fabs worldwide for measuring CDs, trench depths and positive and negative sidewall angles. The product capabilities also include critical measurements of the surface, line and sidewall roughness. 

The powerful measuring technique is completely nondestructive and operates in a noncontact mode, which eliminates wafer and mask scrap costs as compared to traditional measurement procedures. Additionally, the substrates are measured in an ambient environment further reducing cycle times, which greatly increases productivity. 

The complete product family enables the user to select the configuration best suited to their requirements. The Zygo SXM Sierra delivers full factory automation up to 300 mm wafers or 9 x 9 inch masks while the Zygo SXM Dolomite provides the same automated capabilities for up to 200 mm wafers and 6 x 6 inch masks. The Zygo SXM Cascade enables users the ultimate flexibility for measurement modes and substrate dimensions without making hardware modifications. 

Zygo Corporation designs, develops, manufactures, and markets high performance measurement and yield improvement instruments, systems, and accessories used in high technology industries. The Company is headquartered in Middlefield, Connecticut, and also has operations in Asslar, Germany; Longmont, Colorado; and in Newbury Park and Sunnyvale, California. Zygo is traded on the Nasdaq National Market under the symbol ZIGO. Additional information on the Company is available on the Internet at www.zygo.com or contact Zygo Corporation at 1-800-Zygo-Now.

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BW HealthWire)--June 30, 1999--Quantum Dot Corporation announced today that it has obtained exclusive licenses on luminescent nanoparticles from Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the Ernest Orlando Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the University of Melbourne. 

The quantum dot(TM) (Qdot(TM)) nanoparticles are molecular-sized semiconductor material that light up like LEDs and enable the detection and barcoding of biological materials from DNA to proteins. This powerful tool enables dramatic advances in genetic analysis, flow cytometry, high-throughput screening, fluorescence microscopy, drug discovery, and diagnostics. Under the licenses, Quantum Dot Corporation received exclusive, worldwide rights to develop, manufacture, market, and commercialize biological applications of Qdot particles. 

"We have dramatically improved the utility of early Qdot particles by making them bright and robust," commented Moungi Bawendi, W.M. Keck Professor of Energy and Professor of Chemistry at MIT. "The development of semiconductor nanoparticles for biological labeling gives biologists an entire new class of fluorescent probes and multiplexing agents," said Shimon Weiss, Staff Scientist at Lawrence Berkeley Lab. 

"Quantum dot particles," added Paul Alivisatos of Lawrence Berkeley Lab and Chancellor's Professor of Chemistry at UC Berkeley, "offer a distinct advantage over conventional dye-molecules as they emit pure vibrant engineered colors of light. This means they can be used to label and measure a multitude of biological markers simultaneously." 

Adds Paul Mulvaney, Professor of Chemistry at the University of Melbourne, "Quantum dot technology is an exciting application of materials science to biology and provides a simple yet powerful tool for biological measurement." These inventors are the world's leaders in the field of quantum dot particles and are on Quantum Dot Corporation's Scientific Advisory Board. 

Quantum Dot Corporation provides solutions for vastly improving detection and multiplexing in biological assays. The company can custom engineer Qdot particles for the demanding requirements of particular biological assays as used in genetic analysis, diagnostics, and drug discovery. 

According to Joel F. Martin, President, and CEO of Quantum Dot Corporation, "We are developing a broad array of applications for Qdot particles that span improvements to existing products to new massively parallel genetic assays. We are committed to working closely with customers to build partnerships to produce high value-added products." 

Quantum Dot Corporation was founded in November 1998 and is located in Palo Alto. The company and its advisors are the world's leading experts in quantum dot technology and its applications. Additional information on the company and the quantum dot technology can be found at www.qdots.com.

EntreMed, Inc. Signs Contract Manufacturing Agreement for GMP Production of Angiostatin Protein; Protein Manufacturing Underway for Human Clinical Trials 

761 words 
8 July 1999

Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

ROCKVILLE, Md.--(BW HealthWire)--July 8, 1999--EntreMed, Inc. (NASDAQ:ENMD) announced today that it has signed a contract with Covance Biotechnology Services, Inc., of Research Triangle Park, NC, to provide GMP (Good Manufacturing Practices) production of Angiostatin(R) protein for Phase I human clinical studies projected to commence early next year. 

Angiostatin(R) protein, a naturally-occurring antiangiogenic substance, was discovered in 1994 by Drs. Judah Folkman and Michael O'Reilly of Children's Hospital, Boston. In preclinical studies in mice, Angiostatin(R) protein has repeatedly inhibited the growth of a variety of metastatic and primary cancerous tumors, with no drug resistance or toxicity noted. 

EntreMed and Covance began technology transfer for the production of Angiostatin(R) protein in the first quarter of this year. With the technology transfer process now complete, EntreMed and Covance have jointly demonstrated success in numerous small and medium-scale fermentation runs. 

Larger GMP fermentations of Angiostatin(R) protein at the 2,000 liter scale are scheduled to commence at Covance early this quarter. Under the terms of the agreement, Covance will produce enough recombinant human Angiostatin(R) protein for the Phase I clinical trials as well as further preclinical studies. 

Dr. John W. Holaday, EntreMed Chairman, President and Chief Executive Officer commented on the contract with Covance: "After EntreMed's initial evaluation of five separate recombinant expression systems in 1995 and 1996, the Pichia pastoris yeast system emerged as the clear choice for the scale-up expression of Angiostatin(R) protein for human clinical trials. As a result of the molecular engineering of the Angiostatin(R) molecule, and the knowledge gained from biochemical studies performed by EntreMed scientists, we can now report that recombinant human Angiostatin(R) protein is being readily synthesized and purified at Covance." Dr. Kim Lee Sim, EntreMed's Vice President for Preclinical Research and Development, commented on Angiostatin(R) production: "EntreMed first reported on the generation of recombinant human Angiostatin(R) protein in Cancer Research in 1997. Since then, we have continued an active research and development program that has significantly refined our knowledge of this potent antiangiogenic molecule. Our efforts have greatly facilitated the successful engineering of the recombinant human Angiostatin(R) molecule with features that enable protein production at scales required for clinical testing." 

Dr. Sim continued, "EntreMed's research team has also placed a great deal of emphasis on the Angiostatin(R) protein receptor, and the potential for Angiostatin(R) as a gene-based delivery system. By the end of 1998, over 92 publications from around the world confirmed the antiangiogenic properties of this unique molecule; we anticipate that our internal research findings will contribute even further to the scientific literature." 

In 1995, EntreMed signed a Research, Collaboration and License Agreement with Bristol-Myers Squibb Company for Angiostatin(R) protein. As previously reported by EntreMed in February 1999, the agreement was then modified granting EntreMed development rights for Angiostatin(R) protein and rights with respect to future partnering and commercialization of the protein. 

Rockville, Md.-based EntreMed, Inc., The Angiogenesis Company(TM), is a leader in the field of antiangiogenesis research, which involves the inhibition of abnormal blood vessel growth recently associated with a broad range of diseases. 

The Company's strategy is to accelerate development of its core technologies through collaborations and sponsored research programs with university medical departments, research companies and government laboratories. 

For further information, please visit the EntreMed web site at www.entremed.com. 

Key Term Used in This Release 

Pichia pastoris: A methylotropic yeast that has the capability of secreting large quantities of foreign proteins into the fermentation broth in which it survives. Pichia pastoris is an industry accepted production system already being used for several protein-based biopharmaceutical agents currently in clinical trials.

Because engineering is such a dynamic field, there are tremendous opportunities going forward. I hope to build on our current strengths and to initiate some new programs with the help of our superb faculty, staff and students." 

University President Gerhard Casper, who named Plummer to the post, said that "Jim has demonstrated his abilities as an outstanding researcher and as a leader of a complex, multi-use research facility. His interest in continuing to expand the horizons of the School of Engineering, for example in the field of bioengineering, his commitment to undergraduate and graduate teaching, and his personal qualities, as confirmed by the broad support he has within the School, make him superbly qualified to be the next dean. Jim is in the tradition of excellence most recently exemplified by John Hennessy and Jim Gibbons." 

Hennessy, who became dean of the School in 1995 after an international search, was tapped by Casper in April of this year to become university provost, a post he assumed July 1. 

Hennessy praised Plummer's selection: "He's a world class researcher. He's a fantastic teacher. And he's had significant leadership experience. Based on the range of his experience and his long history at Stanford, I am confident that Jim will be an outstanding leader for the engineering school." 

Former engineering dean James Gibbons, who held the post from 1984 to 1995 concurred: "He's firm, thoughtful, and he can focus on what will make the School successful in the future." 

According to Mark A. Horowitz, the professor of electrical engineering who co-chaired the search committee with former Provost Condoleezza Rice, "Jim was on everybody's list. All the members of the committee are quite pleased with the announcement." 

The committee had access to the results of the 1995 search and did consider external candidates, Horowitz said. As was the case with the previous search, however, the committee conformed to the long-standing tradition that engineering deans are chosen from the ranks of veteran engineering faculty. 

Plummer will assume the deanship of a School that is generally considered one of the best in the country. In a 1995 decanal review of the quality of U.S. graduate programs, the National Research Council rated eight of the School's nine departments among the top 10, with three departments ranked number one in scholarly quality. 

About one-quarter of all Stanford students are enrolled in engineering, and the School's faculty of 220 includes 68 members of the National Academy of Engineering and five recipients of the National Medal of Science. 

Plummer said he will spend the summer thinking about the specific directions in which he would like to lead the School. But one direction is clear: biology. Plummer supports Stanford's new Bio-X initiative, designed to increase the amount of collaboration among researchers in medicine, biological sciences, physical sciences and engineering. He foresees that engineering school faculty and students will play a major role in this ambitious program. 

Plummer's own primary research interests lie in making integrated circuits and other devices out of silicon. He has established a national reputation in the area of developing physically based models of silicon structures that can be used to design new devices. 

His research has included a mixture of experimental studies and computer modeling aimed at understanding the basic physical principles that take place in semiconductors. He also has applied the computer modeling tools he has developed to design new devices, including high voltage chips, integrated circuits aimed at special applications, and nanoscale structures. He has written more than 300 articles and holds several patents. 

One of his inventions is a chip, known as an insulated gate bipolar transistor, that has been used in motor controls for washing machines, electric power tools, air conditioners and a variety of other products that contain electric motors. 

Chips made from these transistors can improve the efficiency of AC motors by as much as 40 percent by automatically adjusting the motor's speed to fit the task at hand. The technology was patented by Stanford and has generated substantial royalties for the university. 

The quality of Plummer's research has been recognized with a number of awards, including his election to the National Academy of Engineering in 1996. 

Plummer is also known as a gifted teacher, at both the undergraduate and graduate levels. He has won the Graduate Teaching Award, The Tau Beta Pi Undergraduate Teaching Award and a Best Teacher Award from the Society of Women Engineers. As chairman of the electrical engineering department, he started a highly successful program that allows interested undergraduates to participate in summer research projects. 

During a stint as senior associate dean, Plummer acted as a "chief operating officer" for the School. In that critical position, he demonstrated an ability to work well with all the department chairs, said former dean Gibbons. He also played a central role in working with the engineering departments to integrate computer technology into every aspect of their activities. 

Plummer's long association with the School is another strength, colleagues say. After he earned his doctorate in 1971, Plummer served as a research associate for three years, then became the associate director of the Integrated Circuits Laboratory (ICL). In 1978, he joined the electrical engineering department as an associate professor, becoming a full professor in 1983. 

He directed ICL for nearly nine years, then served as a senior associate dean in the School of Engineering from 1993 to 1996, until he assumed the chairmanship of the electrical engineering department in 1997. At the same time, he has served as director of the Stanford Nanofabrication Facility and as national director of the NSF National Nanofabrication Users Network. 

Joseph Goodman, senior associate dean and professor of electrical engineering, will serve as acting dean until Plummer takes over. 

"I can't think of another individual better suited for the job than Jim," Goodman said. "I'm delighted that he accepted."

Microcosm Leads CAD Portion of $14M Optical MEMS Project 

894 words 
19 July 1999
12:24 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

RALEIGH, N.C.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--July 19, 1999-- 

NIST ATP to Accelerate Efficient Manufacturing of 

Optical MEMS to Support Telecom, IT, Imaging, Medicine, 

and Entertainment Applications 

Microcosm Technologies, Inc. today announced that it will lead the CAD portion of a $14M, three-year optical MEMS project. 

The project, titled "Micro-Opto-Electro-Mechanical Systems Manufacturing," has been funded by the US National Institute for Standards and Technology (NIST). It's goal is to develop and demonstrate technologies for efficient manufacturing of optical MEMS for telecommunications, imaging, medicine, entertainment, and information technology. 

Microcosm shares the NIST Advanced Technology Program (ATP) project with Xerox, Maxim Integrated Products, Optical Micro-Machines, Standard Microsystems Corp., and Microscan Systems, Inc. Xerox is the prime contractor on the project. The companies will share $6.914M in NIST funding and provide matching funds to bring the total project close to $14M over three years. 

This team of companies will also be supported by university efforts, including work at the Industry-Cornell Univ. Alliance for Electronic Packaging, the Cornell Nanofabrication Facility, the Center for Integrated Circuits and Sensors (Univ. of Michigan) and the Washington Technology Center (Seattle). 

MEMS are micro-electro-mechanical systems, tiny electro-mechanical devices machined on silicon using photolithographic technology originally developed for the integrated circuit industry. Already these devices can include actuators, electro-mechanical sensors and a wide variety of mechanisms including beams, diaphragms, gear trains and levers. 

Optical MEMS devices add to this the integration of light sources (e.g. LED's or semiconductor lasers), optical elements (e.g. lenses, mirrors, apertures and beam splitters) and detectors (e.g. photodiodes). 

In the NIST project, Microcosm will extend its CAD software to include modeling of the optical components which are typically incorporated on optical MEMS devices. This is inherently different from ray-tracing optical design at the macroscopic level. In microdevices, the structures being fabricated are often not much larger than the wavelength of the light being manipulated. Thus near-field and diffraction effects are important. 

In addition, due to the high mechanical accelerations inherent in these devices, optical elements can warp dynamically, and this needs to be taken into consideration in a combined dynamic optical-electro-mechanical analysis. Microcosm has already led the MEMS CAD field in the development of software which can co-solve electro-mechanical problems. CAD tools which are needed for optical MEMS development are not however, limited to the component level. 

In addition, system engineers will need accurate (non-linear) reduced order models which can be used in their system simulations. Microcosm expects to be able to extract these automatically from detailed calculations at the device level and to incorporate them in system models which also span the diverse technologies involved (optics, analog and digital electronics, mechanics, heat transfer and packaging). It is this integrated ability to model at both the device level and the system level which is expected to be most valuable in the CAD tools being developed. 

Optical MEMS devices have been in development for several years. Texas Instruments, one of Microcosm's first MEMS customers, has developed devices with over a million individually controllable mirrors. Each mirror can rotate between angular positions in a few microseconds. 

These devices are now used for image projection, including both computer applications and later this year, theater-scale motion picture display. Other areas in which optics and electronics are combined include fiber-optic telecommunications, bar-code scanning and laser printing. 

John West, Microcosm's Marketing Director for Optical MEMS said, "We see potential to link this new optical MEMS work to applications in the area of bio-chips. The latter are microfluidic devices developed to conduct rapid biochemical analyses using minute quantities of samples and reagents. To date, most of these devices are still interfaced however, with macroscopic optical readout systems. 

"As optical MEMS technology advances, it may be possible to develop hybrid or even monolithic devices integrating both microfluidics and optics. Microcosm has already introduced a software package (FlumeCAD) which focuses on the development of biological microfluidic devices and instruments. Microcosm has been funded by DARPA, with partners Perkin-Elmer and Caliper Technologies, to advance microfluidic CAD technology." 

Company Background 

Microcosm Technologies, Inc. (Raleigh, NC) was established in 1995 to develop and market MicroElectroMechanical Systems (MEMS) CAD software and services, which addresses device design, manufacturing analysis, packaging, and system integration. The company has licensed core technology from Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and has engaged in $5.5 million of collaborative development efforts with industry, academia and DARPA. 

Microcosm's products include MEMCAD, an integrated design environment consisting of 3-D design, modeling, and simulation software tools that enable the creation of complex MEMS/ MST devices for automotive, computer, and telecom applications. Microcosm recently introduced FlumeCAD(TM), which targets the requirements for flow, chemical transport, and containment analysis of complex microfluidics networks for the Lab-on-a-Chip market. 

Microcosm has offices and support staff in Cambridge, Mass.; San Mateo, Calif.; Amsterdam, Netherlands and is headquartered in Raleigh. Microcosm is privately held. Microcosm's web site can be found at http://www.memcad.com.

LARCHMONT, N.Y.--(BW HealthWire)--July 23, 1999--Biotechnology companies are taking the lead in the development of novel drug delivery systems for proteins and peptides, according to Genetic Engineering News (GEN) (www.genengnews.com) (http://www.genengnews.com) . "Novel peptide delivery systems are nearing the point of being able to deliver fully functional peptides and proteins on design and over longer periods of time," says John Sterling, managing editor of GEN. "Some estimates suggest that, by the year 2002, drugs administered via these systems will reach $35 billion in the U.S. and $50 billion worldwide." 

For example, Genentech (NYSE;GENE) and Alkermes (NASDAQ;ALKS) recently reported positive results of their Phase III multi-center trial of Nutropin Depot(tm), the first long-acting form of recombinant growth hormone. The product is formulated with Genentech's recombinant human growth hormone and uses Alkermes' ProLease(R) injectable sustained-release drug delivery system. In late June, Genentech filed a New Drug Application (NDA) with the FDA for Nutropin Depot. 

"Designed specifically to reduce the frequency of injections, this formulation encapsulates the drug in biodegradable microspheres that, once injected, release recombinant growth hormone slowly over a sustained period of time," notes Sterling. "Nutropin Depot calls for only one or two dosings a month, compared to the daily injections required by most growth hormone formulations." 

Biotech Australia has developed a very interesting process for the oral delivery of peptide and protein pharmaceuticals. Their system employs a natural process for oral uptake of vitamin B12 in the body to co-deliver proteins and peptides. By riding the vitamin B12 uptake system, the protein or peptide can move through the intestinal wall. 

Researchers at the Australian company have achieved oral bio-availabilities ranging from 10% to 45% of the administered drug using the vitamin B12 process. 

"So far, they have achieved oral delivery of various luteinizing hormone releasing hormone (LHRH) analogs, granulocyte colony stimulating factor (G-CSF) and erythropoietin (EPO) in small animals," says Sterling. "The system has also worked for oral delivery of nanoparticles in rat, dog and pig models." 

MacroMed Inc. has developed the ReGel(R) injectable system for protein and peptide delivery that is thermo-sensitive. Below body temperature, ReGel is an injectable liquid while at body temperature it immediately forms a gel depot that slowly erodes and dissolves into known, safe biodegradable polymers. The active drug is delivered over time as the biopolymers dissolve. While the other drug delivery companies have focused on oral or injection delivery of proteins and peptides, Genetronics Biomedical Ltd. (AMEX;GEB) is moving forward with its electroporation (EPT) system. The MediPulser(R) device delivers a pulsed electric field to cells. This treatment, which increases the permeability of the cell membranes to the drug, results in a significant enhancement of intracellular drug delivery. The company is also testing their ReGel system for administration of drugs to treat anxiety, hepatitis B, type II diabetes, periodontitis, urological disorders and arthritis. 

Other companies developing novel drug delivery systems include Control Delivery Systems Inc., DepoMed, Inc. (AMEX;DMI), Aradigm (NASDAQ;ARDM), Advanced Inhalation Research, Endocyte and Alliance 

Pharmaceutical Corp. (NASDAQ;ALLP). 

"You can be sure that large pharmaceutical companies are watching these biotech firms very closely," adds Sterling. "Some have already formed partnerships with them (e.g., the R.W. Johnson Pharmaceutical Research Institute and DepoMed), and more will jump on board as these technologies continue to validate themselves."

Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) Amplifies Genetic Material (DNA) for 

Diagnostics, Forensics and Research Applications Laser PCR May Make Possible the Analysis of Even Smaller DNA Samples 

Cell Robotics International, Inc. (OTC BB:CRII) announces the allowance by the U.S. Patent Office for a fundamental physics patent to perform Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR) with infrared irradiation, including lasers. 

In-house research and development using the Cell Robotics core technology led to the invention and patent application by Dr. Jerome Conia, Chief Scientist, and Dr. C. Larry Keenan, Cell Robotics Workstation Product Manager. 

PCR technology is key to the following: -- developing the treatments and cures for genetic diseases such as 

cystic fibrosis, Tay Sachs, and sickle cell anemia; -- developing new methods for diagnosis and treatment of cancer, 

viral and bacterial disease; -- detection of genetic markers used in forensic applications to 

solve crimes, determine paternity, and identify remains; -- the current and continuing success of the Human Genome project; 

PCR was developed in 1985 by Dr. Kary B. Mullis while at Cetus Corporation, and is a widely used tool for studying and analyzing the molecules of genetic material. Dr. Mullis was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1993 for this invention that has led to "decisive progress in gene technology". PCR was the advancement in molecular biology making possible the in vitro replication of individual molecules of DNA and RNA; the complicated genetic molecules that direct the development, growth, and reproduction of all organisms from viruses to whales. 

The patent, in part, claims the use of lasers to achieve PCR for samples that may be so small as to contain the genetic information of a single cell or even a few fragments of genetic material. What differentiates the patent from traditional PCR is that small areas within biopsies, single cells, or even single molecules, could be treated . Rapid heating and cooling could be accomplished by the laser irradiation. Reducing the patent to practice could further enhance the capabilities of PCR by decreasing the time of the reaction, and reducing the size of the sample. Just as importantly, with the trend in biotechnology toward miniaturization and nanotechnology, the potential exists to dramatically reduce the size of the instrumentation necessary to carry out the procedures. 

Experiments done by Dr. Jerome Conia and collaborating scientists at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratories will be submitted for publication in the near future. The results identify and quantify the spatial and temporal domains of the thermal effects of laser irradiation that are necessary to achieve PCR. Cell Robotics International, Inc. will seek to license or enter into partnerships with other companies or laboratories to develop this technology. 

Cell Robotics International, Inc. developed and manufactures the Lasette(TM), a laser finger perforator that allows diabetics to sample their blood for glucose measurements in a nearly painless manner. It also manufactures, markets, and sells the In Vitro Fertilization (IVF) Workstation (used in Laser Assisted Hatching and Zona Laser Treatment), and the Cell Robotics Workstation, a research instrument that incorporates the LaserTweezers(R) and LaserScissors(TM) for manipulating and cutting cells and chromosomes. Additional information is available on the Cell Robotics Web Site at http://www.cellrobotics.com, by e-mail at crii@cellrobotics.com, or by telephone at 505/343-1131.

Orthovita Issued Biomaterials Patent For Nano-Structured Technology 

771 words 
26 August 1999
06:14 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

MALVERN, Pa.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 26, 1999--ORTHOVITA (EASDAQ: VITA), an orthopaedic biomaterials company, announced today that it has been granted a U.S. patent for its fine particle synthesis or nano-structured technology. 

The technology was derived from the internal development of VITOSS(TM), Orthovita's platform technology for developing synthetic cancellous resorbable, calcium phosphate bone substitutes. 

Fine particles or nanomaterials are infinitely tiny - approximately one million particles would fit on the head of a pin - and have potential applications in a number of industrial, commercial and medical products, such as in drug delivery and medical imaging. 

"This patent represents a significant product differentiating technology whereby microstructural control at the nanometer level allows for the development of biologically remodelable VITOSS products," said Erik Erbe, Ph.D., Vice President, Research and Development of Orthovita. 

"This microstructural control enabled us to develop our VITOSS Scaffold(TM) product, which has a porosity that closely matches that of trabecular bone. This in turn, allows for cells, growth factors and nutrients to pulse through our material so that it can remodel into natural bone over time." 

"Orthopaedics, and particularly the $1.1 billion spinal market, continues to be the major focus of our product development and commercialization activities," said David S. Joseph, Chairman & CEO of Orthovita. 

"In line with our corporate strategy, we will continue to pursue internally all potential orthopaedic uses for our nano-meter technology. 

"However, because this technology creates new opportunities outside of our focus on orthopaedics, we have assigned this patent to our wholly-owned subsidiary, Partisyn Corporation, to explore other potential medical, industrial and commercial applications through licensing and royalty arrangements." 

About the Company 

Orthovita is a biomaterials company with two broad technology platforms for developing bone substitutes, each providing the potential for multiple product opportunities. 

The ORTHOCOMP(TM) platform is a technology for developing synthetic cortical nonresorbable, load-bearing, resin composite products. Orthovita currently has three products under development that are derived from the ORTHOCOMP platform, and newly branded as CORTOSS(TM) Injectable, CORTOSS(TM) Putty and CORTOSS(TM) Implants. 

Near-term, Orthovita plans to advance the development of its CORTOSS products for a variety of indications, including conducting clinical trials of CORTOSS Injectable for vertebroplasty and screw augmentation in Europe. 

The VITOSS platform, Orthovita's other core technology, is being used to develop synthetic cancellous resorbable, calcium phosphate products. 

Orthovita's products focus primarily on the spine, the fastest growing market in orthopaedics, estimated at $1.1 billion on a worldwide basis. The Company is also developing complementary bone products to address a broad range of clinical needs in the trauma and joint implant fixation markets. 

Orthovita has a worldwide marketing, sales and distribution agreement for joint development of ORTHOCOMP for use in joint implant procedures with Howmedica, a subsidiary of Stryker Corp. -- the PMMA market leader for joint implants. 

The human skeleton consists of two types of bone: cortical bone (80%) and cancellous bone (20%). Cortical bone is dense, structural and tubular in shape and is subject to bending, load bearing and twisting forces. Cancellous bone, on the other hand, is less dense, more vascular and is primarily subject to compressive forces. 

Skeletal integrity is maintained by an ongoing process of regeneration and remodeling; however, both types of bone can be damaged in many ways, including traumatic incidents and degenerative disease, such as osteoporosis.

LA JOLLA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 31, 1999-- 

Virtual Explorer Environment Makes Learning Complex Concepts Fun, Developers Also Release Source Code To Encourage Extensions and 

New Applications 

A research group at the University of California at San Diego (UCSD) today announced that the Virtual Explorer science-based virtual reality adventure is now available at no cost to schools, museums and researchers. This interactive simulation of a voyage through the human immune system makes it fun to learn about the highly complex mechanisms that help fight disease. 

The research group, known as the Senses Bureau, also said that the software framework used to develop Virtual Explorer is also available on an "open source" licensing basis to groups or individuals that wish to use it to develop other educational applications or to extend the currently available adventure. 

Virtual Explorer is a science-fiction styled immersive adventure, in which the viewer pilots a microscopic "nanobot" ship through his or her own blood stream and lymph system. After choosing which cellular character to play, the user performs functions such as cellular navigation, white blood cell recognition and molecular docking, all within a richly rendered computer animation with four-channel spatialized sound. 

The Virtual Explorer adventure is a collaborative project of the Senses Bureau, a primarily undergraduate group of students at UCSD that focuses on advanced exploration of computer science, computer graphics, chemistry, biology and physics. In its 30-year history, the group has executed a wide range of professional-level projects including the development of virtual reality technologies, commercially distributed films, and numerous published articles. 

The adventure is designed for viewing through stereoscopic shutter-glasses on three large rear-projection monitors arranged at angles to create a wrap-around field of view. The sense of immersion is further enhanced through navigation with a force feedback joystick and throttle, and operators can even use verbal cues to enter commands. At UCSD the virtual environment is powered by a four-processor SGI Onyx(TM) supercomputer system. Any SGI computer, ranging from the Onyx to the O2(TM) (which displays a non-stereo version), can also drive the adventure. The Senses Bureau also hopes to port Virtual Explorer to the Windows NT(R) platform. 

The software framework is written in C++, and based on the IRIS Performer(TM) toolkit. Details on the Open Source licensing agreement, for developers who wish to work with the Virtual Explorer software framework, are available on the Internet at http://www-wilson.ucsd.edu/ve/. Individuals and organizations that would like to obtain Virtual Explorer, delivered on three CDs, can contact the Senses Bureau office by telephone at 619-822-0162, or by e-mail at ve@ucsd.edu. 

The Senses Bureau is an undergraduate research group in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at the University of California at San Diego, which has a 30-year history of innovations in multimedia for scientific visualization and education. The Virtual Explorer development team includes: Kevin L. Dean, Xylar S. Asay-Davis, Evan M. Finn, Jeremy A. Friesner, Bret J. Naylor, Sarah R. Wustner, Scott S. Fisher, and Kent R. Wilson. More information about the Senses Bureau and the Virtual Explorer project is available at http://www-wilson.ucsd.edu/ve/. Images that illustrate the Virtual Explorer experience can be downloaded from this site.

New Ultra Low-k SPEEDFILM BX IC Dielectric Now Available from Gore; New BX Material Offers Enhanced Properties, Lowering IC Production Costs 

491 words 
7 September 1999

Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

EAU CLAIRE, Wis.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Sept. 7, 1999--W. L. Gore and Associates announced today prototype availability of its new SPEEDFILM(TM) BX IC Dielectric, an ultra low-k dielectric material for logic chips with the lowest dielectric constant of any thermally stable, non-porous material. The new material is thermomechanically stable with an effective glass-transition temperature (Tge) of over 400 C. 

Gore's SPEEDFILM BX has a nominal dielectric constant of 2.1 with a very low effective dielectric constant, allowing for production of high performance logic wafers using the fewest metalization layers than with any other dielectric. The low effective dielectric constant is achieved by using much thinner capping layers than those used with brittle, porous dielectric materials. Gore's ultra low-k spin-on dielectric (SOD) can be processed using conventional back-end processes and equipment. By reducing the number of metalization layers required and utilizing existing resources, manufacturers can decrease their production cost per wafer. 

SPEEDFILM BX is a water-based polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE)/siloxane nanocomposite and is the only solid ultra low-k IC dielectric available. It is chemically inert with respect to all known semiconductor processor chemicals - it presents no known diffusion problems when used with aluminum, and is highly compatible with copper when titanium nitride is used as a barrier material. With these common IC materials, PTFE is extremely stable and the fluorine presents no known diffusion problems. 

Thermomechanically stable at 400 C, SPEEDFILM BX is easy to process and exhibits high fracture toughness. It presents an excellent profile for trench and via structures, eliminating any significant etching concerns. 

To support its SPEEDFILM program, Gore has process engineers available to assist with developmental work. Coated 200mm wafers as well as partially processed wafers with dielectric, hardmask and patterned photoresist, ready for dielectric etch processing, are available from Gore. 

For more information on Gore SPEEDFILM IC Dielectric, call Buck Bakhru at 800-689-0701 or visit www.gore.com. 

W. L. Gore & Associates, Inc., is an innovative, high technology manufacturing company based in Newark, Del. Gore has pioneered the use of expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE) to manufacture electronics, GORE-TEX(R) fabrics, and a wide range of industrial and medical products. A member of SEMI-SEMATECH since 1989, Gore is an established supplier to the semi-conductor industry. With more than 6,000 associates, more than $1 billion in annual sales, and nearly 50 sites worldwide, Gore is well known for its unique corporate culture and was recently named as one of the top 100 companies to work for in America.

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BW HealthWire)--Oct. 5, 1999--Quantum Dot Corporation (QDC) today announced a Collaborative Research and Development Agreement with the laboratories of Drs. Jeffrey Trent and Michael Bittner, at the Cancer Genetics Branch, National Human Genome Research Institute (NHGRI) of the National Institutes of Health. 

The CRADA will aim to develop significantly more sensitive techniques for hybridization-based detection of nucleic acids by utilizing Quantum Dot(TM) (Qdot(TM)) particles, a new class of luminescent tags derived from semiconductor materials. 

Qdot nanoparticles are molecular-sized semiconductor material that light up like LEDs and enable the detection and barcoding of biological materials from DNA to proteins. This powerful tool enables dramatic advances in genetic analysis, flow cytometry, high-throughput screening, fluorescence microscopy, drug discovery, and diagnostics. 

"QDC and the Cancer Genetics Branch (CGB) of NHGRI have complementary skills and common goals in developing improved methods of multi-color fluorescent detection in the areas of cDNA microarrays and in situ hybridization," commented Joel Martin, Ph.D., President and CEO, Quantum Dot Corporation. "We are extremely excited to have the opportunity to work with world-class scientists at NHGRI. Both QDC and CGB can merge their efforts and expertise to obtain the increased sensitivity and color multiplexing that is needed today in gene expression studies using microarrays." 

"The current methods of generating high quality labeled cDNA is dependent upon many parameters such as the purity and amount of the RNA template, type of fluor tag on the nucleotide, and photobleaching of the fluors used," said Mike Bittner, Ph.D., CRADA Principal Investigator. 

"The primary goal of this CRADA," commented Joel Martin, "is to determine how to use Qdot particle detection to increase the robustness of mRNA labeling to allow accurate, more sensitive gene expression profiling. We will also be conducting experimentation aimed at using Qdot particle detection with reduced levels of cellular total RNA." 

CGB has developed and is continuing to improve, methodologies for the fabrication of cDNA microarrays, the production of fluor labeled cDNA representations of cellular mRNA pools, confocal laser scanning microscopy of microarrays, the analysis of fluorescent images that result from cDNA microarray analysis and analysis of gene expression profiles revealed by microarray analysis.

The system acquires slider images (nano, pico, or femto), using a 4 megapixel digital camera, and the user can define the desired combination of inspection views of the air bearing surface and the pole tip. The system is supplied with flexible software to meet the differing specifications of volume head manufacturers. OASIS(TM) technology is extendable to meet the inspection needs of other precision applications such as printer heads and biotechnology. 

Veeco Instruments Inc., headquartered in Plainview, New York is a worldwide leader in Metrology tools for the data storage and semiconductor industries, and Process Equipment etch and deposition tools for the data storage industry. Manufacturing and engineering facilities are located in New York, California and Arizona. Global sales and service offices are located throughout the United States, Europe, Japan and Asia Pacific.

Nanovation to Celebrate 120th Anniversary of Edison Breakthrough With Introduction of World's First Fully Integrated Optical Circuit 

864 words 
18 October 1999
11:17 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 18, 1999-- 

Light-Based Technology Up to 1,000 Times More Powerful 

Than Electron Semiconductors, 

100 Times Smaller Than Width of Single Human Hair 

Nanovation Technologies Inc., the ground-breaking pioneer of photonic research and instrumentation, will celebrate the 120th anniversary of Thomas Edison's creation of electric light by introducing the world's first fully integrated optical circuit, which integrates optical processes to relay information. 

The company will unveil the technology behind the new circuit at 9 a.m. Thursday, Oct. 21, at the New York Hall of Science, located at 47-01 111th St. in Flushing Meadows. 

Nanovation's event recognizes the anniversary of Edison's invention and showcases the huge technological advances made in light and communications over the past century. The world's first successful test of an electric light began on Oct. 21, 1879. The experiment lasted only 13 hours, but it forever changed the world with its possibilities for the ongoing evolution of light. 

"Edison said, 'We are striking it big in the electric light, better than my vivid imagination first conceived; where this thing is going to stop Lord only knows,'" said Nanovation President and CEO G. Robert Tatum. "Nanovation is now striking it big in another area of light technology, and our results are bigger than anyone first believed possible." 

Nanovation's breakthrough technology harnesses the power of photons, the fundamental particles of light. Photons are to optical fibers what electrons are to copper wires, with two major differences: photons are 1,000 times faster and can move up to 1,000 times more information than today's conventional chip technology. Nanovation's light-based chips also are 100 times smaller than the width of a single human hair. 

As a result, fiber optic communications systems will become more productive and efficient. With 4,000 miles of fiber optic cable installed in the United States every day, communications companies will benefit by giving their customers faster, more efficient connections to the Internet and private networks. 

The results also include a diverse range of uses in many industries: 


--   Faster transmission speeds will bring about a convergence of
     video, voice and data. Video conferencing via the telephone will
     finally become a reality, becoming as commonplace as today's
     voice calls.
--   When today's heat-intense computer chips are replaced by
     nanophotonic chips, laptop computers will become smaller and can
     handle more tasks.
--   In the defense industry, optical chips can replace heavy
     copper-wired communications systems, reducing a single fighter
     jet by more than 180 pounds, which allows for extra fuel and
     munitions.
--   High resolution transmissions allowed by optical technology will
     enable top surgeons to advise on surgeries occurring in another
     state or remote location. Its cost-effectiveness will make these
     transmissions more accessible to a greater number of medical
     professionals.


"We're standing on the threshold of a communications revolution and Nanovation has thrown the door wide open," Tatum said. "Just as Edison's technology revolutionized industry in his time, Nanovation's technology will revolutionize the communications industry in our time. This is a significant, dramatic step forward within the communications networking industry. Networks based on our technology will have more bandwidth, less latency and greater throughput than anything ever witnessed before." 

Nanovation has created the first facility in the United States that is fully dedicated to nanophotonics research. Scientists from the research unit, located on the campus of Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois, will attend the Oct. 21 event to discuss their new technology. 

"As a result of Nanovation's intense research and development program, communications companies will finally have a cost-effective way to eliminate network bottlenecks and upgrade their existing fiber optic infrastructure into a powerful, 100-percent optical system," Tatum said. "Nanovation's technology literally moves information at the speed of light. Our technology is a testament to the foresight of innovators like Edison and our researchers at Northwestern University. Nanovation is making the technology of tomorrow possible today." 

In late September, Nanovation announced its acquisition of Toronto-based Apollo Photonics. The company also recently closed $16.5 million in financing through private placement of common stock shares. 

About Nanovation Technologies Inc. 

Nanovation Technologies is a high-tech company that designs and develops integrated optical devices based on its patented microcavity lasers and resonators for the growing fiber communications market. Nanovation will offer a full line of products that will include optical cross-connect switches, subnanosecond add/drop switches and wave division multiplexers. In addition, Nanovation will develop and deliver advanced photonic devices with the ability to integrate laser sources and optical switches on the same device. Nanovation initially will sell its components to telecommunications and data networking equipment manufacturers, and to original equipment manufacturers that supply subsystems. Nanovation is headquartered in Miami with facilities in Evanston, Illinois. Its Web site is located at www.nanovation.com.

National Inventors Hall of Fame Announces Collegiate Winners 

828 words 
19 October 1999
20:17 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

AKRON, Ohio---(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 19, 1999--They are some of the country's best and brightest (and youngest) creative minds, with inventions ranging from "Luminescent Quantum Dots for Ultrasensitive Biological Detection" to a "Planing Hull Catamaran", to "The Twistmaster: An Automated Jar-Opening Device." 

Recently, the National Inventors Hall of Fame recognized their 1999 Collegiate Inventors Program winners. 

Current and past winners have demonstrated promise for the world's future technologies through inventions such as a sensor for carbon monoxide detection, a new dynamic random access memory (DRAM) cell, a safety electric outlet, a paraplegic ski machine, an ozone generator for reduced auto emissions, minimally-invasive optical biopsy, a variable surface area parafoil, and a non-electric incubator. 

Each year, the National Inventors Hall of Fame which presents the Collegiate Inventors Competition, honors the most outstanding students/advisor teams for their innovative work. This year's competition solicited entries from the finest colleges and universities across the country. Chosen by the National Inventors Hall of Fame, thirty-eight judges participated in the selection process representing the top of their fields in mathematics, engineering, applied sciences, computers, and medicine. 

Jennifer Davis, Lee Collins and Marcus Malinosky (Yale University) were one group of three winners in the Undergraduate Category for their work with an invention called, "The Twistmaster: An Automated Jar-Opening Device." This device enables anyone, especially those with arthritis or other minor handicap, to open most containers with a twist-off cap. "Opening jars is often difficult for most people at one time or another," Collins, Davis and Malinosky wrote in their application, "many people simply do not have enough strength in their hands to both grip a jar securely and twist off the lid." 

Warren Chan (Indiana University) was announced as a winner in the All-Collegiate Category for his "Luminescent Quantum Dots for Ultrasensitive Biological Detection." These semiconductor nanoparticles are used to label biological molecules such as proteins and oligonucleotides. They are extremely bright and photostable as compared to current dyes and would allow for the development of ultrasensitive detection schemes for the early detection of diseases such as AIDS, cancer or Down Syndrome. 

Amy Smith (Massachusetts Institute of Technology) is not as young as the other 1999 winners in the All-Collegiate category because she has spent her life responding to appeals for help. She spent four years in the Peace Corps, twice as long a commitment as normal, in a place where existence for many is difficult - Botswana. Upon returning to the United States, Smith's commitment to the people she spent four years with, did not stop. The 1999 BFGoodrich Collegiate Inventors program recognized Amy for her work with "The Amtek Phase-Change Incubator". Designed to be used in field laboratories or remote clinics in developing countries, this device performs the same function as a standard, electric incubator but can operate where no electricity is available. 

Additional winners include, in the All-Collegiate category: Kevin Linthicum and Thomas Gehrke (North Carolina State University) for "Pendeo-epitaxial Growth of III-Nitrides", and in the Undergraduate Category: Andrew Neice (University of Colorado) for "Porous Membrane", Tobin Fisher and Marcus Malinosky (Yale University) for "Planing Hull Catamaran". Honorable Mention went to Hirad Samavati (Stanford University) for his "Fractal Capacitors", and Ibrahim Merchant, Joel Hegg, Ash Wise and Andrew Wu (University of Illinois) for their "3-D Drunk Driving Simulator." All winners and their faculty advisors received cash prizes and a crystal award. 

The competition gained prominence through the 1990s as the BFGoodrich Collegiate Inventors Program. The National Inventors Hall of Fame is now actively seeking a new corporate sponsor to expand the program. The U.S. Department of Commerce, Patent and Trademark Office, an original founder of the National Inventors Hall of Fame, continues to play a strong supporting role in this program. Q. Todd Dickinson, commissioner of patents and trademarks, adds, "We are proud to be a part of what has become the world's leading program honoring collegiate inventors." "This is a tremendous opportunity for a corporation to increase its campus visibility and become involved with the most innovative students at the finest colleges and universities in the country," adds National Inventors Hall of Fame CEO David Fink. 

The National Inventors Hall of Fame was founded in the early 1970s by the National Council of Intellectual Property Law Associations and the United States Patent and Trademark Office. In 1987, Akron, Ohio was selected as the permanent home for the National Inventors Hall of Fame, which is dedicated to recognizing and fostering invention, creativity and imagination. 

The collegiate inventors competition is open to full-time college students and their faculty advisors, for additional information call 330-762-4463 or contact Megan Gottschalk at 330-849-6912, or visit http://www.invent.org.

Feynman Prize in Nanotechnology Awarded to IBM, Caltech Researchers: Nanotech Researchers Meet to Announce Advances Toward Ultimate Limits 

554 words 
21 October 1999
21:00 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

SANTA CLARA, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Oct. 21, 1999--The 1999 Feynman Prizes in nanotechnology were awarded this weekend to Phaedon Avouris of IBM for experimental work, and to a team led by William A. Goddard III at Caltech for theoretical work. 

Dr. Avouris, of the IBM T.J.Watson Research Center in Yorktown Heights, NY, is a leader in the development of carbon nanotubes for potential computing device applications. This work is considered directly on the pathway to molecular-scale computation -- necessary for the computer industry to stay on the Moore's Law curve, which predicts atomic-level precision before 2015. 

Professor William Goddard, Dr. Tahir Cagin, and Ms. Yue Qi shared the theory prize for their work in modeling the operation of molecular machine designs. Proposed designs for future molecular machine systems can be tested today on powerful supercomputers using sophisticated programs that accurately model the laws of chemistry, giving us a clearer picture both of what works and what doesn't work. Goddard's group -- which operates out of the Materials and Process Simulation Center, Caltech, in Pasadena, CA -- does some of the most advanced modeling possible today. 

The Prizes include a cash award of $5000 per team. They are named in honor of the late Nobel Prizewinning physicist Richard Feynman, whose 1959 talk "There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom" inspired many researchers to pursue the ultimate in miniaturization. 

From nanostructured materials to biological motors, work on new nanoscale tools, devices, and designs were presented to an international audience of 300 in Silicon Valley this weekend at the Seventh Foresight Conference on Molecular Nanotechnology. Molecular nanotechnology is expected to enable atomic precision in fields ranging from medicine to manufacturing, extending lifespan and curing disease, and eliminating waste and chemical pollution. 

Keynoted by Nobel Prizewinning chemist John Polanyi of the University of Toronto, the four-day meeting brought together representatives of nanoscale ventures in academia, national laboratories, Fortune 500 companies, and nanotechnology startups drawn from nearly twenty countries and five continents. 

Attendees were treated to a field trip to NASA Ames where they were shown a simulation of Virtual MechanoSynthesis (VMS) in a realtime 3D virtual environment. 

Also presented at the meeting was the Foresight Distinguished Student Award, which went to Anita Goel, an MD/PhD candidate at the Harvard/MIT Division of Health Sciences and Technology and also a PhD candidate at Harvard's Physics Department. Ms. Goel was selected for her work on using optical and magnetic "tweezers" to probe the real-time single molecule dynamics of motor enzymes "dancing on DNA."

Quantum Dot Corporation Obtains Exclusive License to Luminescent Nanoparticles From Indiana University 

291 words 
2 November 1999
13:45 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BW HealthWire)--Nov. 2, 1999--Quantum Dot Corporation announced today that it has obtained an exclusive license on luminescent nanoparticles from Indiana University. 

Under the license, Quantum Dot Corporation received exclusive, worldwide rights to develop, manufacture, market, and commercialize biological applications of Quantum Dot(TM) (Qdot(TM)) particles. 

Qdot particles, nanometer-sized semiconductor material that light up like molecular-sized LEDs, enable the detection and barcoding of biological materials from DNA to proteins. Applications of the technology include genetic analysis, flow cytometry, high-throughput screening, fluorescence microscopy, drug discovery, and diagnostics. 

"The license from Indiana University is the forth of its kind for Quantum Dot Corp and further strengthens our patent portfolio and position," commented Joel Martin. "We are committed to further enhancing our leadership in the commercialization of biological applications of Qdot particles." Quantum Dot Corp has three other exclusive, world-wide licenses from Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the Ernest Orlando Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory and the University of Melbourne. 

According to Dr. Shuming Nie, professor of chemistry at Indiana University, "Quantum Dots have captured the imagination of biological researchers. Scientists immediately appreciate the improvements in sensitivity and multiplexing." Dr. Nie is an expert in the field of quantum dot particles and is on Scientific Advisory Board at Quantum Dot Corp. 

Quantum Dot Corporation was founded in November 1998 and is located in Palo Alto. The company and its advisors are the world's leading experts in quantum dot technology and its applications. Additional information on the company and the quantum dot technology can be found at www.qdots.com.

PLAINVIEW, NY--(BUSINESS WIRE)--November 5, 1999--Veeco Instruments Inc. (NASDAQ:VECO) and Monarch Labs, Inc., have executed a worldwide partnership agreement for the marketing, distribution and support of magnetic performance test equipment. This agreement, combined with the recent acquisition of OptiMag, Inc., marks the continued expansion of Veeco's metrology line for the data storage industry. 

Monarch's QSW(TM) is a fully automated test system for characterizing the magnetoresistance of bulk films and patterned devices. The instrument monitors the device performance of giant magneto-resistive (GMR) heads used in high-density disk drives, providing essential feedback for process control and device performance improvement. 

Veeco's Metrology Group will add Monarch's QSW and other quasi-static test products to its metrology family, which currently includes optical profilers, atomic force microscopes (AFMs), stylus profilers, optical defect review stations, and X-Ray fluorescence systems. 

Edward H. Braun, Chairman, President and CEO of Veeco, commented, "Monarch's device testing capabilities ideally fit our strategy to provide one-stop metrology and test support for our data storage customers. We are pleased to add this technology, as it both complements and expands our metrology family." 

Dennis Cahalan, President of Monarch Labs, said, "Our agreement with Veeco allows us to rapidly expand our channels of distribution and to draw upon Veeco's excellent worldwide support network. By combining our strengths, we look forward to fulfilling new testing needs for next-generation head and drive designs." 

Monarch Labs, Inc., located in Longmont, CO., develops and manufactures automated quasi-static test systems for research and manufacturing applications in the data storage industry. 

Veeco Instruments Inc., headquartered in Plainview, New York is a worldwide leader in metrology tools for the data storage and semiconductor industries, and process equipment etch and deposition tools for the data storage industry. Manufacturing and engineering facilities are located in New York, California and Arizona. Global sales and service offices are located throughout the United States, Europe, Japan and Asia Pacific.

Powdermet Announces Expansion Plans 

392 words 
9 November 1999
16:15 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

SUN VALLEY, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 9, 1999--Powdermet Inc. Tuesday announced its plans to expand to 2,000,000 lb/year capacity for its nanoengineered powder products. 

Powdermet's engineered raw materials enable dramatic increases in material wear, corrosion, strength, and toughness to be achieved while reducing costs to metal and ceramic component and coatings manufacturers. 

Powdermet's objective is to change the way advanced materials are designed, manufactured, and used both domestically and globally. 

Powdermet achieves this vision through its unique capability to manufacture engineered particles using its patented Fast-Fluidized Bed Chemical Vapor Deposition (FFBCVD) process. The FFBCVD process enables atomic level control over metal and ceramic microstructures, and hence the final material properties, to be designed and built in to the raw material at very low added cost. 

Powdermet's specialty powder products are distributed to component manufacturers in the electronic packaging, automotive, tool and die, heavy equipment, and aerospace and defense market segments, and to thermal spray and wire arc transfer coatings suppliers. 

Customers using Powdermet's engineered raw materials report up to a 500% increase in tool life compared to current coated carbide tools. Other customers have reported that a 32% cost savings was achieved through the elimination of additional processing, a savings enabled through the use of Powdermet's engineered raw materials. 

On November 10th, Powdermet will be presenting its expansion and marketing plans to investors from throughout southern California at the California Venture Forum at Claremont McKenna College. 

Powdermet has also been selected to present its technology at the 1999 Advanced Technology Program National Meeting on Nov 16, 1999 at the San Jose DoubleTree hotel. 

Founded in 1996, Powdermet is a world leader in nanoengineered materials. The Company acquired 22 years worth of development technology from Ultramet Inc. in 1997, and has secured over $2M in development funds from government and industry customers to develop its next generation of engineered materials. 

Powdermet's President Andrew Sherman, anticipates securing required financing for Powdermet's expansion within the next quarter. "We expect to exceed our (50 ton) capacity within five months, and I have no intention of letting our customers down. This investor's forum has absolutely ideal timing for us."

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BW HealthWire)--Nov. 16, 1999--Quantum Dot Corporation (QDC) reported today that the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has issued pioneering U.S. Patent No. 5,990,479 to the Regents of the University of California for semiconductor nanoparticle (QDOT(TM)) conjugates and their uses in biological, biomedical and biochemical applications. This patent, exclusively licensed for these applications to QDC, claims compositions including semiconductor nanocrystals capable of being linked to biological affinity molecules, methods for preparing QDOT(TM) probes using these compositions and methods for determining the presence of analytes in biological systems using the QDOT(TM) probes. Their work is already improving the sensitivity and speed of biological measurements including everything from DNA arrays to diagnostics." 

"We are delighted that this powerful patent has been issued by the U.S. Patent Office," commented Ken Barovsky, Ph.D., Vice President and Intellectual Property Counsel at QDC. "QDC has further strengthened the extensive patent portfolio it has licensed exclusively from Berkeley Lab, MIT, Indiana University and the University of Melbourne." IBM Technology helps U.S. Airforce Design Safer Planes; RS/6000 SP Supercomputer Selected by Wright-Patterson 

706 words 
17 November 1999
22:54 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

DAYTON, Ohio--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 17, 1999--IBM today announced that the Aeronautical Systems Center (ASC) Major Shared Resource Center (MSRC) at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base has installed an IBM RS/6000 SP supercomputer to support its aircraft safety research. 

This Wright-Patterson system ranks fifty-ninth on the TOP500 list of the world's fastest supercomputers issued this week. (www.top500.org) 

The RS/6000 SP enables the ASC MSRC to carry out complex calculations and simulations pertaining to computational fluid dynamics, computational chemistry and materials, signal/image processing, computational electronics and nanoelectronics, computational electro-magnetics and acoustics, and computational structural mechanics to improve the safety and security features of airplanes. 

These simulation tests are designed to analyze how certain factors like wind flow, heat and combustion processes affect the aerodynamics and structural composition of aircraft. Engineers using the RS/6000 SP to identify the ideal compound for designing the interior and exterior structures of planes. The aim is build a stronger, safer aircraft. 

"Wright Patterson's use of an RS/6000 SP gives them access to the world's leading high performance computing platform." says Michael Henesey, director worldwide sales and marketing for scientific and technical computing, IBM RS/6000. "More and more researchers are turning to the SP for critical research in many industries including transportation, energy, and health care." 

The strength in the RS/6000 SP lies in its gigaflops (GFLOPS) performance allowing it to complete as many as 211 billion calculations per second. The new SP installed at Wright Patterson has 132 SMP nodes. Each node contains two POWER3 processors, 2 gigabytes of memory, 18 gigabytes of disk, the newest IBM compilers, and AIX, IBM's UNIX operating system. This parallel processing platform is more than ten times as powerful as the system made famous during Deep Blue's historic 1997 victory over world chess champion Garry Kasporov. 

"Defense scientists and engineers must constantly push the boundaries of known science to keep the technological edge for America's aviation industry. We need to keep America's fighting forces out of harm's way and the only way to do this is to be able to depend on a reliable and scalable supercomputing platform that has become synonymous with the SP," said John Blair, Deputy Director, ASC Major Shared Research Center, Wright-Patterson Airforce Base. "Its hard work but the payoff is that our military systems are top-notch." 

To assist users in large scale computing, the new SP system at Wright Patterson will provide one terabyte (one trillion bytes) of disk storage. 

The Aeronautical Systems Center at Wright Patterson Air Force Base was selected as the site of a Major Shared Resource Center, one of four, high-performance computing locations in the United States. The MSHC forecasts the needs of the Department of Defense well into the 21st century and tackles large-scale problems previously beyond the reach of current processing platforms. The MSRC, which will facilitate teaming with industry and several colleges and universities,(a) features computer-system upgrades enabling a three-fold and ultimately, 10-fold computing increase in capabilities.

(JRI) as Senior X-ray Research Scientist. 

JRI is the advanced laser and X-ray research and development arm of JMAR Technologies. 

Prior to joining JMAR, Dr. Vladimirsky participated in establishing synchrotron-based X-ray lithography processing facilities at the Singapore Synchrotron Light Source (SSLS) at the National University of Singapore where he also provided student guidance and supervised the technical and engineering staffs. Previously, he served as a Senior Scientist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison's Center for X-ray Lithography (CXRL), where he played a key role in X-ray, EUV and e-beam lithography development programs for next-generation integrated circuit fabrication and micromachining. During his tenure at CXRL, Dr. Vladimirsky received a lifetime appointment as Honorary Fellow of the Center for Nanotechnology.

It is a photographic technique using advanced light sources to transfer electronic circuit designs onto the semiconductor wafers and is the key to the industry's ability to produce ever-smaller and faster-operating integrated circuits. The annual market for semiconductor lithography equipment is several billion dollars. 

As semiconductor circuit sizes shrink, the cost of the more advanced lithography system light sources increase, making them an ever-greater portion of the total lithography system market. JMAR is developing laser and X-ray technologies to produce cutting-edge light sources to meet the needs of this growing market for next generation lithography equipment as well as other important new products.

SI Diamond Technology Inc. (OTC BB:SIDT) Tuesday announced that researchers from Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL), Berkeley, Calif., presented investigation results of carbon film samples provided by Field Emission Picture Element Technology Inc. (FEPET) a subsidiary of SI Diamond Technology Inc., at the 46th annual International Symposium of the American Vacuum Society that took place in Seattle in October 1999. 

FEPET has achieved carbon film samples showing one million emission sites per centimeter square. 

The results, presented as "Field emission from Flat Diamond-like Carbon Films Characterized by Scanning Force Microscopy," demonstrate that electron emitting carbon films grown by hot filament CVD techniques are very flat, with a roughness of 20 nanometers (=0.02 microns). This confirms FEPET's claim of a flat emitting cathode with no geometrically enhanced features at the surface, such as microtips. 

Furthermore, Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM) measurements at fields of approximately 50 volts per micrometer showed emission site densities to be on the order of 1 million emission sites per centimeter square. These recent results significantly enhance the understanding of the nature of these films and give new directions for further investigation and improvement. 

FEPET gratefully acknowledges the assistance of the Office of Energy Research, U.S. Deptartment of Energy, under CRADA contract DE-AC03-76SF00098 for supporting this work.

Ballistic Nanotransistor From Lucent's Bell Labs May Lead to Smaller and Faster Silicon Chips 

700 words 
6 December 1999
16:27 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(c) 1999 Business Wire

WASHINGTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Dec. 6, 1999--Researchers at Lucent Technologies' Bell Labs have developed a method to significantly improve the flow of current in nanoscale transistors -- a characteristic that may help the semiconductor industry continue making smaller and faster silicon chips. 

Dubbed a "ballistic nanotransistor" for its virtually unimpeded flow of current -- similar to a bullet whizzing through the air -- the device is roughly four times smaller than today's transistors. 

In recent years, the semiconductor industry has increased the performance of chips by decreasing the size of their transistors, which increases their switching speed. However, one component of a transistor - its insulating layer - will limit the continued shrinkage because a short circuit will occur when it becomes too thin; the insulating layer lies between the transistor's gate, which turns the current on and off, and the channel, through which current flows. 

To overcome the limitations posed by the insulating layer, the Bell Labs researchers decided to tackle another major factor that limits a transistor's speed: the resistance encountered by current as it flows through the channel. 

In today's silicon-based transistors, only 35 percent of the input current flows, via the channel, from a transistor's "source" to its "drain;" the remainder scatters as it collides with the rough edges of the insulating layer. 

"The electrons going through the channel are like a ball going through a pinball game," said Bell Labs researcher Greg Timp, who presented his research findings today at the International Electron Devices Meeting. "In our device, we not only made the channel very short to minimize the channel resistance, but we also removed nearly all the `pinball bumpers' by making the insulating layer smoother than it is in conventional transistors. This results in 85 percent of the current being transmitted from the source to the drain, which yields the ballistic transport." 

Although other researchers have attained ballistic effects in nanotransistors, they needed to cool their devices to nearly minus 200 degrees Centigrade to reduce the scattering, or they used exotic materials. 

"This is the first ballistic nanotransistor that operates at room temperature with conventional silicon technology," Timp said. 

The Bell Labs nanotransistor has a 40-nanometer gate, which is roughly 2,000 times smaller than the width of a human hair, and its channel length is 25 nanometers. 

There were several key elements involved in making a ballistic nanotransistor. Timp and his colleagues used an unconventional process, known as rapid thermal oxidation, to "grow" the insulating layer, or gate oxide, on the silicon wafer. This process adds oxygen to silicon at 1,000 degrees Centigrade for 10 seconds. 

"This results in a smooth interface between the silicon wafer and the gate oxide," Timp said. 

When Timp and his colleagues tested the new devices, they were surprised by a counterintuitive finding, which may have implications for the semiconductor industry. At first, the researchers tested nanotransistors with gate oxides that were only 1.3 nanometers thick, compared with today's average of 2.8 nanometers. The drive current efficiency was about 75 percent. However, when the researchers performed a computer simulation of a slightly thicker gate oxide -- 1.6-nanometers -- they predicted an 85 percent efficiency, which appeared odd because thicker gate oxides typically hinder current flow. Experimental results confirmed the prediction, which may ease the industry's need for making thinner gate oxide layers. 

"It appears that electrons travel better when the gate oxide is slightly thicker because the electrons are not as attracted to the gate, which is directly above the gate oxide layer," Timp said. 

Lucent Technologies, headquartered in Murray Hill, N.J., designs, builds and delivers a wide range of public and private networks, communications systems and software, data networking systems, business telephone systems and microelectronics components. Bell Labs is the research and development arm for the company. For more information on Lucent Technologies, visit the company's web site at http://www.lucent.com.
