Concurrent View Needed 

There are four major SoC design-closure issues: timing, signal integrity, power, and clock. All are interdependent, necessitating a concurrent view to resolve them. Resolving them calls for a blend of extraction, timing analysis, signal-integrity analysis, and optimization in a single engine. Failure to account for these effects concurrently inevitably leads to diminished performance and increased time to market. 

PhysicalStudio optimizes chip timing and signal-integrity issues concurrently, both before and after routing. It is fully interoperable with industry-standard routing tools, permitting existing physical design flows to reach fast, predictable design closure in silicon geometries below 180 nanometers. 

About PhysicalStudio 

PhysicalStudio allows system-on-chip designers to: 


   --  reach 35% higher clock speeds
   --  achieve a 5-15% reduction in power over traditional physical
        design flows
   --  compensate for signal integrity effects, such as
        crosstalk-induced "setup" violations and "hold" violations and
        functional "glitch" errors
   --  accurately predict and immunize against noise during placement
   --  surgically correct timing and signal-integrity issues "along
        the route" using a patent-pending FullContext post-route
        technique


By unifying placement-driven optimization and post-route optimization into a single engine, the product ensures that every net in a design is correctly driven and all timing and signal integrity violations are eliminated. PhysicalStudio operates on large, hierarchical designs with varying abstractions at the top-level such as register-bounded blocks, STAMP, LIB and CLF.

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 8, 2002--The Institute for Molecular Manufacturing (IMM), a non-profit organization established to provide funding to develop molecular nanotechnology, established the IMM Prizes in Computational Nanotechnology. Presented for the first time at a recent conference, the prizes were given to top researchers in three categories: design, rendering, and simulation. 

"The purpose of the IMM Prizes is to stimulate research in the design, analysis and visualization of molecular machines," said David Forrest, President of IMM. "In order for the general public, technical community, and policy makers to understand molecular manufacturing, there needs to be scientifically accurate and vivid visualizations of what this technology will make possible. These prizes recognize and highlight the very best of this work being done by researchers." 

The Design Prize, which involves a new design of molecular machine systems or component part, was presented to the team of Santiago Solares, Mario Blanco, and William A. Goddard III at the California Institute for Technology for their entry "Design of Nanomechanical Fluid Control Valve Based on Functionalized Silicon Cantilevers: Coupling Molecular Mechanics and Classical Engineering Design." The team provided and analyzed a novel design for the transport and precise flow control of molecules through a carbon nanotube. This design, based on the ability to constrict a nanotube by kinking it, could be constructed with existing technology. 

The Rendering Prize, which recognizes a new rendering that enables better visualization of an existing molecular machine system or component part, was awarded to Dr. Carl D. Montemagno at the University of California, Los Angeles for "Engineering the Molecular Sorter." Montemagno rendered compelling visual representations of the sorting and purification of target molecular using the molecular motors that have spindles coated with antibodies. 

The Simulation Prize, which is a new animation enabling better visualization over time of a molecular machine system, was given to Lawrence Fields and Jillian Rose of Phlesch Bubble Productions for their animation of a Freitas respirocyte, which is a machine that would function as a red blood cell, absorbing CO2 and releasing oxygen. The team's highly detailed, scientifically accurate and visually impressive animation simulated how a respirocyte would operate in the bloodstream. 

The IMM prizes include a $1,000 cash award in each category made possible by the generosity of IMM Senior Associate Dan Kindsvater. 

About Institute for Molecular Manufacturing

The Institute for Molecular Manufacturing (IMM) is a nonprofit foundation formed in 1991 to provide funding to develop molecular nanotechnology. Molecular nanotechnology, or MNT, is a technology based on assemblers able to build systems to complex atomic specification under programmable control. For more information visit the IMM Web site at www.IMM.org.

Sunlin Chou's Background 

Born in 1946 in Hong Kong, Chou joined Intel in 1971 -- less than three years after the company was founded -- and his career took him into multiple disciplines related to silicon technology. He designed Intel's first charge-coupled device (CCD) serial memory, then managed several generations of DRAM design and process development. 

In the mid-1980s, Chou led his team to develop high-yielding wafer fabrication processes and to ramp them into production using "copy exactly" techniques. By shortening technology introduction cycles from three years to two, his team made Intel the industry leader in manufacturing with new process technologies. 

In the 1990s, Chou spread this successful approach to other technology areas, including packaging and testing. He expanded Intel's long-range research efforts and is leading the Extreme Ultraviolet (EUV LLC) consortium to bring a new scalable lithographic technology into production in the second half of this decade.

HP Receives Another Key Molecular Electronics Patent; Invention Portfolio Continues to Grow 

629 words 
12 November 2002
16:01 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

PALO ALTO, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 12, 2002--Continuing its groundbreaking efforts in the emerging field of nanotechnology, HP (NYSE:HPQ) today announced it has received a key U.S. patent that helps consolidate and strengthen its growing portfolio of inventions in molecular electronics. 

"We aim to do nothing less than reinvent the computer and this patent is the foundation of the effort," said R. Stanley Williams, HP Fellow and director, Quantum Science Research (QSR), HP Labs. 

The patent, "Chemically Synthesized and Assembled Electronic Devices" (US 6,459,095), describes a simple, inexpensive and scalable chemical process that could be used in creating a variety of molecular-scale electronic devices -- including logic, memory, communications and signal routing devices -- using two crossed wires "sandwiching" electrically addressable molecules. 

Although much of the work has been disclosed in three previous patents issued to HP and UCLA(1), the current patent reflects HP's effort to create a complete, manufacturable molecular electronics technology. 

The inventors are James R. Heath, currently UCLA chemistry professor and former director of the California NanoSystems Institute, whose group collaborates with HP Labs; Philip J. Kuekes, HP senior scientist and computer architect in QSR, and Williams. (Heath will become Elizabeth W. Gilloon Professor and professor of chemistry at the California Institute of Technology Jan. 1, 2003.) 

The three also have just been named to the Scientific American 50, the noted magazine's first list recognizing scientific and technological contributions from the past year that provide a vision of a better future. 

Their invention relates to a method for going beyond the theoretical material limits of conventional silicon processes -- expected to be reached in about a decade -- by creating electronic devices made by trapping electrically switchable molecules between crossed wires only a few atoms wide. A bit of logic or memory could be stored at each intersection of wires. 

In conventional integrated circuit fabrication, complex patterns of wires and switches must be precisely built up a layer at a time. With the new invention, however, the wires need not cross at precise points or angles, and the function of the molecules can be defined after the device has been built. 

"This is an approach that we believe will enable the industry to extend Moore's Law for another 50 years," said Heath. Moore's Law states that integrated circuits essentially double in power every 18 months. It is widely recognized in the semiconductor industry and named after Intel co-founder Gordon Moore. 

"We believe that this basic architecture can be used to build nanoscale electro-chemical cells that are useful electronically in a variety of ways," Kuekes added. 

"It's important to recognize that this is a whole new field and a lot of work remains to be done," Williams said. "That's why we're talking about it -- to encourage others to pursue research as well. The more people working on it, the stronger it will become, and that will benefit everybody." 

About HP 

HP is a leading global provider of products, technologies, solutions and services to consumers and businesses. The company's offerings span IT infrastructure, personal computing and access devices, global services and imaging and printing. HP completed its merger transaction involving Compaq Computer Corporation on May 3, 2002. More information about HP is available at http://www.hp.com.

Cray Inc. Announces Cray X1 System, World's Most Powerful Supercomputer Product; ``Extreme Performance'' Supercomputer Will Help Advance the Frontiers of Science and Engineering

(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

SEATTLE--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 14, 2002-- 

Company Accepts Challenge to Provide Sustained Petaflop Computing 

Speed -- 1,000 Trillion Calculations Per Second -- by 2010 

Global supercomputer leader Cray Inc. (Nasdaq:CRAY) today announced the Cray X1(TM) system, the world's most powerful supercomputer product. 

The new product is available with up to 52.4 trillion calculations per second (teraflops) of peak computing power and 65.5 terabytes of memory. U.S. list pricing starts at about $2.5 million. 

The high-efficiency, extreme-performance system is aimed at the critical computing needs of classified and unclassified government, academic research, and the weather-environmental, automotive, aerospace, chemical and pharmaceutical markets. 

Cray also announced today that it is the first company to accept the challenge, as stated in a 1999 report of the President's Information Technology Advisory Committee, to provide actual, sustained (not merely "theoretical peak") petaflop computing speed -- 1,000 trillion calculations per second -- for critical next-generation applications by 2010. 

Along with previously announced initial orders for Cray X1 systems, Cray expects substantial additional orders in the year-end 2002 timeframe. The company recently reported that five early-production Cray X1 units passed acceptance tests at the U.S. Army High Performance Computing Research Center (AHPCRC) and undisclosed customer sites, and that Spain's National Institute of Meteorology (INM) placed an $8.4 million, multi-year order for a Cray X1 system. Cray plans to ship the first production system later this year, with the manufacturing ramp-up scheduled to begin in early 2003. 

The AHPCRC is the first site in the DoD High Performance Computing Modernization Program to acquire a Cray X1 system. AHPCRC scientists already have implemented widely used weather forecasting, computational mechanics, and computational fluid dynamics application codes on their two early production systems. 

In August 2002, the U.S. Department of Energy announced that Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) had been selected to test the effectiveness of the Cray X1 system in solving important scientific problems in climate, fusion, biology, nanoscale materials and astrophysics. Dr. Raymond L. Orbach, director of the department's Office of Science, said the program is part of an effort to provide the U.S. scientific community with computing resources to match or exceed those of the new Japanese "Earth Simulator," which has an effective speed more than 20 times that of the fastest U.S. civilian supercomputer. Under the program, ORNL initially will acquire a 32-processor Cray X1 supercomputer for evaluation. 

"The Cray X1 system is designed to scale to deliver performance for key scientific applications greater than the performance of currently available U.S. computers. It is the first U.S. computer to offer vector processing and massively parallel processing capabilities in a single architecture," said ORNL's Associate Director for Computing and Computational Sciences, Thomas Zacharia. "We are pleased to partner with Cray to provide U.S. scientists with the computational power to solve the most demanding science applications." 

Sustained Petaflop Goal 

"The Cray X1 product is a major milestone en route to our goal of enabling the world's most creative scientists and engineers to run challenging applications at sustained petaflop speed by the end of this decade," said Cray Chairman and CEO James Rottsolk. "Our product roadmap is focused on this commitment. Other key initiatives, including our previously announced $90 million contract to develop and deliver the 'Red Storm' supercomputer to Sandia National Laboratory, our DARPA HPCS contract for advanced research on trans-petaflops computer systems, and further experience with our multithreaded MTA-2(TM) system will accelerate our progress toward this goal." 

Rottsolk said that in meetings such as the Petaflops I (1994) and Petaflops II (1999) conferences, experts identified crucial problems requiring petaflop speed. "These problems range from basic science to severe weather forecasting, full-fidelity automotive crash testing, advanced aircraft and spacecraft design, rapid detection of wildfires, virtual surgery planning, national economic modeling, combating pandemics and bioterrorism, improving electrical power generation and distribution, advanced drug discovery methods, and many more." The Cray X1 system will allow users to begin addressing these next-generation applications, he said. 

World's Most Powerful Supercomputer Product 

With innovative processors more than four times faster than in today's typical cluster products, and seven to 40 times more memory bandwidth for solving big, complex problems efficiently, the Cray X1 supercomputer promises to help advance the frontiers of science and engineering across a broad spectrum of disciplines. Cluster products are collections of individual servers or PCs, rather than tightly integrated supercomputers, and are adept at handling smaller, less complicated problems. 

"Current 'clustered' systems provide a low initial purchase price and can be broadly deployed, but they do not necessarily provide the highest levels of performance for next-generation scientific and engineering problems," said Debra Goldfarb, IDC group vice president, Worldwide Systems and Servers. "The Cray X1 is masterfully designed to address these strategically important requirements and, based on early indications, has the potential to return Cray to leadership in the high-end supercomputer segment." 

The new product features ultra-fast (12.8 gigaflops) individual processors, up to 819 gigaflops (billions of calculations per second) of peak computing power in a single chassis, and a high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnect for substantially more efficient scaling than on clustered SMP systems. Cray X1 systems are available with 8-4,096 processors (2-1,024 nodes) and 32 gigabytes-65.5 terabytes of memory. 

"The Cray X1 supercomputer is the successor to Cray MPP and vector products," said Steve Scott, chief architect of the Cray X1 system. "Programmers with experience using clustered systems will also find the Cray X1 environment familiar: MPI, cache-based, distributed memory, 32- and 64-bit IEEE support. Shmem, Co-array Fortran and UPC programming models are available for leading-edge work benefiting from the very low latency and communication overhead of true shared memory." 

Broad Applicability 

"It is not just large government projects or major university research sites that desire an alternative to standard parallel systems built from off-the-shelf processors," according to Rich Partridge, Enterprise Systems analyst at D.H. Brown Associates. "Automotive design/analysis, biotech research such as protein folding, petrochemical seismic analysis, and other compute-intensive fields eagerly await the arrival of Cray's new high-bandwidth, low-latency X1 design. Cray has not succumbed to the attack of the low-priced commodity providers, but instead is in the process of re-establishing its leadership as the premier high-performance computing provider." 

"A lot of people have argued that cluster systems are cheaper than semi-custom systems such as the Cray X1. The fact of the matter is, they're not cheaper," said Paul Muzio, AHPCRC Support Infrastructure Director. "When we did our total life-cycle cost analysis, it turns out that clusters are fairly expensive -- a lot more expensive than people would think, especially when you look at the relatively low level of sustained performance that you get out of the processors on a cluster system, and compare that with the higher levels of sustained performance on the Cray X1. The Cray X1 will allow AHPCRC, Army, and DoD researchers to address a set of key problems in computational mechanics, battlefield weather forecasting, and biological process modeling that are of great importance to the defense of the United States." 

Rottsolk said he also expects the Cray X1 product to benefit the automotive and aerospace industries. "For example, the computational capability of the Cray X1 system is very applicable to the types of problems Ford Motor Company is trying to solve. Ford has utilized Cray capability-class systems in the past, and we look forward to partnering with Ford in the future on their most challenging problems." 

"In the next eight years, the Cray X1 and its successors are going to enable users for the first time to do very, very complex simulations that are biologically and medically relevant," said Dr. Frederick Hausheer, chairman and CEO of BioNumerik Pharmaceuticals, Inc. As part of a previously announced agreement, Germany's Konrad-Zuse-Zentrum fur Informationstechnik Berlin (ZIB) and Bielefeld University will be given access to the Cray X1 system to develop advanced software solutions for some of the most challenging problems in the new field of bioinformatics. 

"The new Cray X1 system will dramatically increase the computing capability of INM for operational numerical weather prediction and for research in climate and atmospheric modeling. The new system will play a major role in the improvement of short and very short range forecasting in Spain in coming years," said Ricardo Riosalido, Head, Observations and Instruments at INM. 

Ohio Supercomputer Center helped Cray evaluate I/O node technologies and data archiving tools for the Cray X1 product. Cray recently announced an agreement for Iowa State University to test software products developed by the company for the Cray X1(TM) system, and that it will use the StorNext(R) File System from Advanced Digital Information Corporation (Nasdaq:ADIC) as the primary SAN file system for the new supercomputer. Separately today, Samsung Semiconductor, Inc., announced that Cray selected Samsung RDRAM as the memory technology for the Cray X1 product.

MENLO PARK, Calif. and TOKYO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 14, 2002-- 

The Takeda Techno-Entrepreneurship Award Funds R&D Which Creates 

and Applies Engineering Intellect and Knowledge 

The Takeda Foundation has announced the recipients of this year's Takeda Techno-Entrepreneurship Award. This international award is presented to researchers and engineers who are engaged in the challenge to create new technology that contribute positively to people's lives. The monetary value of each award, presented in six application areas, is a maximum of 7,000,000 yen (approximately US$55,000). 

The Takeda Foundation has created an innovative screening process for selecting research proposals. Award winners are selected through an open process based on competitive "cyber (online) workshops." Applicants have the opportunity to comment on each other's proposals, as well as to respond to the selection committee's inquiries. Research proposals that display an outstanding level of techno-entrepreneurship are selected for the award. At the same time, the selection process provides a forum for information exchange and collaboration by participants. This year, 6 winners were selected from 132 applicants. 

The Takeda Techno-Entrepreneurship Award ceremony will be held jointly with the Takeda Award ceremony at the ANA Hotel in Tokyo, Japan, on November 20, 2002.

JMAR Technologies Reports Third Quarter 2002 Results 

2,194 words 
14 November 2002
13:30 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

SAN DIEGO--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 14, 2002--JMAR Technologies Inc. (Nasdaq\NM:JMAR) 


   --  Revenues Up 35% From Prior Year First Nine Months on Continued
        Expansion of Lithography Program Revenues
   --  Collimated Plasma Lithography Beta Test Model Source Meets 20
        Watts Average Sustained Power Goal


JMAR Technologies, Inc. (Nasdaq\NM:JMAR), a provider of advanced lasers, Collimated Plasma Lithography (CPL(TM)) systems, precision microelectronic products, and semiconductor industry services today announced results for its third quarter and nine months ended Sept. 30, 2002. 

For its third quarter, the company reported that revenues increased 34% to $7,325,395 from $5,447,090 in the comparable year-ago period, and that, on a sequential basis, revenue improved 19% from the $6,133,686 reported in the second quarter of this year. For the third quarter ended Sept. 30, 2002, JMAR reported a net loss of $2,836,656, or $0.12 per share, compared to a net loss of $2,555,466, or $0.11 per share for the same quarter last year. The net loss for the 2002 quarter included a charge of $1,074,324, or approximately $0.05 per share, relating to the obligation to pay certain retirement benefits to former Chairman and Chief Executive Officer John S. Martinez, Ph.D. who retired on Aug. 16, 2002. This included a non-cash charge related to the modification of options and warrants held by Dr. Martinez. 

JMAR's improvement in revenues for the quarter was attributable to increases in contract revenue at JMAR Research Inc. (JRI), JMAR/SAL NanoLithography Inc. (JSAL), and the semiconductor process technology business of JMAR Semiconductor Inc. (JSI). JMAR Precision Systems Inc. (JPSI) experienced a decrease in revenues as the semiconductor industry continued to suspend purchases of the capital equipment produced by JPSI and other manufacturers. 

For the first nine months of 2002, JMAR reported that revenues improved 35% to $17,995,597 from $13,311,632 in the comparable period of 2001. The net loss for the 2002 nine months was $4,586,442, or $0.20 per share including a loss of $1,548,861, or $0.07 per share, related to the discontinuation of the standard chip business at JSI, and $1,074,324, or nearly $0.05 per share, related to the obligation to pay retirement benefits to Dr. Martinez discussed above. The net loss for the comparable nine-month period of 2001 was $4,027,453, or $0.18 per share, including a loss from discontinued operations of $1,397,407, or $0.06 per share. 

The increase in revenues for the three- and nine-month periods of 2002 was primarily attributable to a significant increase in contract revenues for JMAR's CPL(TM) technology. Part of that increase was due to the addition of contracts held by JSAL, the company's semiconductor lithography system division, which became part of JMAR in August 2001. 

JMAR's total Research, Development and Engineering (RD&E) expenditures from both customer and company-funded programs for the development of high-performance microelectronics manufacturing equipment represented 65% and 59% of sales for the three months ended Sept. 30, 2002 and 2001, respectively, and 60% and 47% of sales for the first nine months of those years. Contract RD&E funds supported the continued development of the company's high-power laser technology and its CPL source and stepper systems. 

JMAR's strategy for commercializing CPL calls for initially using it to produce high-performance Gallium Arsenide (GaAs) semiconductors for military and commercial markets. While pursuing the technology's acceptance by those markets, the company is seeking the additional funding required to develop the next generation of its CPL systems. JMAR believes that the higher power and wafer throughput levels of these advanced systems will earn CPL recognition as the most cost-effective means of delivering reduced feature size lithography to the high-volume silicon semiconductor market. 

Commenting on the company's results and its continued progress in commercializing CPL, JMAR President and Chief Executive Officer Ronald A. Walrod said, "I feel very fortunate to have joined JMAR at such an exciting time in its history. Although the prolonged downturn of the semiconductor industry continues to exert a negative influence on our sales and earnings, particularly as that downturn is impacting our precision equipment business, I find the strong increase in contract revenues achieved at JRI and JSAL to be extremely encouraging. 

"The ongoing progress that is being made to advance CPL to market introduction is another very encouraging indication of what I believe lies ahead for JMAR," Walrod said. "After more than a decade of research and development aimed at delivering a viable next-generation lithography alternative to the semiconductor industry, JMAR's efforts are now nearing fruition. In San Diego, JRI has built, and is currently beta testing, its first CPL light source. I am very pleased to report that this source has already met its fundamental performance requirement, producing an average 20 watts of 1-nanometer light on a sustained basis. In Vermont, JSAL has now successfully beta tested the customized stepper it designed for our CPL system, achieving a stepper limited throughput rate of 17 wafers per hour that is right on target." 

"I am gratified by the patience and understanding shown by JMAR shareholders as we've worked to overcome the technical obstacles that are inherent in the development of this, or any other, leading-edge technology, and I'm confident that patience will be rewarded in the not-too-distant future," Walrod noted. "With that said, I'm sure those who have followed CPL's development will appreciate the fact that we will not try to compensate for the delays of the past by moving too quickly through CPL's pre-shipment source testing, which must be meticulous if we are to give this important technology, which has taken so long to develop, its best chance to succeed in the marketplace. As part of that discipline, we intend to complete the source's characterization and reliability testing in San Diego before shipping it to JSAL in Vermont for integration. 

"The rigorous testing now being conducted on the CPL source is essential in order to detect and remedy the engineering issues that inevitably surface when any complex, state-of-the-art system is worked up to full operational status," Walrod emphasized. "As part of that effort, and to facilitate the transition of the source from San Diego to Vermont, JSAL technical staff will soon come to JRI to participate in the source's operational reliability testing, to be trained on source operation and maintenance and to perform demonstrations of static lithography. I am confident that careful CPL source testing and the training of the JSAL team in San Diego will make the first integrated CPL stepper system demonstrations in Vermont all the more impressive and will save JMAR both time and money in the long run," said Walrod. 

Referring to JMAR's Precision Systems division, Mr. Joseph G. Martinez, acting president of JPSI said, "Unfortunately, despite the acceptance of our precision products by the semiconductor and other industries, we do not believe we have yet seen the bottom of the downturn in our precision equipment business. Although our motion and metrology products compete well at the high end of the market, many of our customers are delaying their equipment purchases out into 2003. We cannot predict when the semiconductor and other technology industries will rebound, but when it does we will be ready to react with a competitive product line that should generate attractive gross margins. In the meantime, we have responded with aggressive cost reductions that have substantially reduced JPSI's use of cash and its operating losses. At the same time, we are expanding our sales activity using both direct sales staff and manufacturer's representatives in the U.S. and internationally, and we are also looking outside the semiconductor industry for new markets for our metrology products." 

As previously reported in the first quarter of 2002, the company discontinued its standard specialty memory semiconductor products business at JSI, but retained its semiconductor fabrication technical support operation that services the Defense Microelectronics Activity's (DMEA) flexible foundry in Sacramento. JSI also continues to provide custom ASIC design services to its commercial and government customers. 

"Our semiconductor process technology operation in Sacramento is a stable and profitable service business. We are considering ways to leverage our core competence in semiconductor design and fabrication processes and operations to create growth in this business," Walrod said. 

"JMAR has been talking about the potential of its CPL technology for a long time as it worked to prove the physics and the feasibility of implementation," Walrod added. "Today we have both a beta test model source that is going through the reliability `hardening' process, and a thoroughly-tested stepper suitable for GaAs patterning. Soon the industry will see the complete beta test model CPL Stepper System in operation," he said. "I believe that 2003 will be a watershed year for JMAR as the value and full potential of CPL becomes more fully appreciated by the semiconductor industry. As interest builds, we will continue to actively seek alliances with dynamic industry players to augment JMAR's resources for advanced source and stepper development and to assure that mask and resist sources of supply are available to complement the CPL Stepper System itself. We believe JMAR and its prospective alliance partners will demonstrate a superior lithography technology and infrastructure, first for relatively low-volume compound semiconductors, then for specialty silicon semiconductors, and finally, for high-volume silicon semiconductors," Walrod concluded. 

JMAR Technologies Inc. is the world's leading developer and manufacturer of collimated laser plasma lithography sources and systems and X-ray lithography stepper systems for the semiconductor industry. It also develops proprietary advanced laser, one nanometer and EUV light sources for other high-value microelectronics applications. In addition, JMAR provides semiconductor process technologies and services and manufactures precision measurement, positioning and light-based manufacturing systems for inspection, repair, and fabrication of semiconductors, data storage devices, biomedical and optical communications products. 

The statements herein regarding JMAR's expectations for the successful development and introduction of its CPL systems and future sales and potential business opportunities are forward-looking statements based on current expectations that are subject to risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those set forth in the forward-looking statements. These risks include unanticipated delays in the first-time assembly and operation of a complex lithography system, delays in receipt of funding of its government contracts and delays in or the inability to obtain other financing in a timely manner to further commercialize the CPL products, the failure of the CPL technology to perform as predicted or to be fully developed and engineered into a commercial product that is accepted by gallium arsenide chip manufacturers, the failure to make improvements to the company's laser technology and to third party collimator, X-ray mask and resist technologies required to increase the throughput of the company's X-ray and CPL systems to meet the requirements of silicon chip manufacturers, the continued downturn in the semiconductor market and delays in receipt of orders from customers of precision systems products, the failure of pending patents to be issued, competition from alternative technologies, including electron beam, deep ultraviolet and extreme ultraviolet lithography technologies which have been more heavily funded than JMAR's CPL program, the failure of future orders to materialize as expected, delays in development, shipment or production, parts and labor shortages, cancellation or re-scheduling of orders, the inability to obtain financing when required on terms acceptable to the company, and the other risks detailed in the company's 2001 Form 10-K and other reports filed with the SEC.

HAYWARD, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 14, 2002--Quantum Dot Corporation (QDC), the leader in quantum dot biotechnology applications, announced today the launch of its first Qdot(TM) product. The Qdot(TM) 605 Streptavidin Conjugate, the first in a line of Qdot products, enables dramatic improvements in a wide range of bio-sensing applications. 

"This first product launch is an enormously significant milestone in our evolution into a commercial organization," said Carol C. Lou, QDC's President and Chief Operations Officer. "We have made many significant innovations in converting an academic curiosity into a business reality. Our core expertise in the commercialization of biologically active nanomaterials will enable the rapid launch of many additional products in 2003 and beyond. Our Qdot products give substantial performance improvements with a wide variety of installed instruments. We anticipate rapid adoption by the large number of scientists who require sensitive detection and visualization of biomolecules." 

The Qdot(TM) product comprises a multi-layered semiconductor nanocrystal attached to streptavidin, a specific biomolecule. Initial users of the Qdot(TM) technology have observed order-of-magnitude improvements in sensitivity, brightness, and stability in their bio-sensing applications. Currently supported applications include cell and tissue analysis, with many more applications scheduled for 2003. 

"We are selling our products directly to customers in life science and drug discovery research," added Andy R. Watson, VP of Business Development at QDC. "However, the breadth of applications for the Qdot technology is quite overwhelming, so we will be partnering with market-leading companies to open additional sales channels for quantum dot-based products. In vitro diagnostic testing and specific multiplexed research applications are our focus areas for partnering in the short term." 

Qdot(TM) nanocrystals, or quantum dots, are nanometer-sized semiconductor crystals that brightly light up specific biological events. These nano-scale molecular light emitting diodes (LEDs) allow rapid, parallel, and ultra-sensitive detection of biomolecular interactions. 

Founded in 1998, Quantum Dot Corporation is located in Hayward, CA. The company and its advisors are the world's leading experts in semiconductor nanocrystal (Qdot(TM)) technology and its biological applications. Additional information on QDC can be found at www.qdots.com.

CLEVELAND--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 18, 2002--Copernicus Therapeutics, Inc. a Cleveland company developing novel targeting and gene delivery systems with broad applications in human therapeutics and vaccines, announced today that it has completed a first close of $2 million toward a private placement financing round of $2.5 million. 

"We are pleased to report the first closing of a bridge financing round of over $2 million to support continued development of a cystic fibrosis (CF) gene therapy product," said Robert C. Moen, M.D., Ph.D., President and CEO of Copernicus. "This round will provide the resources required for continued development of our cystic fibrosis aerosol product as well as other products based on our DNA nanoparticle technology." 

Cystic fibrosis is the most common fatal genetic disease in the United States and Europe and represents a potential market size exceeding $2 billion.

"This is a significant event for Copernicus, Bob Moen, and the universities involved in the project, and it demonstrates that a Cleveland company can successfully raise capital from outside the region, even in a tough market," said BioEnterprise President Matt Jennings. 

"This is a win for both the company and the universities' technologies, and we are proud to be associated with it," said Mark Coticchia, CWRU Vice President of Research and Technology Management.

Copernicus Therapeutics, Inc. is advancing novel targeting and delivery systems with broad applications in human therapeutics and vaccines. Copernicus' technologies include a multi-component delivery platform that can be applied to nucleic acids to develop therapies for a variety of human diseases and a targeting platform enabling the efficient uptake of drugs by specific cells and tissues. The Company's targeting and delivery platforms are complementary and can be combined to enhance the efficacy and safety of existing drugs or to create novel therapeutics.

GLASGOW, Scotland--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 19, 2002-- 

Dr. Simon Hicks will detail the value of integrated 

optoelectronics & electronics approach 

At the Lightspeed Europe conference, Dr. Simon Hicks, Chief Technology Officer of Essient, will describe how his company's innovative use of Indium Phosphide enables a significant change in both economic and technical structures. Hicks will present "Unlocking Transponder Value using Ultra-Low Power Integrated Optoelectronics & Electronics." The conference will run from December 3 - 5 in London, and Dr. Hicks will speak on Wednesday, December 4, 10:15 to 11:30 a.m., as part of the Tomorrow's Technology Hot Startups Track. 

Essient, a supplier of integrated III-V optoelectronic components, recently introduced the Essient EA-MDA-10G - Electro Absorption Modulator-Detector with Integrated Amplification at 10Gbps, its first product. Essient will also be exhibiting at the show, Booth #324. 

During his presentation, Dr. Hicks will explore the benefits and challenges facing the integration of optoelectronics and electronics, and will illustrate how Essient's technology, realized through a fabless manufacturing model, can enhance electronic transceivers at 2.5, 10 and 40 Gbps. Through monolithic integration, Essient has combined electronic and optoelectronic functions on a single chip using standard III-V fabrication processes, resulting in reduced module costs, power requirements and module size. 

Previously, Dr. Hicks was the Chief Operations Officer of Kelvin Nanotechnology, during which time he built the company from initial creation to having a worldwide customer list of more than 50 companies. He has over 10 years' experience in R&D of fabrication processes for the high frequency electronics sector and the optoelectronics sector, concentrating mainly on optical WDM devices. In addition, Dr. Hicks was actively involved with the incubation, spinout and subsequent support of Kymata Ltd and Intense Photonics Ltd, and has authored 17 papers in international journals and is named on more than 5 patents. 

Now in its second year, Lightspeed Europe is sponsored by Light Reading and Penton Technology Media. TEL Announces Participation in Albany NanoTech Initiative

Business Wire

(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

AUSTIN, Texas--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 21, 2002--Tokyo Electron (TEL), today announced their participation in Albany NanoTech's new 300mm semiconductor research center at a press conference held on the campus of the University at Albany-State University of New York (UAlbany). TEL, the world's second largest supplier of semiconductor manufacturing equipment, has agreed to participate in the new center through a joint TEL-Albany NanoTech program, which is expected to generate more than $300 million in spending over seven years and support more than 300 research jobs. TEL's participation with Albany NanoTech is complementary to its current and future activities in Austin, Boston and Phoenix. 

The new NanoTech center will allow advanced semiconductor material and process research to be performed on 300mm equipment rather than laboratory scale systems, which will shorten the time from research and development to production. The center will be housed in two 300mm wafer cleanroom buildings. The first of these buildings is nearing completion and will begin operations in late 2003. Once both buildings are completed, they will house a fully-integrated semiconductor fabrication line capable of developing materials and processes for advanced semiconductor devices at the 45nm generation and beyond. 

TEL's participation in the Albany NanoTech project will provide them with significant opportunities to collaborate with leading industry companies, as well as the highly respected researchers from NanoTech. At this time, the exact details of TEL's participation in the Albany Initiative have not been finalized, but will include the installation of TEL tools at the facility, placement of TEL researchers and engineers, and joint leadership on a variety of advanced research projects. The new program will supplement TEL's global internal research and development activities and will complement its participation in leading industry consortia, such as International SEMATECH, SELETE and IMEC. 

Tetsuro Higashi, CEO, president TEL said, "TEL is very pleased with the opportunity to participate in Albany NanoTech's 300mm research facility. As a global leader in the semiconductor equipment industry, we constantly strive to find new and innovative ways to advance the science of semiconductor fabrication. By participating in this center, we will significantly enhance our internal development efforts, ultimately allowing us to shorten the time required to bring critical technology from the research lab to the production floor. This exemplifies our commitment to providing our customers with production-worthy, enabling technology according to the requirements and timing of their roadmaps." 

About TEL 

TEL, established in 1963, is a leading supplier of innovative semiconductor and FPD production equipment worldwide. Product lines include coater/developers, thermal processing systems, dry etchers, CVD systems, sputtering systems (PVD), wet cleaning systems, and test systems. In Japan, TEL distributes other leading edge semiconductor equipment tools, such as metrology tools and process control systems. In addition, TEL distributes high quality computer systems, semiconductor devices and electronic components of other leading suppliers, as well as computer network related products from around the world. To support this diverse product base, TEL has strategically located research & development, manufacturing, sales, and service locations all over the world. TEL is a publicly held company listed on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. http://www.tel.co.jp.

Altair Nanotechnologies' New Swimming Pool Treatment Eliminates Algae; This New Safe and Efficient Algae Treatment Is Not a Biocide 

786 words 
25 November 2002
14:45 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

RENO, Nev.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 25, 2002--Altair Nanotechnologies (Nasdaq:ALTI) today announced that it has developed a novel nano-structured compound that effectively prevents the growth of algae in swimming pools. 

This new compound is highly insoluble in water and easily filters through existing conventional pool filtration systems without the use of flocculants or auxiliary chemicals. The company emphasizes that the algae prevention compound is not a biocide and is safe and effective with no pool downtime required during the algae prevention treatment. 

"The amazing thing about this new compound is that it not only works to prevent algae growth in a highly efficient manner but continues to work even when embedded in a pool filtration system and is insoluble in water," said Altair Nanotechnologies President Dr. Rudi E. Moerck. 

Unwanted algae growth in swimming pools is a major problem for pool owners worldwide and generally requires aggressive chemical treatment to remedy the problem, particularly if algae bloom takes place. 

"The use of Altair's low-cost algae prevention treatment prevents the unsightly occurrence of visible black or green algae growth, eliminates filter fowling caused by biomass accumulation and avoids the use of chemical shock or algaecide treatments required if an algae bloom does occur," noted Moerck. 

"With Altair's product there is no need to purchase expensive algaecides or costly electrolysis equipment often employed to prevent algae growth. 

"We want to emphasize that the technology and intellectual property Altair is employing in this application already exists within the company and we are simply applying it to a new and potentially large market which, according to statistics provided by the National Swimming Pool and Spa Institute, consists of approximately 8 million pools and 4 million existing spas and hot tubs worldwide, with an additional 360,000 pools and approximately 260,000 spas and hot tubs being installed on a yearly basis." 

The company's goal is to license its technology to a company that already serves the swimming pool industry, as Altair does not plan to either manufacture or distribute the new compound. Altair believes it can have the new swimming pool algae product in the market through a partner by late spring. 

According to Moerck, the company is also investigating the use of this new compound for prevention of algae growth in cooling towers and in commercial fish farming. 

"We believe it is important to note that the company has discussed the potential delisting issue with NASDAQ," commented Dr. Moerck. "Management has developed and is implementing a plan that is expected to extend the listing of the company's common stock on the NASDAQ System until June 2003. The company expects to meet the minimum bid criteria prior to the June 2003 date." 

Altair Nanotechnologies Inc. 

In addition to supplying a unique titanium dioxide pigment process technology to pigment manufacturers, Altair Nanotechnologies is positioning itself through product innovation within the emerging nanotechnology industry. Altair owns a proprietary technology for making nanocrystalline materials of unique quality both economically and in large quantities. 

The company is currently developing special nanomaterials with potential applications in pharmaceuticals, fuel cells, solar cells, advanced energy storage devices, thermal spray coatings, catalysts, cosmetics, paints and environmental remediation. For additional information on Altair's nanoparticle materials, visit www.altairnano.com.

ISE Announces Expanded Usage of Its TCAD Software in 3D Device Simulation At Major Customer; ISE TCAD Performs Accurate Simulation of DSM and LDMOS Power Device Semiconductor Technologies 

498 words 
25 November 2002
15:00 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

SAN JOSE, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 25, 2002--Integrated Systems Engineering (ISE) today announced that Texas Instruments (TI) is expanding usage of ISE's technology-leading TCAD (Technology CAD) simulation software. Under prior agreement (see press release dated March 22, 2001), ISE 2D device simulation tools had already been in use by TI to develop its latest, most advanced semiconductor fabrication processes. Deployment of ISE tools will now be expanded to 3D device simulation applications in TI, Dallas and TI, Manchester, New Hampshire. 

"Our current research in the area of ultra-thin SOI and double gate structures, including fully depleted SOI structures and FinFETs, underscored the importance to investigate 3D effects in such structures," said Dennis Buss, Vice President of Si Technology Development at TI. "Moreover, ultra thin and ultra short devices demand that we address velocity overshoot and quantization effects. We found that ISE DESSIS 3D is the best choice to address these issues that are so important in nanoscale devices. DESSIS 3D is clearly an efficient tool for investigation of complicated issues which we face in the current state of DSM technology development." 

As semiconductor companies face the development of advanced semiconductor processes and microelectronic devices, the role of fast and accurate simulation tools has become essential to successful process and device development. TCAD provides early feedback describing the impact of process and device design changes at any stage of the product design and process development cycles. 

"Advances in power device design lead to high-performance, reliable power ICs at low cost," said Taylor Efland, a TI Fellow and power device technology expert. "With DESSIS 3D we are able to capture true three-dimensional effects essential for the accurate modeling of the advanced LDMOS structures in our SOI technology." 

"TI's existing agreement with ISE already provided TI with access to the most advanced TCAD simulation capabilities available," said Wolfgang Fichtner, Founder and CEO of ISE. "TI's expanded usage under this agreement to take advantage of our advanced tools for 3D device simulation in both power and DSM semiconductor applications speak to the superiority of ISE tools in a broad application space." 

About ISE 

ISE AG is a leading provider of TCAD tools worldwide. ISE focuses on TCAD, and offers software solutions and consulting services for the world's largest semiconductor fabrication facilities. Founded in 1993, the company is privately held with headquarters in Zurich, Switzerland at Balgriststrasse 102 CH-8008 Zurich, and a subsidiary ISE, Inc. located in San Jose, California at 111 N. Market Suite, Suite 710, San Jose, CA 95113. For more information, please visit our website at http://www.ise.com.

Transducers '03: The 12th International Conference on Solid-State Sensors, Actuators and Microsystems will take place at the Boston Marriott Copley Place from June 8-12, 2003. Transducers '03 continues a series of biennial conferences that began in Boston in 1981, and are held in odd-numbered years, alternating between North America, Asia and Europe. These conferences have been the premier forum for reporting research results in microsensors, microactuators, MEMS (micro-electro-mechanical systems) and microsystems. Transducers '03 is sponsored by the IEEE Electron Device Society. Transducers '03 will bring new important advances in materials and microfabrication processes; innovative designs for physical, chemical, and bio sensors, and microactuators; applications areas such as wireless sensor networks, optical MEMS, RF MEMS, micro total analysis systems; interface electronics; and modeling and CAD tools. As the largest gathering worldwide in this rapidly-expanding field, Transducers '03 is where the latest research results are presented to the broadest possible audience. 

Dr. G. Benjamin Hocker, Transducers '03 General Chairman, said, "Transducers '03 provides a unique opportunity for professionals engaged in microsensor, microactuator, MEMS and microsystems technology to report the results of their research, to learn of the work of others conducted in this area, and to meet and network with fellow researchers. Our technical program committee will be faced with a challenge to select the final presentations and posters from the large number of high-quality papers we expect to be submitted. An outstanding group of plenary and invited speakers has already been arranged. We will provide our attendees with an exceptional technical experience."

Altair Nanotechnologies President Provides Project Update; Expects to Achieve Profitability in 2003 

1,376 words 
26 November 2002
14:02 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

RENO, Nev.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Nov. 26, 2002--Altair Nanotechnologies Inc. (Nasdaq:ALTI) today announced that it has increased sales in both battery materials and thermal spray coatings and, according to Altair Nanotechnologies President Dr. Rudi E. Moerck has made significant progress in the company's development of RenaZorb(TM) a new pharmaceutical for controlling serum phosphate levels in kidney dialysis patients and in chemically related products. 

"These developments, coupled with Altair's momentum in bringing the Altair Hydrochloride Process, an advanced process for producing white titanium dioxide pigment, closer to commercial realization suggest that Altair Nanotechnologies can achieve profitability in 2003," commented Moerck. 

"In keeping with our commitment to keep our lines of communications open," said Moerck, "I am providing an update of recent developments within the company." 

Pharmaceuticals 

Two pharmaceutical companies have expressed interest in testing RenaZorb in animal models. Altair expects to announce positive results of these negotiations during the first week of December. The testing is expected to be conducted in several species of animals. This testing is a significant step towards proving that RenaZorb is effective and safe in vivo. 

Based on the company's previous in vitro laboratory testing, Altair expects positive results in the animal models. Upon completion of animal testing, Altair expects to finalize a licensing agreement pertaining to RenaZorb. This is expected to occur in late February 2003. 

The company remains in discussions with six pharmaceutical companies who are interested in the possibility of developing and eventually seeking FDA and foreign approvals for RenaZorb. Each of these companies has entered into confidentiality agreements with Altair. Two other pharmaceutical companies have decided not to expand their work with RenaZorb. 

In a related development, an official at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) has invited Altair to apply for a grant in the area of "Transition Metals in Medicine." 

Developments in the manufacturing process of RenaZorb(TM) "A" and "B" have improved in vitro phosphate binding results in the laboratory. Altair has achieved the binding of 140 mg phosphate per gram of drug in 20 minutes of exposure of the drug to simulated stomach acid containing phosphate. This is an unprecedented binding rate for this class of pharmaceutical -- RenaZorb is very selective for phosphate ions. 

Altair has also developed RenaZorb "H" a hardened form of the drug that shows the lowest solubility in stomach fluid while rapidly absorbing dietary phosphate. 

The chemistry of RenaZorb has been extended to the development of a new non-toxic ceramic nanomaterials that effectively stop the growth of algae in swimming pools. 

Thermal Sprays 

The National Resource Council of Canada (NRC) has informed Altair that its nano-titanium dioxide product produces superior thermal spray coatings exhibiting unprecedented toughness while displaying excellent smoothness and lack of porosity. Altair will shortly issue a news release on this subject when it obtains the NRC written findings. 

The company has recently completed manufacturing 1,500 pounds of nano-titanium dioxide for F.W. Gartner Thermal Spray Co. to coat ball vales for severe-duty applications in high-quality valves manufactured by Mogas Industries of Houston. 

Shipment of material has begun and the company believes that Gartner will order additional tons of this material for repair and replacement services. The entire 1,500 pounds is expected to be shipped and invoiced before year-end. 

Batteries 

Electrodes made with Altair materials enable lithium ion batteries to charge and discharge up to 100 times faster than current commercial batteries. Patents have been field jointly with the company's partner, NTera/Xoliox, who continues to buy nano lithium titanate spinel for their battery development work. 

The critical requirement to enable commercialization of rapid charge and discharge lithium ion batteries is a new electrolyte that can withstand the higher temperature caused by faster charge and discharge cycles. Several laboratories are actively working with nanomaterials to develop a satisfactory electrolyte and the company is optimistic of a near-term solution. 

The company has terminated its marketing agreement with FMC Corp. since the agreement did not progress as expected. The company has received an order for 55 pounds of nano-sized lithium titanate spinal -- an indication that large-sized test batteries are being fabricated and tested. 

Altair Hydrochloride Pigment Process 

Altair announced that it has received a contract to determine the suitability of an existing ore concentrate for making white titanium dioxide pigment. Extraction and iron removal work has proceeded very well and the purification and pigment production steps will begin in the near future. A second agreement based on an ore body located in Vietnam was recently signed. 

Advances have been made in producing an inexpensive white pigment using the company's patented, environmentally friendly Altair Hydrochloride Process. Established process parameters produce a white pigment without a separate coating step; this process could potentially save millions of dollars in investment and operating costs for the companies licensing the Altair Hydrochloride Pigment Process. 

Existing titanium dioxide production processes generally require additional wet chemical treatment processes to be successfully used in semi-durable paints. 

Government Research Funds 

Following a review of project priorities, management has determined to actively solicit funding for projects that may benefit from the company's new, unique nanomaterials. 

Fuel Cells 

Work continues in the development of solid oxide fuel cells for stationary, always on, electrical power. The goal of the company is not to manufacture fuel cells, but rather to build prototypes that showcase the company's nanomaterials. 

Altair is negotiating supply contracts with a major company that is seeking to be a manufacturer of solid oxide fuel cells. The company is supplying materials such as nano sized yttria stabilized zirconia and nanoparticle slurries that can be used to manufacture fuel cells using tape-casting technology. 

Nasdaq Listing 

"As we recently announced, Altair Nanotechnologies is in the process of implementing a plan that will allow the extension of Altair's Nasdaq listing through May 2003," commented Moerck. "If our profitability forecast is accurate, maintaining a minimum bid of $1 for the company's common stock should not be a concern." 

Altair Nanotechnologies Inc. 

Nanotechnology is rapidly emerging as a unique industry sector. Altair Nanotechnologies is positioning itself through product innovation within this emerging industry to become a leading supplier of nanomaterial technology and nanomaterials worldwide. Altair owns a proprietary technology for making nanocrystalline materials of unique quality both economically and in large quantities. 

The company is currently developing special nanomaterials with potential applications in pharmaceuticals, batteries, fuel cells, solar cells, advanced energy storage devices, thermal spray coatings, catalysts, cosmetics, paints and environmental remediation. For additional information on Altair and its nanoparticle materials, visit www.altairnano.com.

HAYWARD, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Dec. 2, 2002--Quantum Dot Corporation (QDC), the leader in Qdot(TM) biotechnology applications and products, announced today the publication of a seminal scientific paper in the prestigious journal Nature Biotechnology. The paper, entitled "Immunofluorescent labeling of cancer marker Her2 and other cellular targets with semiconductor quantum dots", was published in the on-line version of Nature Biotechnology, following collaborative work performed by scientists at Genentech and QDC. The print version will be published in January 2003. 6 "The promise of Qdot conjugates to revolutionize biological detection has now become a reality. Our work with Genentech is the first practical application of the Qdot technology in an important biological system - specific detection of breast cancer markers. 

These results demonstrate the dramatic sensitivity and stability benefits enabled using Qdot detection," said Xingyong Wu, Ph.D., senior staff scientist at QDC, and the lead author of the paper. "We have also demonstrated cancer marker detection in live cancer cells, an extremely difficult task using conventional methods," continued Dr. Wu. 

"This work demonstrates how Qdot technology allows the detection of many biological analytes simultaneously, using a range of different colored Qdot nanocrystals," stated Charlie Hotz, Ph.D., director of chemistry at QDC. "This range of colors is achieved using different sized nanocrystals. Our unique ability to precisely tune the size of these nanoscale structures, at tolerances below one nanometer, is critical," continued Dr. Hotz. 

"Coming so rapidly on the heels of our first product launch last month, this work is a strong validation of the commercial value of the Qdot technology," said Carol C. Lou, QDC's President and Chief Operations Officer. "We highly value the relationship with our colleagues at Genentech, and we look forward to working with them on further innovative applications of our products." 

Qdot(TM) nanocrystals, or quantum dots, are nanometer sized semiconductor crystals that brightly light up specific biological events. These nano-scale molecular light emitting diodes (LEDs) allow rapid, parallel, and ultra-sensitive detection of biomolecular interactions. 

Founded in 1998, Quantum Dot Corporation is located in Hayward, CA. The company and its advisors are the world's leading experts in semiconductor nanocrystal (Qdot(TM)) technology and its applications. QDC sells and markets products to life science researchers worldwide, and is seeking marketing partners for its diagnostic applications. LAS VEGAS--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Dec. 2, 2002--Emergency Filtration Products Inc. (EFP) (OTCBB:EMFP) today announced that it is commencing with testing of its nanotechnology-enhanced 2H Technology(TM) filtration system to be incorporated into an Environmental Isolation Mask. 

The development of methods to deliver small amounts of biological agents that can potentially inflict large scale damage to people, the lack of adequate personal protection against biochemical contamination and the perception that this is a viable threat, drove EFP's search for filtration-compatible nanotechnologies. EFP believes that the technology development constitutes the natural progression in filtration research in addressing viral and bacterial concerns, without regard to biochemical delivery contamination. 

EFP entered into an agreement with NanoScale Materials, a Manhattan, Kan.-based company in September 2002. Nanoscale manufactures and markets the proprietary NanoActive(TM) materials and technologies EFP will utilize in its Environmental Isolation Mask design. The reactive nanoparticle materials will enhance the capture and isolation characteristics of 2H technology by eradicating biological contaminants that come in contact with the coated filters. 

Testing will be conducted at Nelson Laboratories, Salt Lake City, and are expected to be completed by Dec. 12, 2002. Nelson Laboratories is an independent testing laboratory that has served the medical device and pharmaceutical industries for over 15 years. Nelson Laboratories is ISO 9001 certified (BSI) and EN45001\IEC\ISO Guide 25 Accredited (AMTAC). 

Commenting on the purpose of the testing, Douglas Beplate, EFP president, said, "We have been looking forward to entering into this phase of the project where we will validate the mask design and efficiency along with establishing which nanomaterials are best suited to enhance our core 2H Technology. However, it should also be noted that there is nothing at this time to base an assumption that in the event the testing results in a favorable outcome, that there will be any new market in the so-called biochemical contamination defense arena, or that any stand-alone product that we may be able to develop will be sold profitably." 

About Emergency Filtration Products 

EFP is an air filtration products manufacturer whose patented 2H(TM) technology provides filtration efficiencies of greater than 99.9 percent at a particle size of 0.027 microns. Its initial products were developed for the medical market and include: RespAide(TM), a CPR mask used for resuscitation of respiratory/cardiac arrest cases; an A.E.D. prep kit; and the 2H(TM) Breathing Circuit Filter. In addition to filtration products, the company also supplies Superstat, a modified hemostatic collagen, to military and commercial medical markets.

Triton BioSystems and Thermonix Announce Merger; Merger to Develop Low Side Effect Non-Invasive Therapy for Advanced Breast Cancer 

725 words 
2 December 2002
16:49 GMT
Business Wire 
English
(Copyright (c) 2002, Business Wire) 

BOSTON--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Dec. 2, 2002--Triton BioSystems, Inc. and Thermonix, Inc. today announced they have merged operations to focus on pre-clinical product development of their Targeted Nano-Therapeutics system for advanced breast cancer. Under the terms of the merger, the combined companies will continue as Triton BioSystems, Inc., with Dr. Samuel Straface as its Chief Executive Officer. The two companies have independently pursued the development of therapeutics based on non-invasive inductive heating of prosthetic devices and injectable targeted-nanomaterials. "Combined, we possess stronger intellectual property and know-how to pursue the Targeted Nano-Therapeutics system for cancer as well as a much accelerated product development effort," said Dr. Straface. "We believe this merger will leverage existing partnerships and development activities to expedite our path to human clinical trials in 2004, starting with breast cancer which affects nearly two million Americans today." 

"The Targeted Nano-Therapeutics system will become the new standard for antibody guided cancer therapies," said Philip Smith, President and Chief Executive Officer of Thermonix, Inc., who will remain with Triton BioSystems and lead its business development efforts. Thermonix will relocate its operations and team to Triton BioSystems' facilities in Chelmsford Massachusetts. Mr. Rudy Mazzocchi, Chairman of Thermonix, Inc., will join the Triton BioSystems' board of directors. 

The Targeted Nano-Therapeutic system consists of magnetic nanomaterials bound to monoclonal antibodies (which, combined, are referred to as bioprobes) and a device capable of generating a magnetic field. A simple injection into a patient's bloodstream will release millions of bioprobes, each many times smaller than a cancer cell, where they will detect the unique chemical signature of a cancer cell and attach themselves to the cell's surface. Their payload of nanomaterial then sits ready for the doctor to activate at will. By applying magnetic field energy through the patient's body, the doctor chooses the time to energize the bioprobes, which will selectively kill the cancer cells. The magnetic energy activates the bioprobes by rapidly heating them, thus killing adjacent cancer cells without damaging healthy tissue or organs. The Company believes that the Targeted Nano-Therapeutics system will enable doctors to non-invasively treat cancer patients with substantially less collateral damage compared to current treatments such as chemotherapy and radiation. 

"A major opportunity for treating cancer is targeting cancer cells while sparing surrounding tissue," says Professor Emeritus Gerald DeNardo, M.D., of the Division of Hematology Oncology at the University of California's School of Medicine. "The Targeted Nano-Therapeutic system offers the promise of a cancer-specific killing approach with little of the collateral damage seen with current therapies." 

Doctors will be able to visualize bioprobes attached to cancer cells using MRI and then directly activate them by sending a magnetic field through the body. "I am excited by the possibility of having a therapeutic system that potentially offers the physician dual control over the targeting of cancer cells and the ability to assess uptake by the tumors of bioprobes before switching them on and killing the cancer," said David E. Fisher, M.D., Ph.D., Associate Professor at Harvard Medical School and Dana Farber Cancer Institute, in Boston, Massachusetts. By targeting individual cancer cells instead of healthy tissues or organs, Triton BioSystems believes that the Targeted Nano-Therapeutic system will offer cancer patients and their doctors a new precision weapon in the war against cancer. 

About Triton BioSystems 

Triton BioSystems, Inc, is based in Chelmsford, Massachusetts, USA, and is a development-stage company focused on the discovery and development of non-invasive targeted therapeutics that use heat to treat cancer and other life threatening and debilitating diseases. For more information about Triton BioSystems, call Dr. Samuel Straface on +1-978-856-4203. 

About Thermonix 

Thermonix, Inc, is based in Minneapolis, Minnesota, USA, and is a leader in the development of therapeutics based on non-invasive inductive heating of prosthetic devices, directed at various inflammatory diseases such as arterioscleroses and cancer. For more information about Thermonix, call Mr. Philip Smith on +1-612-221-8863.

and Facilitate Demanding Research and Development Applications 

n&k Technology, Inc., a manufacturer of proven, production worthy process diagnostic tools for reliable, accurate, and precise thin film characterization as well as trench and critical dimension measurements, today announced the successful installation and demonstration of the company's 1280 Analyzer at the Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) and of the company's 1500 Analyzer at the University of Maryland's Laboratory of Physical Sciences (LPS). The n&k Analyzer 1280, which performs real-time non-destructive characterization of the key properties of thin film materials, will be used at NRL in the research and development of a wide variety of advanced materials to meet important naval needs for electronics, sensors, and photonics. The n&k 1500, which performs real-time non-destructive characterization of the key properties of thin film materials, will be used at LPS in the research and development of a wide variety of advanced communication and computer technologies. 

Naval Research Laboratory (NRL) 

"NRL conducts research that includes investigations of a broad spectrum of materials - not only semiconductors, optical materials, and metals - but also very advanced materials such synthetic biomolecular films, as in organic LEDs," said Dr. Rahim Forouhi, president and CEO of n&k Technology. "These materials present new challenges for measurement and characterization instrumentation. n&k's 1280 Analyzer has again proved its versatility in a demanding R&D environment by the rapid and accurate characterization of various films, including photoluminescent material." 

NRL is the Navy's corporate laboratory, administering a multidisciplinary research and development program for new and improved materials, systems, techniques, and equipment, for maritime as well as atmospheric and space applications. Within NRL the Materials Science and Component Technology Directorate conducts research into the discovery and exploitation of new materials, and the development of advanced components based on these new and improved materials. Theoretical and experimental research is carried out to determine the basis of materials behavior and to develop these materials to meet important naval needs for advanced platforms, electronics, sensors, and photonics. The n&k 1280 analyzer will be used in investigations of a broad variety of materials including insulators, semiconductors, superconductors, metals and alloys, optical materials, polymers, plastics, and synthetic biomolecular materials and composites. 

University of Maryland's Laboratory of Physical Sciences (LPS) 

"The research conducted at LPS covers a wide range of applications using many different film and substrate materials, which places great demands on the instrumentation used for characterization," said Dr. Forouhi. "At LPS, the n&k 1500 demonstrated its versatility, surpassing expectations in a demanding R&D environment" 

LPS, located adjacent to the University of Maryland's College Park Campus, is a unique facility where university and federal government personnel collaborate on research in advanced communication and computer technologies. Research is conducted in microelectronics, quantum computing, photonics, nanostructures, and various other fields. n&k's 1500 Analyzer is being used by the Microelectronics Research Program, whose work is focused on the process of Heterogeneous Integration, where semiconductor components and circuits, with different functionality or material systems, are physically and electrically combined together into a common 3-dimensional structure. 

n&k 1280 and 1500 Analyzers 

Based on the company's proven measurement technology, the n&k 1280 and the n&k 1500 Analyzers use broadband spectrophotometry over a wavelength range of 190 to 1000 nm, with innovative optics in conjunction with the Forouhi-Bloomer dispersion equations and other proprietary algorithms. These n&k Analyzers determine film thickness, the spectra of refractive index (n) and extinction coefficient (k), as well as energy band gap, interface roughness, and other optical properties. The spectra on n and k can be correlated to various other physical parameters, such as composition, resistivity, and degree of crystallinity. A wide variety of materials can be characterized including dialectrics, semiconductors, polymers, transparent conductors, and metals. Structures such as thin films (less than 20 angstroms), thick films (up to 300 microns), and multi-layer stacks, deposited on transparent, opaque, or rough substrates, all fall within the capabilities of n&k's technology. Furthermore, n&k's methodology is non-destructive and fast, providing results within seconds. The n&k 1500 Analyzer has the added capability of mapping the uniformity of the measured quantities of the samples, using a computerized X-Y stage. 

About n&k Technology, Inc. 

n&k Technology is a manufacturer of proven, production worthy process diagnostic tools for reliable, accurate, and precise thin film characterization as well as trench and critical dimension measurements serving a variety of industries including semiconductor, photo mask, flat panel display, and data storage. The company's cost-effective, easy to use systems, ranging from table-top models to fully automated 300mm production tools, deliver "the true measure" with superior resolution, enabling users to characterize virtually any combination of thin films, substrates, and structures. n&k's products are also ideally suited for challenging integrated metrology applications. More information about n&k Technology can be found on the Internet at www.nandk.com.
